title: Songs of Grace, Book VI, Volume 1

intro.title: Introduction: Thiru Arutpa
paras: Thiru Arutpa, which means Divine Songs of Grace, is a collection of poems written by Ramalinga Adigal, lovingly known as Vallalar.

The entire poetic work is divided into 6 volumes or Thirumurais. The poems narrate the spiritual journey of Vallalar. From his early days of worship into the Saiva Siddhanta doctrine, the suffering from separation from the divine, to the final realization of the ArutPerunJothi (Vast Grace-Light) in his late stage of Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam Sathya Sangam philosophy and way of life. The core philosophical pillars of the Thiru Arutpa include:
Active Compassion: The foundation is Jeeva Karunyam, or active compassion for all living beings as basis to spiritual life
Unity of All Beings: The Arutpa teaches Anma Neya Orumaipadu, or the Unity of Souls, asserting that every creature shares the exact same spiritual essence.
Rejection of Division: Vallalar wholly rejected caste systems, religious divisions, and sectarian hierarchies.
The Divine Light: The ultimate recognition is that ArutPerunJothi, the supreme divine light, dwells within every single soul without exception.
Ultimately, the Thiru Arutpa is a spiritual guide toward boundless compassion to all life, self-realization, and what Vallalar taught as the physical body's ability to reach a deathless state.

intro.title: Introduction: Thiru Arutpa Sixth Thirumurai
paras: The Thiru Arutpa is the collected poetry of Ramalinga Adigal, and it is arranged in six parts called Thirumurai. This is the sixth and last.

The first five volumes were written by a younger Ramalinga inside a tradition. They are temple hymns. They name places, they address deities by their local names, and they follow forms Tamil devotional poetry had used for a thousand years.

The Sixth is what came after. These are the works of his final years, written at Vadalur and at Mettukuppam, in the same period when he opened a kitchen that fed anyone who came and built a hall with no god in it.

In the earlier volumes he is a devotee. Here he is teaching something, and it has a name: Suddha Sanmarkkam, the pure true path. He describes it, he sets out what it asks, and he tells people to enter it.

He says caste, creed and sect are false. Not incomplete. False. He uses the word poy, a lie, and he says he was told so from the beginning. The man writing the Sixth Thirumurai has stopped working within the religions and has begun speaking past them.

He says the body does not have to die. The teaching on deathlessness, on the body remade by grace, appears here and nowhere earlier. It is the hardest part of his work and the part most often argued over.

He puts compassion at the gate. Jeeva Karunyam, mercy toward every living thing, is not presented as one virtue among many. It is the condition. Without it, he says, nothing else opens. This is why the free kitchen and these poems belong to the same act.
The form changes too. The temple hymn gives way to direct address. He is no longer singing about the divine from a shrine. He is speaking to it, and reporting what it said back.

A note on the arrangement. Ramalinga did not publish these works himself. He wrote as occasion demanded and left the ordering to others. His disciple Thozhuvur Velayutha Mudaliar, who had edited the earlier volumes during his lifetime, gathered the late writings after 1874 and arranged them. The six-part division is the work of the disciples, not of Ramalinga. Later editors, chiefly Ooran Adigal, reordered the volumes by date of composition, which is why some poems sit in different Thirumurai in different editions.

A note on this volume. The Sixth Thirumurai is published in three volumes, and the ArutPerunJothi Agaval, at 1,596 lines a book in itself, has a book of its own: The Hymn of the Vast Grace-Light. This is Volume One of three, with pathigams 001 to 048. All of them are free to read at sanmarkkamlife.org.
The Tamil text follows the arrangement of Ooran Adigal, as given at thiruarutpa.org, checked against the printed editions of 1885 and 1932 where it was damaged.

works.title: The Hymn of the Vast Grace-light

blocks.html: The ArutPerunJothi Agaval, the Hymn of the Vast Grace-Light, is the greatest work of Ramalinga Adigal, the Tamil saint lovingly known as Vallalar. He wrote it in his last and most mature years, at Mettukuppam in south India. It is said that he wrote it in one unbroken session, in a single night.

It has 1,596 lines. Its subject is the ArutPerunJothi, the Vast Grace-Light. The poem describes what that Light is, how everything that exists came out of it and is still held by it, and what happens inside a person when it is let in.

It begins by naming it. For 437 couplets, every second line ends in the same word. Then the naming stops, and the poem calls the same thing mother, father, friend, medicine, gold, mountain, ocean, lamp. At the end the first name returns, and the poem closes on the line it opened with.
Three things are said clearly. Caste, creed and sect are false. The path of non-violence is the path of grace. Every living thing is to be seen as your own.
More than a century later, devotees all over the world still wake up before dawn to sing these blissful lines.

translit: ellām ceyalkūṭum eṉāṇai ampalattē ellāmval lāṉtaṉaiyē ēttu.
translation: Praise the all-powerful One in the divine hall. By my oath, all things will become possible.
commentary: The Sixth Thirumurai opens with an oath. Vallalar swears that all things can be accomplished, and he names the One to praise: the All-powerful One in the Ambalam (the hall of consciousness). He does not offer a doctrine to be believed. He gives his word from experience and points to the One who alone can do all.

translit: iṉṟuvaru mōnāḷaik kēvarumō allatumaṟ ṟeṉṟuvaru mōaṟiyēṉ eṅkōvē - tuṉṟumala vemmāyai aṟṟu veḷikkuḷ veḷikaṭantu cummā irukkum cukam.
translation: My King, I do not know if the bliss of simply being still will come today, tomorrow, or on some other day. This state transcends the space within space and is completely free from the cruel illusion of dense impurities.
commentary: Vallalar longs for one thing: the bliss of simply being (cummā irukkum cukam). It comes when the dense impurity of malam and the fierce delusion of māyai fall away, and the soul passes beyond even the inner space. He does not know when it will come, today, tomorrow or later. He knows only that he wants nothing else.

translit: tiruviḷaṅkac civayōka cittielām viḷaṅkac civañāṉa nilaiviḷaṅkac civāṉupavam viḷaṅkat teruviḷaṅku tiruttillait tirucciṟṟam palattē tirukkūttu viḷaṅkaoḷi ciṟantatiru viḷakkē uruviḷaṅka uyirviḷaṅka uṇarcciyatu viḷaṅka ulakamelām viḷaṅkaaruḷ utavuperun tāyām maruviḷaṅku kuḻalvalli makiḻntorupāl viḷaṅka vayaṅkumaṇip potuviḷaṅka vaḷarntacivak koḻuntē.
translation: O divine lamp of supreme light, you make the sacred dance shine in the holy little hall of sacred Tillai with its radiant streets. You shine so that divine wealth, the attainments of Siva yoga, the state of divine wisdom, and the supreme experience all radiate brilliantly. O tender shoot of Siva, you grew so that the gleaming hall of gems may shine, while at your side rejoices the creeper-like goddess with fragrant hair, the great Mother who grants grace so that forms, lives, feeling, and all the worlds may shine.
commentary: Everything Vallalar treasures is named here as something God makes shine: the powers of Siva-yoga, the wisdom and experience of Siva, the sacred dance in the Chitrambalam of Thillai. The same light makes every form, every life and every feeling shine. Beside God stands the Divine Mother, who gives grace so that all worlds may shine. God is the Lamp; all of this is its light.

translit: aṉpeṉum piṭiyuḷ akappaṭum malaiyē aṉpeṉum kuṭilpukum aracē aṉpeṉum valaikkuṭ paṭuparam poruḷē aṉpeṉum karattamar amutē aṉpeṉum kaṭattuḷ aṭaṅkiṭum kaṭalē aṉpeṉum uyiroḷir aṟivē aṉpeṉum aṇuvuḷ ḷamaintapē roḷiyē aṉpuru vāmpara civamē.
translation: O mountain caught in the grasp of love! O King who enters the hut of love! O supreme reality caught in the net of love! O nectar resting in the hands of love! O ocean contained within the pot of love! O shining wisdom in the soul of love! O great light dwelling within the atom of love! O Parasiva whose very form is love!
commentary: The infinite is held by love alone. Vallalar turns each image around: the mountain is caught in the grip of love, the ocean fits in the pot of love, the great light dwells in the atom of love. Nothing else can contain God, yet love can, because God's own form is love. Parasivam, beyond all reach, is reached through love.
NOTES

translit: tāḷaiēttu - mutaṟpatippu, po. cu. patippu.
translation: tāḷaiēttu — reading of the first edition and of the Po. Su. edition.

sections.title: The Hymn of the Vast Grace-light

blocks.html: This hymn of 1,596 lines is published as a separate volume; see its introduction at the front of this book.

translit: aruṭperu veḷiyil aruṭperu ulakat taruṭperun talattumēl nilaiyil aruṭperum pīṭat taruṭperu vaṭivil aruṭperun tiruvilē amarnta aruṭperum patiyē aruṭperu nitiyē aruṭperuñ cittieṉ amutē aruṭperuṅ kaḷippē aruṭperuñ cukamē aruṭperuñ cōtieṉ aracē.
translation: Seated in great sacred splendor, in a great form of Grace, on a great throne of Grace, in the supreme state at the great sacred site of Grace, in the great world of Grace, in the great expanse of Grace, O great Lord of Grace, O great treasure of Grace, O great Siddhi that is my nectar, O great rapture of Grace, O great happiness of Grace, O Supreme Grace-Light, my King!
commentary: This opening verse establishes that God’s very substance and dwelling place is Grace. Everything about the divine reality, from its form to its location, is an expression of this all-encompassing Grace. The verse addresses this reality directly as the Supreme Grace-Light (ArutPerunJothi), a source of supernatural perfection (siddhi), joy, and personal guidance, making the relationship both cosmic and deeply intimate.

translit: kulavupē raṇṭap pakutiōr aṉanta kōṭikō ṭikaḷumāṅ kāṅkē nilaviya piṇṭap pakutikaḷ muḻutum nikaḻntapaṟ palaporuḷ tiraḷum vilakuṟā takattum puṟattumēl iṭattum meyyaṟi vāṉantam viḷaṅka alakuṟā toḻiyā tatuvatil viḷaṅkum aruṭperuñ cōtieṉ aracē.
translation: O Supreme Grace-Light, my King, you who shine immeasurably, ceaselessly, and perfectly, causing True Knowledge-Bliss to manifest; you who are inseparably present inside, outside, and in the space above the countless, magnificent cosmic realms, all the microcosmic realms, and the various multitudes of existing things.
commentary: The divine is not confined to a single heaven or temple; it fills and surrounds everything that exists. From vast cosmic realms down to individual beings and objects, the Grace-Light is present within, without, and above all things. Its presence is what allows True Knowledge and Bliss to manifest everywhere, ceaselessly and perfectly.

translit: kaṇmutal poṟiyāl maṉamutal karaṇak karuviṉāl pakutiyiṉ karuvāl eṇmutal puruṭa tarattiṉāl parattāl icaikkumōr parampara uṇarvāl viṇmutal paraiyāl parāpara aṟivāl viḷaṅkuva tariteṉa uṇarntōr aṇmutal taṭittup paṭittiṭa ōṅkum aruṭperuñ cōtieṉ aracē.
translation: O Supreme Grace-Light, my King! For those who realize how hard it is to know you, whether by the senses beginning with the eye, by the inner faculties beginning with the mind, by the root of Prakriti, by the level of Purusha, by Param, by the one awareness of Paramparam, by Parai who begins from space, or by the knowledge of Paraparam, for them you rise up so they can approach, grasp, and praise you.
commentary: You cannot grasp the divine through your eyes, your mind, or even through sophisticated philosophical concepts. Vallalar lists the entire range of perception, from the senses to primal matter (Prakriti), the conscious self (Purusha), and even transcendent spiritual states (Para, Parai). All are inadequate. The key is to realize this limitation. Paradoxically, it is only when you understand that you cannot grasp God on your own terms that the Grace-Light rises up and makes itself known to you.

translit: nacaittamēl nilaiī teṉa:uṇarn tāṅkē naṇṇiyum kaṇṇuṟā tantō ticaittamā maṟaikaḷ uyaṅkiṉa mayaṅkit tirumpiṉa eṉilataṉ iyalai icaittaleṅ ṅaṉamō aiyakō ciṟitum icaittiṭu vēmeṉa nāvai acaittiṭaṟ kariteṉ ṟuṇarntuḷōr vaḻuttum aruṭperuñ cōtieṉ aracē.
translation: When even the great Vedas that proclaimed you, having realized ‘This is that longed-for supreme state,’ approached it only to suffer, become confused, and turn back without perceiving it, then how can anyone describe your nature? You are the Supreme Grace-Light, my King, praised by those who, realizing this, understand how difficult it is even to move the tongue to say, ‘Alas, let us describe it, if only a little.’
commentary: This verse makes a powerful claim about the limits of scripture. Even the Vedas, the most revered sacred texts, failed in their attempt to describe the ultimate reality; they approached it, but were overwhelmed and had to turn back. If even the Vedas could not succeed, Vallalar asks, how can anyone else hope to put that reality into words? True sages are those who are left speechless, knowing the divine is beyond all description.

translit: cuttavē tānta mavuṉamō alatu cuttacit tāntarā ciyamō nittanā tānta nilaiaṉu pavamō nikaḻpiṟa muṭipiṉmēl muṭipō puttamu taṉaiya camaracat tatuvō poruḷiyal aṟintilam eṉavē attakai uṇarntōr uraitturait tēttum aruṭperuñ cōtieṉ aracē.
translation: Is it the silence of pure Vedanta, or the kingdom of pure Siddhanta? Is it the experience of the eternal state of Nadanta? Is it the crown upon the end of all other ends? Or is it that Sāmarasya (perfect harmony), which is like fresh nectar? You are the Supreme Grace-Light, my King, praised again and again by those who, realizing this state, say, ‘We do not know its true nature.’
commentary: Those who have reached the highest state cannot name it. Is it the silence of Vedanta, the kingdom of Siddhanta, the state beyond sound (Nadanta), or perfect harmony (Samarasam)? They confess they do not know its nature, and they keep praising it all the same. Vallalar gives this nameless summit one name: ArutPerunJothi, his King.

translit: ēkamō aṉṟi aṉēkamō eṉṟum iyaṟkaiyō ceyaṟkaiyō cittō tēkamō potuvō ciṟappatō peṇṇō tikaḻntiṭum āṇatō atuvō yōkamō pirivō oḷiyatō veḷiyō uraippateṟ ṟōeṉa uṇarntōr ākamō ṭuraittu vaḻuttaniṉ ṟōṅkum aruṭperuñ cōtieṉ aracē.
translation: "Is It one or many? Natural or artificial? Consciousness or body? Common or special? Is It female, shining male, or 'that'? Union or separation? Is It light or space? How can we even speak of It?" Thus the realized ones, speaking with the Āgamas , praise and extol You, who stand and soar, O Vast Grace-Light, my King!
commentary: The Divine cannot be defined by any human category. It is not one or many, male or female, light or space. Even the most sacred scriptures, the Āgamas, can only gesture toward this reality that transcends all our concepts of opposition and form. To recognize this limit of language is itself a form of praise.

translit: tattuvam aṉaittum taṉittaṉi kaṭantēm tattuvā tītamēl nilaiyil cittiyal muḻutum terintaṉam avaimēl civanilai terintiṭac ceṉṟēm ottaan nilaikkaṇ yāmumem uṇarvum oruṅkuṟak karaintupō yiṉameṉ ṟattakai uṇarntōr vaḻuttaniṉ ṟōṅkum aruṭperuñ cōtieṉ aracē.
translation: "We have crossed beyond all the tattvas one by one. In the state beyond the tattvas, we came to know the full nature of all siddhis. We went beyond them to know the state of Siva. In that supreme state, we and our consciousness completely dissolved and vanished as one." Thus those who have realized praise You, who stand and soar, O Vast Grace-Light, my King!
commentary: The spiritual path is a process of transcending every layer of existence. One must go beyond the fundamental principles of reality (tattvas) and even the spiritual powers (siddhis) that may arise on the path. The final goal is to reach the state of Siva (the ultimate divine consciousness) where the individual ego dissolves completely. This total surrender is the ultimate realization.

translit: eṅkumāy viḷaṅkum ciṟcapai iṭattē ituatu eṉa:uraip paritāyt taṅkumōr iyaṟkait taṉiaṉu pavattait tanteṉait taṉmayam ākkip poṅkumā ṉanta pōkapōk kiyaṉāyp puttamu taruttieṉ uḷattē aṅkaiyil kaṉipōṉ ṟamarntaruḷ purinta aruṭperuñ cōtieṉ aracē.
translation: O Vast Grace-Light, my King! In the Chit Sabhai that shines forth as everywhere, You gave me a unique, natural experience, impossible to describe as 'this' or 'that'. You made me one with Yourself, the enjoyer of overflowing bliss, fed me fresh ambrosia, and within my heart, sat and bestowed grace as clearly as a fruit in the palm of the hand.
commentary: After describing the supreme state as beyond words, Vallalar shifts to a deeply personal testimony. The experience of grace, received in the Chit Sabhai (the inner hall of consciousness), is both indescribable and unmistakably real. It is a direct, intimate encounter that removes all doubt, like holding a solid fruit in your own hand. This verse brings the immense, abstract Grace-Light into the intimate space of the human heart.

translit: akaranilai viḷaṅkucattar aṉaivarukkum avarpāl amarntacatti māravarkaḷ aṉaivarukkum avarāl pakaravarum aṇṭavakai aṉaittiṉukkum piṇṭap pakutikaḷaṅ kaṉaittiṉukkum pataṅkaḷaṉait tiṉukkum ikaramuṟum uyirevaikkum karuvikaḷaṅ kevaikkum epporuṭkum aṉupavaṅkaḷ evaikkummutti evaikkum cikaramutal cittivakai evaikkumoḷi vaḻaṅkum tirucciṟṟam palantaṉilē teyvamoṉṟē kaṇṭīr.
translation: For all the Shaktars who shine in the state of the letter 'A', for all their attendant Shaktis, for all the kinds of universes spoken by them, for all parts of the microcosm, for all realms, for every life that embodies the letter 'I', for all their inner instruments, for every object, for all experiences, for all kinds of liberation, and for all types of siddhi beginning with the highest, know that in the Thiru Chitrambalam that bestows light, there is only one God.
commentary: The one God is the single source of light for everything that exists, from the highest divine principles to the smallest particle of matter. Vallalar lists an all-encompassing catalog: the cosmic powers (Shaktars as male and Shaktis as female), the universes they create, all living beings and their inner faculties, every object, every experience, and even spiritual liberation (mutti) and the powers (siddhis) that come with it. All of this, he says, is illuminated by the one God found in the Thiru Chitrambalam, the sacred hall of consciousness.

translit: vaṇṇamiku pūtaveḷi pakutiveḷi mutalā vakukkumaṭi veḷikaḷelām vayaṅkuveḷi yāki eṇṇamuṟu māmavuṉa veḷiyāki ataṉmēl icaittapara veḷiyāki iyalupaya veḷiyāy aṇṇuṟuciṟ paraveḷiyāyt taṟparamām veḷiyāy amarntaperu veḷiyāki aruḷiṉpa veḷiyāyt tiṇṇamuṟum taṉiiyaṟkai uṇmaiveḷi yāṉa tirucciṟṟam palantaṉilē teyvamoṉṟē kaṇṭīr.
translation: Becoming the radiant space that is all the foundational spaces, from the space of the colorful elements and the space of primordial matter; becoming the great silent space of thought, and above that, the declared transcendent space; becoming the natural dual space, the supreme space of consciousness, the space of the self-transcendent, the serene great space, and the space of blissful Grace; in the Thiru Chitrambalam which is the firm, unique, natural space of Truth, know that there is only one God.
commentary: God is more than in a place; God is the very 'space' in which everything exists. Vallalar describes a progression of spaces, from the physical space of the elements and primordial matter (prakriti) to the inner space of thought, and finally to the highest spiritual spaces of consciousness, grace, and truth. The Thiru Chitrambalam is this ultimate, true space which contains and becomes all other spaces.

translit: cārpūta viḷakkamoṭu pakutikaḷiṉ viḷakkam tattuvaṅkaḷ viḷakkamelān taruviḷakka māki nērāti viḷakkamatāyp paraiviḷakka māki nilaittaparā paraiviḷakka mākiakam puṟamum pērācai viḷakkamatāyc cuttaviḷak kamatāyp peruviḷakka mākielām peṟṟaviḷak kamatāyc cīrāṭa viḷaṅkukiṉṟa iyaṟkaiviḷak kamatām tirucciṟṟam palantaṉilē teyvamoṉṟē kaṇṭīr.
translation: Becoming the light that reveals the light of the dependent elements, the light of the primordial parts, and the light of all the tattvas; becoming the light of Nada and what is beyond; becoming the light of Parai and the steadfast light of Paraparai becoming the light of great love, both within and without; becoming the pure light, the great light, and the light that contains all others; in the Thiru Chitrambalam which shines as the glorious natural light, know that there is only one God.
commentary: The divine is the ultimate light that makes all other forms of light and perception possible. This light illuminates the physical world, the principles of reality (tattvas), the primal divine sound (Nada), and even the highest expressions of divine power, Parai (the supreme Shakti) and Paraparai (that which is beyond her). It is the light of love and the pure, natural light that is the source of all knowing.

translit: iṭampeṟumin tiriya:iṉpam karaṇa:iṉpam ulaka iṉpamuyir iṉpammutal eytumiṉpa mākit taṭampeṟumōr āṉma:iṉpam taṉittaaṟi viṉpam cattiyappē riṉpammutti iṉpamumāy ataṉmēl naṭampeṟumeyp poruḷiṉpam niraticaya iṉpam ñāṉacittip perumpōka nāṭṭaraciṉ pamumāyt tiṭampeṟaōṅ kiya:iyaṟkait taṉiiṉpa mayamām tirucciṟṟam palantaṉilē teyvamoṉṟē kaṇṭīr.
translation: Becoming the bliss of the senses, the bliss of the inner instruments, the bliss of the world, and the bliss of life; becoming the vast bliss of the soul, the bliss of unique consciousness, the great bliss of truth, and the bliss of liberation; and beyond that, becoming the bliss of the true substance that dances, unsurpassed bliss, and the bliss of the sovereign reign which is the great experience of perfected wisdom; in the Thiru Chitrambalam which is the embodiment of firm, exalted, natural, unique bliss, know that there is only one God.
commentary: Every form of happiness and bliss, from the most basic to the most exalted, has its source in the one God. Vallalar traces a path from the simple bliss of the senses and the mind (karanas) to the bliss of the soul (anma), of pure consciousness, and of liberation. The final state is the unsurpassed bliss of perfected wisdom (jnana-siddhi), and the Thiru Chitrambalam is the very substance of this natural, unique bliss.

translit: ellāntāṉ uṭaiyatuvāy ellāmval latuvāy ellāntāṉ āṉatuvāy ellāntāṉ alatāyc collālum poruḷālum tōṉṟumaṟi vālum tuṇintaḷakka muṭiyātāyt turiyaveḷi kaṭanta vallāḷar aṉupavattē atuatuvāy avarum matittiṭuṅkāl ariyatuvāyp periyatuvāy aṇuvum cellāta nilaikaḷiṉum celluvatāy viḷaṅkum tirucciṟṟam palantaṉilē teyvamoṉṟē kaṇṭīr.
translation: It possesses everything, is all-powerful, has become everything, yet is also none of it. It cannot be measured by word, by meaning, or by apparent knowledge. In the experience of the mighty ones who have crossed beyond the space of Turiya it becomes whatever they perceive it as. Yet when even they try to comprehend it, it is rare and great. It shines, penetrating even realms where an atom cannot enter. In the Thiru Chitrambalam that so shines, know that there is only one God.
commentary: God possesses all, can do all, becomes all, and yet is none of it. No word, meaning or knowledge can measure God. Even the great ones who have passed beyond the fourth state (turiyam) find God rare and vast when they try to grasp it. What enters where not even an atom can go shines in the Thiru Chitrambalam. There is only one God.

translit: ayarvaṟupē raṟivāki avvaṟivuk kaṟivāy aṟivaṟivuḷ aṟivāyāṅ kataṉuḷḷōr aṟivāy mayarvaṟumōr iyaṟkaiuṇmait taṉiaṟivāyc ceyaṟkai maṉṉumaṟi vaṉaittiṉukkum vayaṅkiyatā rakamāyt tuyaraṟutā rakamutalāy ammutaṟkōr mutalāyt turiyanilai kaṭantataṉmēl cuttaciva nilaiyāy uyarvuṟuciṟ ṟampalattē ellāntā māki ōṅkukiṉṟa taṉikkaṭavuḷ oruvaruṇṭē kaṇṭīr.
translation: He is the unwavering great intelligence, the intelligence of that intelligence, the intelligence within the intelligence of intelligence, and the intelligence within that. He is the one natural, true, unique intelligence free from delusion. He is the radiant foundation for all established, artificial knowledge; the origin of that sorrow-ending foundation; and the origin of that origin. He is the state of pure Sivam beyond the transcendent Turīya state In the exalted Chitrambalam becoming everything Himself, see, there is one unique God who reigns supreme.
commentary: God is pure intelligence, the source of all knowing. This verse describes a consciousness so fundamental that it is the "intelligence within intelligence," the ultimate awareness that lies behind every thought and perception. All of our worldly or "artificial" knowledge is built upon this natural, true intelligence. This supreme state of pure Sivam (the ultimate divine reality) is experienced beyond even Turīya (the fourth state of consciousness), in the inner space of the Chitrambalam (hall of consciousness).

translit: aṇṭamelām piṇṭamelām uyirkaḷelām poruḷkaḷ āṉaelām iṭaṅkaḷelām nīkkamaṟa niṟaintē koṇṭaelāṅ koṇṭaelām koṇṭukoṇṭu mēlum koḷvataṟkē iṭaṅkoṭuttuk koṇṭucalip piṉṟik kaṇṭamelāṅ kaṭantuniṉṟē akaṇṭamatāy atuvum kaṭantaveḷi yāyatuvum kaṭantataṉi veḷiyām oṇtakuciṟ ṟampalattē ellāmval lavarāy ōṅkukiṉṟa taṉikkaṭavuḷ oruvaruṇṭē kaṇṭīr.
translation: He completely fills, without exception, all universes, all microcosms, all living beings, all existing things, and all spaces. He holds all that is held, continues to hold it, and gives space for more to be held, all without growing weary. Standing beyond all divisions, He becomes the indivisible whole, and then the space that transcends even that. In the radiant and worthy Chitrambalam, which is the unique space beyond even that space, He is all-powerful. See, there is one unique God who reigns supreme.
commentary: God is both the infinite container and the entire contents of existence. He fills all universes and all individual beings so completely that there are no gaps, yet He also exists as the boundless space beyond them. This space is not static; it tirelessly holds all of creation and makes room for more, showing God as an inexhaustible, ever-present reality that is at once within everything and beyond everything.

translit: pāroṭunīr kaṉalkāṟṟā kāyameṉum pūtap pakutimutal pakarnātap pakutivarai yāṉa ērpeṟutat tuva:uruvāyt tattuvakā raṇamāy iyampiyakā raṇamutalāyk kāraṇattiṉ muṭivāy nēruṟumam muṭivaṉaittum nikaḻntiṭupū raṇamāy nittiyamāyc cattiyamāy niṟkuṇaciṟ kuṇamāy ōrtarucaṉ māttiramām tirucciṟṟam palattē ōṅkukiṉṟa taṉikkaṭavuḷ oruvaruṇṭē kaṇṭīr.
translation: He is the beautiful form of all tattvas, from the elemental categories of earth, water, fire, wind, and sky up to the proclaimed category of Natham. He is the cause of the tattvas, the origin of that cause, and the culmination of causation. He is the Pūranam where all these culminations manifest. He is eternal, true, both Nirgunam and possessing attributes of consciousness. In the sacred Chitrambalam, which is pure being-consciousness itself, see, there is one unique God who reigns supreme.
commentary: God is the single thread running through all of reality, from its most basic building blocks to its most sublime principles. The verse traces creation from the physical elements up to Natham , showing God as the source, substance, and destination of this entire spectrum of tattvas . God is described as both Nirgunam and possessing the qualities of consciousness, meaning the Absolute is beyond all description, yet its essential nature is pure, conscious being.

translit: iravimati uṭukkaḷmutal kalaikaḷelām tammōr ilēcamatāy eṇkaṭantē ilaṅkiyapiṇ ṭāṇṭam paravumaṟṟaip poruḷkaḷuyirt tiraḷkaḷmutal ellām pakarakattum puṟattumakap puṟattuṭaṉap puṟattum viravieṅkum nīkkamaṟa viḷaṅkianta māti viḷampariya pēroḷiyāy avvoḷippē roḷiyāy uravuṟuciṉ māttiramām tirucciṟṟam palattē ōṅkukiṉṟa taṉikkaṭavuḷ oruvaruṇṭē kaṇṭīr.
translation: The sun, moon, stars, and all their phases are but a tiny fraction of Him. He pervades the countless shining microcosms and macrocosms, the vast array of other objects, the multitudes of lives, and everything else: their inside, outside, inside-outside, and beyond-the-outside. Shining everywhere without exception, He is the great light whose end and beginning no one can tell, and the great light of that light. In the sacred Chitrambalam, which is powerful, pure consciousness itself, see, there is one unique God who reigns supreme.
commentary: The immense light of the sun, moon, and stars is just a tiny spark of God's infinite radiance. His presence permeates every level of existence: inside things, outside them, and in the mysterious space that is both internal and external. He is the great, self-luminous light that is both the beginning and the end of all things, a pure consciousness.

translit: āṟṟuviṭa yāṉantam tattuvā ṉantam aṇiyōkā ṉantammatip paruñāṉā ṉantam pēṟṟuṟumāṉ māṉantam paramāṉan tañcēr piramāṉan tamcāntap pērāṉan tattō ṭēṟṟiṭumē kāṉantam attuvitā ṉantam iyaṉṟacacci tāṉantam cuttacivā ṉanta ūṟṟamatām camaracā ṉantacapai taṉilē ōṅkukiṉṟa taṉikkaṭavuḷ oruvaruṇṭē kaṇṭīr.
translation: Along with the bliss of worldly objects, the bliss of the tattvas, the beautiful bliss of yoga, the bliss of esteemed supreme wisdom, the attained bliss of the Self, supreme bliss, the conjoined bliss of Brahman, and the great bliss of peace, together with the elevated bliss of oneness, the bliss of non-duality, and inherent Satchitānanda, in the hall of the bliss of total integration, which is the very wellspring of the bliss of pure Sivam, see, there is one unique God who reigns supreme.
commentary: God is the ultimate source of every kind of bliss imaginable. This includes the joy we find in worldly things, the bliss from understanding reality, the bliss of yoga, of wisdom, and of knowing the Self. All these different joys flow from and merge into the ultimate bliss of Samarasa Ānandam (the bliss of total integration), which is the experience of God Himself.

translit: vakutta:uyir mutaṟpalavām poruḷkaḷukkum vaṭivam vaṇṇanala mutaṟpalavāṅ kuṇaṅkaḷukkum pukutal pukuttaluṟal mutaṟpalavām ceyalkaḷukkum tāmē pukalkaraṇam upakaraṇam karuviupa karuvi mikunta:uṟup patikaraṇam kāraṇampal kālam vitittiṭumaṟ ṟavaimuḻutum ākiallār āki ukappuṟumōr cuttacivā ṉantacapai taṉilē ōṅkukiṉṟa taṉikkaṭavuḷ oruvaruṇṭē kaṇṭīr.
translation: For the many entities beginning with life, for their many qualities beginning with form and fine color, and for their many actions beginning with entering and causing entry, He Himself is the proclaimed primary instrument, secondary instrument, tool, and sub-tool. He is the abundant parts, the locus, the cause, the many divisions of time, and all else that is ordained. He becomes all of it, yet is not it. See, in the joyous Assembly of Pure Siva-Ananda, there is one unique God reigning supreme.
commentary: God is the hidden machinery behind everything that exists. He is the creator and the very tools, processes, and even the unfolding of time that allow beings, qualities, and actions to come into being. Yet, even as He becomes all these things, He remains completely separate from them, untouched and whole in the joyous Assembly of Pure Siva-Ananda (the bliss of Sivam).

translit: iyaṟkaiyilē pācaṅkaḷ oṉṟumilār kuṇaṅkaḷ ētumilār tattuvaṅkaḷ ētumilār maṟṟōr ceyaṟkaiillār piṟappillār iṟappillār yātum tiripillār kaḷaṅkamillār tīmaioṉṟum illār viyappuṟavēṇ ṭutalillār vēṇṭāmai illār meyyēmey ākieṅkum viḷaṅkiiṉpa mayamāy uyattarumōr cuttacivā ṉantacapai taṉilē ōṅkukiṉṟa taṉikkaṭavuḷ oruvaruṇṭē kaṇṭīr.
translation: In His very nature, He is without any bonds, without any qualities, and without any constituent principles. He is without contrived action, without birth, without death, without any change, without blemish, and without any evil. He has no desires and no aversions. Being Truth itself, He shines everywhere, full of bliss. See, in the salvific Assembly of Pure Siva-Ananda, there is one unique God reigning supreme.
commentary: God exists in a state of absolute perfection, completely free from everything that defines our limited existence. He has no karma-like bonds (pāsaṅkaḷ), no defining qualities, no birth or death, and no flaws. Because He is without desire or aversion, He is simply pure Truth and bliss, a presence that offers salvation.

translit: oṉṟumalār iraṇṭumalār oṉṟiraṇṭum āṉār uruvumalār aruvumalār uruaruvum āṉār aṉṟumuḷār iṉṟumuḷār eṉṟumuḷār tamakkōr ātiyilār antamilār arumperuñcō tiyiṉār eṉṟukaṉal matiakattum puṟattumviḷaṅ kiṭuvār yāvumilār yāvumuḷār yāvumalār yāvum oṉṟuṟutām ākiniṉṟār tirucciṟṟam palattē ōṅkukiṉṟa taṉikkaṭavuḷ oruvaruṇṭē kaṇṭīr.
translation: He is not one and not two, yet He became both one and two. He is not form and not formless, yet He became both form and formless. He existed then, He exists now, and He exists forever. He has no beginning and no end. He is the rare, great Light. He shines both inside and outside the sun and moon. He possesses nothing, He possesses everything, and He is none of it, yet He stands as the One who has become all things. See, in Thiru Chitrambalam, there is one unique God reigning supreme.
commentary: The divine nature resolves all paradoxes. God is neither one nor many, but both; neither form nor formless, but both. He is the eternal great Light (arum peruñcōti) who contains everything while being bound by nothing, a mystery realized in Thiru Chitrambalam, the inner space of consciousness.

tamil: உரைவளர் கலையே கலைவளர் உரையே உரைகலை வளர்தரு பொருளே
விரைவளர் மலரே மலர்வளர் விரையே விரைமலர் வளர்தரு நறவே
கரைவளர் தருவே தருவளர் கரையே கரைதரு வளர்கிளர் கனியே
பரைவளர் ஒளியே ஒளிவளர் பரையே பரையொளி வளர்சிவ பதியே.
translit: uraivaḷar kalaiyē kalaivaḷar uraiyē uraikalai vaḷartaru poruḷē viraivaḷar malarē malarvaḷar viraiyē viraimalar vaḷartaru naṟavē karaivaḷar taruvē taruvaḷar karaiyē karaitaru vaḷarkiḷar kaṉiyē paraivaḷar oḷiyē oḷivaḷar paraiyē paraiyoḷi vaḷarciva patiyē.
translation: O Art that grows from the word, O Word that grows from art, O Meaning that grows from word and art! O Flower that grows from fragrance, O Fragrance that grows from the flower, O Nectar that grows from the fragrant flower! O Tree that grows from the bank, O Bank that grows from the tree, O Ripening fruit that grows from the bank-side tree! O Light that grows from Parai, O Parai that grows from light, O Sivapati who grows from Parai and light!
commentary: Each line presents a pair of things that create and sustain each other: word and art, flower and fragrance, a riverbank and the tree it supports. The final line reveals the point of this pattern: the Supreme Lord, Sivapati, is the ultimate reality that arises from the interplay of divine power (Parai) and its own manifest light. God is the living relationship that unites all such pairs.

tamil: ஒளிவளர் உயிரே உயிர்வளர் ஒளியே ஒளியுயிர் வளர்தரும் உணர்வே
வெளிவளர் நிறைவே நிறைவளர் வெளியே வெளிநிறை வளர்தரு விளைவே
வளிவளர் அசைவே அசைவளர் வளியே வளியசை வளர்தரு செயலே
அளிவளர் அனலே அனல்வளர் அளியே அளியனல் வளர்சிவ பதியே.
translit: oḷivaḷar uyirē uyirvaḷar oḷiyē oḷiyuyir vaḷartarum uṇarvē veḷivaḷar niṟaivē niṟaivaḷar veḷiyē veḷiniṟai vaḷartaru viḷaivē vaḷivaḷar acaivē acaivaḷar vaḷiyē vaḷiyacai vaḷartaru ceyalē aḷivaḷar aṉalē aṉalvaḷar aḷiyē aḷiyaṉal vaḷarciva patiyē.
translation: O Life that grows from light, O Light that grows from life, O Consciousness that grows from light and life! O Fullness that grows from space, O Space that grows from fullness, O Fruition that grows from space and fullness! O Movement that grows from air, O Air that grows from movement, O Action that grows from air and movement! O Fire that grows from grace, O Grace that grows from fire, O Sivapati who grows from grace and fire!
commentary: The same pattern of mutual creation continues, revealing God's presence in the most fundamental aspects of existence. Consciousness arises from life and light; the universe's potential is fulfilled through space and its inherent fullness; action becomes possible through air and movement. Last, the transforming power of fire and the saving power of grace are also shown to be a divine pair whose unified expression is God Himself.

tamil: அடிவளர் இயலே இயல்வளர் அடியே அடியியல் வளர்தரு கதியே
முடிவளர் பொருளே பொருள்வளர் முடியே முடிபொருள் வளர்சுக நிதியே
படிவளர் விதையே விதைவளர் படியே படிவிதை வளர்பல நிகழ்வே
தடிவளர் முகிலே முகில்வளர் தடியே தடிமுகில் வளர்சிவ பதியே.
translit: aṭivaḷar iyalē iyalvaḷar aṭiyē aṭiyiyal vaḷartaru katiyē muṭivaḷar poruḷē poruḷvaḷar muṭiyē muṭiporuḷ vaḷarcuka nitiyē paṭivaḷar vitaiyē vitaivaḷar paṭiyē paṭivitai vaḷarpala nikaḻvē taṭivaḷar mukilē mukilvaḷar taṭiyē taṭimukil vaḷarciva patiyē.
translation: O Nature that grows from the foundation, O Foundation that grows from nature, O Path that grows from foundation and nature! O Substance that grows from the summit, O Summit that grows from substance, O Treasure of bliss that grows from the summit's substance! O Seed that grows from the earth, O Earth that grows from the seed, O Manifold events that grow from earth and seed! O Cloud that grows from lightning, O Lightning that grows from the cloud, O Sivapati who grows from lightning and cloud!
commentary: Each pair grows from the other: nature and foundation, substance and summit, seed and earth, cloud and lightning. Vallalar uses this circling pattern to show that in God nothing is simply first and nothing simply second; cause and effect arise together. Sivapati, the Lord who is Siva, is the One from whom both grow and in whom both rest.

tamil: சிரம்வளர் முதலே முதல்வளர் சிரமே சிரமுதல் வளர்தரு செறிவே
தரம்வளர் நிலையே நிலைவளர் தரமே தரநிலை வளர்தரு தகவே
வரம்வளர் நிறையே நிறைவளர் வரமே வரநிறை வளர்தரு வயமே
பரம்வளர் பதமே பதம்வளர் பரமே பரபதம் வளர்சிவ பதியே.
translit: ciramvaḷar mutalē mutalvaḷar ciramē ciramutal vaḷartaru ceṟivē taramvaḷar nilaiyē nilaivaḷar taramē taranilai vaḷartaru takavē varamvaḷar niṟaiyē niṟaivaḷar varamē varaniṟai vaḷartaru vayamē paramvaḷar patamē patamvaḷar paramē parapatam vaḷarciva patiyē.
translation: O Origin that grows from the head, O Head that grows from the origin, O Plenitude that grows from the head and the origin! O State that grows from quality, O Quality that grows from the state, O Fitness that grows from quality and state! O Fullness that grows from the boon, O Boon that grows from fullness, O Mastery that grows from the boon of fullness! O State that grows from the Supreme, O Supreme that grows from the state, O Sivapati who grows from the supreme state!
commentary: The same pattern continues: origin and head, state and quality, boon and fullness, the Supreme and its state, each growing from the other. The repetition is itself the teaching. Whatever we call highest, God is also its source; whatever we call source, God is also its fullness. Sivapati is both the root and the crown.

tamil: திருவளர் வளமே வளம்வளர் திருவே திருவளம் வளர்தரு திகழ்வே
உருவளர் வடிவே வடிவளர் உருவே உருவடி வளர்தரு முறைவே
கருவளர் அருவே அருவளர் கருவே கருவரு வளர்நவ கதியே
குருவளர் நெறியே நெறிவளர் குருவே குருநெறி வளர்சிவ பதியே.
translit: tiruvaḷar vaḷamē vaḷamvaḷar tiruvē tiruvaḷam vaḷartaru tikaḻvē uruvaḷar vaṭivē vaṭivaḷar uruvē uruvaṭi vaḷartaru muṟaivē karuvaḷar aruvē aruvaḷar karuvē karuvaru vaḷarnava katiyē kuruvaḷar neṟiyē neṟivaḷar kuruvē kuruneṟi vaḷarciva patiyē.
translation: O Abundance that grows from holiness, O Holiness that grows from abundance, O Splendor that grows from holy abundance! O Form that grows from shape, O Shape that grows from form, O Order that grows from form and shape! O Formless that grows from the manifest-form, O Manifest-form that grows from the formless, O New path that grows from the formless and the manifest-form! O Path that grows from the Guru, O Guru that grows from the path, O Sivapati who grows from the Guru and the path!
commentary: God is found in the dynamic interplay of opposites. Holiness and abundance grow from each other. The form you can see and the formless reality you cannot see are also a unified, living process, and God is the source from which they arise.

tamil: நிறைவளர் முறையே முறைவளர் நிறையே நிறைமுறை வளர்பெரு நெறியே
பொறைவளர் புவியே புவிவளர் பொறையே புவிபொறை வளர்தரு புனலே
துறைவளர் கடலே கடல்வளர் துறையே துறைகடல் வளர்தரு சுதையே
translit: niṟaivaḷar muṟaiyē muṟaivaḷar niṟaiyē niṟaimuṟai vaḷarperu neṟiyē poṟaivaḷar puviyē puvivaḷar poṟaiyē puvipoṟai vaḷartaru puṉalē tuṟaivaḷar kaṭalē kaṭalvaḷar tuṟaiyē tuṟaikaṭal vaḷartaru cutaiyē maṟaivaḷar poruḷē poruḷvaḷar maṟaiyē maṟaiporuḷvaḷarcivapatiyē.
translation: O Way where fullness grows! O Fullness where the way grows! O Great Path where fullness and the way grow! O Earth where patience grows! O Patience where the earth grows! O Water that nurtures the growth of earth and patience! O Ocean where the shore grows! O Shore where the ocean grows! O Nectar that nurtures the growth of shore and ocean! O Substance where the scriptures grow! O Scriptures where the substance grows! O Sivapati in whom the substance of the scriptures grows!
commentary: This verse describes a world where everything grows in mutual dependence. The spiritual path and the fullness it brings arise together; the earth and the patience it embodies are inseparable. Even opposites like the ocean and the shore create and define each other. This constant, interconnected growth finds its source in God, here called Sivapati (Lord Siva), who is the ultimate substance from which even the scriptures and their meaning arise.

tamil: தவம்வளர் தயையே தயைவளர் தவமே தவநிறை தயைவளர் சதுரே
நவம்வளர் புரமே புரம்வளர் நவமே நவபுரம் வளர்தரும் இறையே
துவம்வளர் குணமே குணம்வளர் துவமே துவகுணம் வளர்தரு திகழ்வே
சிவம்வளர் பதமே பதம்வளர் சிவமே சிவபதம் வளர்சிவ பதியே.
translit: tavamvaḷar tayaiyē tayaivaḷar tavamē tavaniṟai tayaivaḷar caturē navamvaḷar puramē puramvaḷar navamē navapuram vaḷartarum iṟaiyē tuvamvaḷar kuṇamē kuṇamvaḷar tuvamē tuvakuṇam vaḷartaru tikaḻvē civamvaḷar patamē patamvaḷar civamē civapatam vaḷarciva patiyē.
translation: O Grace where spiritual discipline grows! O Spiritual discipline where grace grows! O Adeptness in which discipline and abundant grace grow! O Abode where newness grows! O Newness where the abode grows! O Lord who nurtures the growth of the new abode! O Quality where "you-ness" grows! O "You-ness" where quality grows! O Splendor that nurtures the growth of "you-ness" and quality! O State where Sivam grows! O Sivam where the state grows! O Sivapati in whom the state of Sivam grows!
commentary: Spiritual effort (tavam) and divine grace (tayai) are not a sequence where one earns the other; they grow together, each strengthening the other. The final line identifies God, Sivapati, as both the ultimate reality, Sivam, and the state (padam) of being one with that reality.

tamil: நடம்வளர் நலமே நலம்வளர் நடமே நடநலம் வளர்தரும் ஒளியே
இடம்வளர் வலமே வலம்வளர் இடமே இடம்வலம் வளர்தரும் இசைவே
திடம்வளர் உளமே உளம்வளர் திடமே திடவுளம் வளர்தரு திருவே
கடம்வளர் உயிரே உயிர்வளர் கடமே கடமுயிர் வளர்சிவ பதியே.
translit: naṭamvaḷar nalamē nalamvaḷar naṭamē naṭanalam vaḷartarum oḷiyē iṭamvaḷar valamē valamvaḷar iṭamē iṭamvalam vaḷartarum icaivē tiṭamvaḷar uḷamē uḷamvaḷar tiṭamē tiṭavuḷam vaḷartaru tiruvē kaṭamvaḷar uyirē uyirvaḷar kaṭamē kaṭamuyir vaḷarciva patiyē.
translation: O Goodness where the Dance grows! O Dance where goodness grows! O Light that nurtures the growth of the Dance and goodness! O Right where the left grows! O Left where the right grows! O Harmony that nurtures the growth of the left and right! O Mind where firmness grows! O Firmness where the mind grows! O Sacred Wealth that nurtures the growth of the firm mind! O Life where the body grows! O Body where life grows! O Sivapati in whom the body and life grow!
commentary: The divine Dance (naṭam) of creation is inseparable from the goodness (nalam) it expresses. The most powerful idea here is that God is the principle by which the body (kaṭam, literally ‘pot’) and life (uyir) grow from one another. The physical and the vital are two aspects of a single divine process.

tamil: அதுவளர் அணுவே அணுவளர் அதுவே அதுவணு வளர்தரும் உறவே
விதுவளர் ஒளியே ஒளிவளர் விதுவே விதுஒளி வளர்தரு செயலே
மதுவளர் சுவையே சுவைவளர் மதுவே மதுவுறு சுவைவளர் இயலே
பொதுவளர் வெளியே வெளிவளர் பொதுவே பொதுவெளி வளர்சிவ பதியே.
translit: atuvaḷar aṇuvē aṇuvaḷar atuvē atuvaṇu vaḷartarum uṟavē vituvaḷar oḷiyē oḷivaḷar vituvē vituoḷi vaḷartaru ceyalē matuvaḷar cuvaiyē cuvaivaḷar matuvē matuvuṟu cuvaivaḷar iyalē potuvaḷar veḷiyē veḷivaḷar potuvē potuveḷi vaḷarciva patiyē.
translation: O Atom where "That" grows! O "That" where the atom grows! O Relationship that nurtures the growth of "That" and the atom! O Light where the moon grows! O Moon where the light grows! O Action that nurtures the growth of the moon and light! O Taste where sweetness grows! O Sweetness where taste grows! O Nature in which sweet taste grows! O Expanse where the Universal Stage grows! O Universal Stage where the expanse grows! O Sivapati in whom the universal expanse grows!
commentary: God is the relationship between the infinite ("That") and the infinitesimal (the atom). The universal stage of existence (potu) and the infinite empty expanse (veḷi) are not separate; they give rise to each other, and God is the reality in which this happens.

tamil: நிதிவளர் நிலமே நிலம்வளர் நிதியே நிதிநிலம் வளர்தரு நிறைவே
மதிவளர் நலமே நலம்வளர் மதியே மதிநலம் வளர்தரு பரமே
கதிவளர் நிலையே நிலைவளர் கதியே கதிநிலை வளர்தரு பொருளே
பதிவளர் பதமே பதம்வளர் பதியே பதிபதம் வளர்சிவ பதியே.
translit: nitivaḷar nilamē nilamvaḷar nitiyē nitinilam vaḷartaru niṟaivē mativaḷar nalamē nalamvaḷar matiyē matinalam vaḷartaru paramē kativaḷar nilaiyē nilaivaḷar katiyē katinilai vaḷartaru poruḷē pativaḷar patamē patamvaḷar patiyē patipatam vaḷarciva patiyē.
translation: O Land where treasure grows! O Treasure where the land grows! O Fullness that nurtures the growth of treasure and land! O Goodness where wisdom grows! O Wisdom where goodness grows! O Supreme One who nurtures the growth of wisdom and goodness! O State where the goal grows! O Goal where the state grows! O Substance that nurtures the growth of the goal and the state! O State where the Lord grows! O Lord where the state grows! O Sivapati in whom the Lord and His state grow!
commentary: The poem concludes by stating that God is the ultimate fullness in which all value resides. He is the supreme reality (paramam) that nurtures wisdom, and the very substance of the spiritual goal. Finally, God the Lord (pati) and the state of being with God (padam) are inseparable, each growing from the other.

tamil: எழுவினும் வலிய மனத்தினேன் மலஞ்சார் ஈயினும் நாயினும் இழிந்தேன்
வழுவினும் பெரியேன் மடத்தினும் பெரியேன் மாண்பிலா வஞ்சக நெஞ்சக்
குழுவினும் பெரியேன் அம்பலக் கூத்தன் குறிப்பினுக் கென்கட வேனே.
translit: eḻuviṉum valiya maṉattiṉēṉ malañcār īyiṉum nāyiṉum iḻintēṉ puḻuviṉum ciṟiyēṉpoyviḻain tuḻalvēṉpuṉmaiyēṉ pulaittoḻiṟkaṭaiyēṉ vaḻuviṉum periyēṉ maṭattiṉum periyēṉ māṇpilā vañcaka neñcak kuḻuviṉum periyēṉ ampalak kūttaṉ kuṟippiṉuk keṉkaṭa vēṉē.
translation: My mind is harder than a steel stylus. I am lower than a fly drawn to filth, lower than a dog. I am smaller than a worm, I wander desiring falsehood, I am a base person, the very last among those who do vile deeds. I am immense in my errors, immense in my ignorance, greater than a whole gang of deceitful hearts that lack nobility. What can I do to fulfill the will of the Dancer of the Ambalam?
commentary: The devotee begins by declaring his spiritual state as completely hardened and impure. Comparing his mind to a steel stylus and himself to a fly drawn to filth, he expresses a feeling of being utterly base. The final line, a refrain throughout the poem, is a cry of despair: feeling so unworthy, how can he possibly do God's will? The "Dancer of the Ambalam" is The Vast Grace-Light, whose cosmic dance creates and sustains the universe.

tamil: கற்றமே லவர்தம் உறவினைக் கருதேன் கலகர்தம் உறவினிற் களித்தேன்
உற்றமே தகவோர் உவட்டுற இருந்தேன் உலகியற் போகமே உவந்தேன்
செற்றமே விழையும் சிறுநெறி பிடித்தேன் தெய்வம்ஒன் றெனும்அறி வறியேன்
குற்றமே உடையேன் அம்பலக் கூத்தன் குறிப்பினுக் கென்கட வேனே.
translit: kaṟṟamē lavartam uṟaviṉaik karutēṉ kalakartam uṟaviṉiṟ kaḷittēṉ uṟṟamē takavōr uvaṭṭuṟa iruntēṉ ulakiyaṟ pōkamē uvantēṉ ceṟṟamē viḻaiyum ciṟuneṟi piṭittēṉ teyvamoṉ ṟeṉumaṟi vaṟiyēṉ kuṟṟamē uṭaiyēṉ ampalak kūttaṉ kuṟippiṉuk keṉkaṭa vēṉē.
translation: I did not value the company of the learned and noble; instead, I delighted in the company of troublemakers. I behaved in a way that disgusted the truly virtuous. I rejoiced only in worldly pleasures. I followed the petty path that desires hostility. I do not have the awareness that God is One. I am composed entirely of faults. What can I do to fulfill the will of the Dancer of the Ambalam?
commentary: Here, the focus shifts to a lifetime of wrong choices. He has actively preferred the company of troublemakers over the wise and chosen worldly pleasure over virtue. His deepest regret is lacking the simple, core awareness that "God is One," a foundational spiritual truth. He sees himself as a collection of faults, completely misaligned with the divine.

tamil: கடுமையேன் வஞ்சக் கருத்தினேன் பொல்லாக் கண்மனக் குரங்கனேன் கடையேன்
நெடுமைஆண் பனைபோல் நின்றவெற் றுடம்பேன் நீசனேன் பாசமே உடையேன்
நடுமைஒன் றறியேன் கெடுமையிற் கிளைத்த நச்சுமா மரம்எனக்கிளைத்தேன்
கொடுமையே குறித்தேன் அம்பலக் கூத்தன் குறிப்பினுக் கென்கட வேனே.
translit: kaṭumaiyēṉ vañcak karuttiṉēṉ pollāk kaṇmaṉak kuraṅkaṉēṉ kaṭaiyēṉ neṭumaiāṇ paṉaipōl niṉṟaveṟ ṟuṭampēṉ nīcaṉēṉ pācamē uṭaiyēṉ naṭumaioṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ keṭumaiyiṟ kiḷaitta naccumā marameṉakkiḷaittēṉ koṭumaiyē kuṟittēṉ ampalak kūttaṉ kuṟippiṉuk keṉkaṭa vēṉē.
translation: I am a harsh person with a deceitful mind, the lowest of the low, a monkey of wicked sight and mind. I am an empty body, standing useless like a tall male palm tree. I am a vile person, possessing only worldly attachments. I know nothing of impartiality. I have branched out like a great poison tree growing from ruin itself. I intended only cruelty. What can I do to fulfill the will of the Dancer of the Ambalam?
commentary: The self-critique deepens with stark natural metaphors. He feels he is useless, like a male palm tree that can never bear fruit. Worse, he sees himself as a "great poison tree," a being who spreads harm and whose very nature is toxic. He confesses to having only pācam, the entangling bonds of worldly attachment, and knowing nothing of fairness or impartiality.

tamil: புலத்திலும் புரைசேர் பொறியிலும் மனத்தைப் போக்கிவீண் போதுபோக் குறுவேன்
நலத்தில்ஓர் அணுவும் நண்ணிலேன் கடைய நாயினுங் கடையனேன் நவையேன்
குலத்திலும் கொடியேன் அம்பலக் கூத்தன் குறிப்பினுக் கென்கட வேனே.
translit: nilattilumpaṇattum nīḷviḻimaṭavār nerukkilumperukkiya niṉaippēṉ pulattilum puraicēr poṟiyilum maṉattaip pōkkivīṇ pōtupōk kuṟuvēṉ nalattilōr aṇuvum naṇṇilēṉ kaṭaiya nāyiṉuṅ kaṭaiyaṉēṉ navaiyēṉ kulattilum koṭiyēṉ ampalak kūttaṉ kuṟippiṉuk keṉkaṭa vēṉē.
translation: My thoughts multiply, dwelling on land, money, and the closeness of long-eyed women. I waste my time, letting my mind run after the senses and the flawed sense organs. I have not attained even an atom of goodness. I am a flawed person, lower than the lowest dog. I am the cruelest of my kind. What can I do to fulfill the will of the Dancer of the Ambalam?
commentary: This verse targets the restless, uncontrolled mind. He admits his thoughts are consumed by the classic worldly desires for wealth ("land, money") and sensual pleasure ("long-eyed women"). By letting his mind chase after the senses, he feels he has wasted his life and achieved not even an "atom of goodness," making him, in his own eyes, lower than a dog.

tamil: அடிமுடி அறியும் ஆசைசற் றறியேன் அறிந்தவர் தங்களை அடையேன்
படிமுடி வழித்துக் கடிகொளும் கடையர்பணத்திலும் கொடியனேன் வஞ்கக்
கொடிமுடிந் திடுவேன் அம்பலக் கூத்தன் குறிப்பினுக் கென்கட வேனே.
translit: ceṭimuṭin talaiyummaṉattiṉēṉ tuṉpac celliṉālarippuṇṭaciṟiyēṉ aṭimuṭi aṟiyum ācaicaṟ ṟaṟiyēṉ aṟintavar taṅkaḷai aṭaiyēṉ paṭimuṭi vaḻittuk kaṭikoḷum kaṭaiyarpaṇattilum koṭiyaṉēṉ vañkak koṭimuṭin tiṭuvēṉ ampalak kūttaṉ kuṟippiṉuk keṉkaṭa vēṉē.
translation: I have a mind that wanders, entangled in evil. I am a wretched creature, eaten away by the termites of suffering. I have not the slightest desire to know the divine feet and crown. I do not approach those who have realized the truth. I am more vile than the wealth of the lowest robbers who block the roads to plunder travelers. I am completely entangled in the vine of deceit. What can I do to fulfill the will of the Dancer of the Ambalam?
commentary: Vallalar lists his failings: a tangled mind, a life eaten away by suffering, no wish to know God, no company with those who know. He calls himself crueler than robbers who block the roads to plunder travelers, bound in a vine of deceit. The confession ends in one question: how can such a one fulfil the will of the Dancer of the Ambalam?

tamil: அரங்கினிற் படைகொண் டுயிர்க்கொலை புரியும் அறக்கடை யவரினுங் கடையேன்
இரங்கில்ஓர் சிறிதும் இரக்கம்உற் றறியேன் இயலுறு நாசியுட் கிளைத்த
சிரங்கினிற் கொடியேன் சிவநெறி பிடியேன் சிறுநெறிச் சழக்கையே சிலுகுக்
குரங்கெனப் பிடித்தேன் அம்பலக் கூத்தன் குறிப்பினுக் கென்கட வேனே.
translit: araṅkiṉiṟ paṭaikoṇ ṭuyirkkolai puriyum aṟakkaṭai yavariṉuṅ kaṭaiyēṉ iraṅkilōr ciṟitum irakkamuṟ ṟaṟiyēṉ iyaluṟu nāciyuṭ kiḷaitta ciraṅkiṉiṟ koṭiyēṉ civaneṟi piṭiyēṉ ciṟuneṟic caḻakkaiyē cilukuk kuraṅkeṉap piṭittēṉ ampalak kūttaṉ kuṟippiṉuk keṉkaṭa vēṉē.
translation: I am lower than even the lowest of the unrighteous, who take up arms on the battlefield and slaughter living beings. I have never known the slightest compassion for those in distress. I am more vile than a sore that festers inside the nose. I do not follow the path of Siva. I have clung to the depravity of the lesser path like a troublesome monkey. What can I possibly do about the intention of the Dancer of the Hall?
commentary: Vallalar measures himself against those who kill living beings on the battlefield and finds himself lower still, for he has felt no compassion for those in distress. He does not hold to the path of Siva and clings to lesser paths like a restless monkey. The verse sets killing and the absence of compassion side by side: both are failures of the same heart.

tamil: வாட்டமே உடையார் தங்களைக் காணின் மனஞ்சிறிதிரக்கமுற் றறியேன்
கோட்டமே உடையேன் கொலையனேன் புலையேன் கூற்றினும் கொடியனேன் மாயை
ஆட்டமே புரிந்தேன் அறத்தொழில் புரியேன் அச்சமும் அவலமும் இயற்றும்
கூட்டமே விழைந்தேன் அம்பலக் கூத்தன் குறிப்பினுக் கென்கட வேனே.
translit: vāṭṭamē uṭaiyār taṅkaḷaik kāṇiṉ maṉañciṟitirakkamuṟ ṟaṟiyēṉ kōṭṭamē uṭaiyēṉ kolaiyaṉēṉ pulaiyēṉ kūṟṟiṉum koṭiyaṉēṉ māyai āṭṭamē purintēṉ aṟattoḻil puriyēṉ accamum avalamum iyaṟṟum kūṭṭamē viḻaintēṉ ampalak kūttaṉ kuṟippiṉuk keṉkaṭa vēṉē.
translation: When I see those who are suffering, my mind has never known even a little compassion. I am full of crookedness. I am a killer, a base one. I am crueler than the God of Death. I have only performed the dance of delusion. I do not perform righteous deeds. I desired only the company of those who create fear and misery. What can I possibly do about the intention of the Dancer of the Hall?
commentary: Vallalar accuses himself without mercy: no compassion for those who suffer, a killer, vile, crueler than Death. He names the lack of compassion first, because for him it is the root of every other fault. Measured against Jeeva Karunyam, the compassion for all life he holds as the foundation, he finds himself guilty, and he leaves his case with the Dancer of the Hall.

tamil: கலைத்தொழில் அறியேன் கள்உணுங் கொடியேன் கறிக்குழல் நாயினும் கடையேன்
விலைத்தொழில் உடையேன் மெய்எலாம் வாயாய் விளம்புறும் வீணனேன் அசுத்தப்
புலைத்தொழில் புரிவேன் பொய்யனேன் சீற்றம் பொங்கிய மனத்தினேன் பொல்லாக்
கொலைத்தொழில் புரிவேன் அம்பலக் கூத்தன் குறிப்பினுக் கென்கட வேனே.
translit: kalaittoḻil aṟiyēṉ kaḷuṇuṅ koṭiyēṉ kaṟikkuḻal nāyiṉum kaṭaiyēṉ vilaittoḻil uṭaiyēṉ meyelām vāyāy viḷampuṟum vīṇaṉēṉ acuttap pulaittoḻil purivēṉ poyyaṉēṉ cīṟṟam poṅkiya maṉattiṉēṉ pollāk kolaittoḻil purivēṉ ampalak kūttaṉ kuṟippiṉuk keṉkaṭa vēṉē.
translation: I do not know the noble arts. I am a wretch who drinks liquor. I am lower than a dog that eats from the cooking pot. I am a man who sells himself. I am a worthless man who is all mouth. I perform impure and base deeds. I am a liar, a man whose mind seethes with rage. I commit the wicked act of killing. What can I possibly do about the intention of the Dancer of the Hall?
commentary: Vallalar lists his faults without mercy: drinking liquor, lower than a dog that eats from the cooking pot, selling himself, all mouth, impure deeds, lies, rage, and the wicked act of killing. He does not leave killing out of the list; he names it last and strongest. With nothing left to plead, he leaves his case with the Dancer of the Hall.

tamil: பணமிலார்க் கிடுக்கண் புரிந்துணுஞ் சோற்றுப் பணம்பறித் துழல்கின்ற படிறேன்
மணமிலா மலரிற் பூத்தனன் இருகால் மாடெனத் திரிந்துழல் கின்றேன்
குணமிலாக் கொடியேன் அம்பலக் கூத்தன் குறிப்பினுக் கென்கட வேனே.
translit: paṇamilārk kiṭukkaṇ purintuṇuñ cōṟṟup paṇampaṟit tuḻalkiṉṟa paṭiṟēṉ eṇamilā taṭuttārk kuṟuperuntīmai iyaṟṟuvēṉ eṭṭiyēaṉaiyēṉ maṇamilā malariṟ pūttaṉaṉ irukāl māṭeṉat tirintuḻal kiṉṟēṉ kuṇamilāk koṭiyēṉ ampalak kūttaṉ kuṟippiṉuk keṉkaṭa vēṉē.
translation: I am a fraud who wanders about, causing hardship for the penniless and snatching the money they have for their food. Without any thought, I commit great evil against those who approach me. I am like the poisonous etty tree. I have blossomed like a flower without fragrance. I wander around like a two-legged beast. I am a villain with no good qualities. What can I possibly do about the intention of the Dancer of the Hall?
commentary: He compares himself to a poisonous tree and a fragrantless flower, powerful metaphors for a life that fails to offer any goodness to the world. By seeing himself as a "two-legged beast," he expresses the deep spiritual distress of feeling disconnected from his own humanity and purpose.

tamil: கடியரில் கடியேன் கடையரில் கடையேன் கள்வரில் கள்வனேன் காமப்
பொடியரில் பொடியேன் புலையரில் புலையேன் பொய்யரில் பொய்யனேன் பொல்லாச்
செடியரில் செடியேன் சினத்தரில் சினத்தேன் தீயரில் தீயனேன் பாபக்
கொடியரில் கொடியேன் அம்பலக் கூத்தன் குறிப்பினுக் கென்கட வேனே.
translit: kaṭiyaril kaṭiyēṉ kaṭaiyaril kaṭaiyēṉ kaḷvaril kaḷvaṉēṉ kāmap poṭiyaril poṭiyēṉ pulaiyaril pulaiyēṉ poyyaril poyyaṉēṉ pollāc ceṭiyaril ceṭiyēṉ ciṉattaril ciṉattēṉ tīyaril tīyaṉēṉ pāpak koṭiyaril koṭiyēṉ ampalak kūttaṉ kuṟippiṉuk keṉkaṭa vēṉē.
translation: Among the cruel, I am the cruelest. Among the low, I am the lowest. Among thieves, I am the greatest thief. Among lustful degenerates, I am the most degenerate. Among the defiled, I am the most defiled. Among liars, I am the greatest liar. Among the wicked, I am the wickedest. Among the wrathful, I am the most wrathful. Among the evil, I am the most evil. Among sinful villains, I am the most villainous. What can I possibly do about the intention of the Dancer of the Hall?
commentary: This verse brings the poem's self-reproach to a climax. In a torrent of comparisons, Vallalar declares himself a sinner and the very worst among every category of sinner. This is the ultimate expression of emptying the self, a state of complete humility before God where no trace of self-righteousness remains.

translit: kulattiṭaiyum koṭiyaṉoru kuṭittaṉattum koṭiyēṉ kuṟikaḷilum koṭiyaṉaṉṟik kuṇaṅkaḷilum koṭiyēṉ malattiṭaiyē puḻuttaciṟu puḻukkaḷilum kaṭaiyēṉ vaṉmaṉattup perumpāvi vañcaneñcap pulaiyēṉ nalattiṭaiōr aṇuaḷavum naṇṇukilēṉ pollā nāykkunakai tōṉṟaniṉṟēṉ pēykkummika iḻintēṉ nilattiṭaināṉ ēṉpiṟantēṉ niṉkaruttai aṟiyēṉ nirkkuṇaṉē naṭarāja nipuṇamaṇi viḷakkē.
translation: I am cruel in my lineage and cruel in my family life, cruel in my aims and also cruel in my character. I am lower than the tiny worms that breed in filth, a great sinner with a hardened heart, a base one with a deceitful mind. I have not attained even an atom's worth of goodness; I am a laughing stock even to a wicked dog, more base than even a demon. Why was I born on this earth? I do not know Your intention, O Nirguna, O Nataraja ), O expert gem-like lamp!
commentary: This verse opens with a litany of self-blame, with Vallalar portraying himself as lower than a worm in filth. He then poses the poem's central, haunting question: "Why was I born?" By addressing God as both Nirguna (the abstract, quality-less Absolute) and Nataraja (the personal, dancing Lord), he shows that this desperate cry comes from a place where deep philosophy and intense devotion meet.

translit: viḷakkaṟiyā iruṭṭaṟaiyil kaviḻntukiṭan taḻutu vimmukiṉṟa kuḻaviyiṉum mikapperitum ciṟiyēṉ aḷakkaṟiyāt tuyarkkaṭalil viḻuntuneṭuṅ kālam alaintalaintu melintaturum pataṉiṉmikat turumpēṉ kiḷakkaṟiyāk koṭumaielām kiḷaittapaḻu marattēṉ keṭumatiyēṉ kaṭumaiyiṉēṉ kiṟipēcum veṟiyēṉ kaḷakkaṟiyāp puviyiṭaināṉ ēṉpiṟantēṉ antō karuṇainaṭat taracēniṉ karuttaiaṟi yēṉē.
translation: I am far more insignificant than a baby lying face down, crying and sobbing in a pitch-dark room. Having fallen into a measureless ocean of sorrow, I have drifted and drifted for a long time, becoming more wasted than a withered blade of grass. I am a rotten tree from which all unspeakable cruelties have branched out. I have a ruined mind, I am harsh, a madman who speaks nonsense. Alas, why was I born on this guileless earth? O King of the compassionate dance, I do not know Your intention!
commentary: The feeling of utter insignificance is deepened with images of a helpless baby, a withered blade of grass, and a rotten tree. This is the voice of someone feeling completely lost and without purpose. The verse ends with a painful paradox, asking the "King of the compassionate dance" why such a miserable and useless being was ever created. This question highlights the gulf between the perfection of God and the devotee's own sense of failure.

translit: aṟiyāta poṟiyavarkkum iḻintatoḻi lavarkkum atikarittut tuṉmārkkat taracuceyuṅ koṭiyēṉ kuṟiyāta koṭumpāvac cumaicumakkum tiṟattēṉ kollāmai eṉpataiōr kuṟippālum kuṟiyēṉ ceṟiyāta maṉakkaṭaiyēṉ tīmaiyelām uṭaiyēṉ ciṉattālum matattālum ceṟintaputal aṉaiyēṉ eṟiyāta puviyiṭaināṉ ēṉpiṟantēṉ uṉṟaṉ itayamaṟi yēṉmaṉṟil iṉittanaṭat tiṟaiyē.
translation: I am the cruel one who reigns supreme in wickedness, surpassing even those with ignorant senses and those who do base work. I am capable of carrying the burden of terrible sins one should never even contemplate. I do not consider non-killing even in the slightest. I am the lowest of the low with an unfocused mind, and I possess all evils. I am like a dense thicket of anger and arrogance. Why was I born on this earth that does not cast me out? I do not know Your heart, O Lord of the sweet dance in the cosmic hall!
commentary: Among all his faults, Vallalar names one plainly: he has not held to non-killing (kollāmai) even in thought. He calls himself a ruler of the evil path, a carrier of terrible sins, a thicket of anger and pride. His question is not a figure of speech: why does the earth bear one like him? He does not know God's heart, and he asks to be shown it.

translit: iṉittapaḻac cāṟuviṭut tiḻittamalaṅ koḷumōr iḻivilaṅkil iḻintuniṉṟēṉ irakkamoṉṟum illēṉ aṉittaneṟi yiṭaittoṭarntu maṉitta:uṭam peṭutta aṟakkaṭaiyar tamakkellām aṟakkaṭaiyaṉ āṉēṉ paṉittamaṉak kuraṅkāṭṭip palikkuḻalum koṭiyēṉ pātakamum cūtakamum payiṉṟapeṟum paṭiṟēṉ taṉittakaṭuṅ kuṇattēṉnāṉ ēṉpiṟantēṉ niṉatu taṉikkaruttai aṟintilēṉ capaikkēṟṟum oḷiyē.
translation: I am more base than a vile animal that forsakes sweet fruit juice to consume disgusting excrement; I have no compassion whatsoever. Persisting in the path of impermanence, I have become the very lowest among all the lowly wretches who have taken a human body. I am a cruel man who wanders for alms, making a spectacle of my trembling, monkey-like mind. I am a great hypocrite practiced in mortal sin and ritual impurity. With my uniquely harsh character, why was I born? I have not understood Your unique intention, O Light that graces the cosmic assembly!
commentary: Vallalar uses a shocking image, feeling lower than an animal that chooses filth over sweet fruit, to show how far he has strayed from his own divine nature. He sees his lack of compassion as the ultimate sign of this degradation. Posing as a holy man while feeling internally corrupt, he asks God the desperate question that drives this poem: given my fallen state, why was I even born?

translit: ēṟukiṉṟēm eṉamatittē iṟaṅkukiṉṟa kaṭaiyēṉ ētamelām niṟaimaṉattēṉ irakkamilāp pulaiyēṉ cīṟukiṉṟa puliyaṉaiyēṉ ciṟutoḻilē purivēṉ ceyvakaioṉ ṟaṟiyāta ciṟiyariṉum ciṟiyēṉ māṟukiṉṟa kuṇappētai matiyataṉāl iḻintēṉ vañcamelām kuṭikoṇṭa vāḻkkaimika uṭaiyēṉ vīṟukiṉṟa ulakiṭaināṉ ēṉpiṟantēṉ niṉatu meykkaruttai aṟintilēṉ viḷaṅkunaṭat taracē.
translation: I am a wretch who descends while thinking I am ascending; my mind is filled with every fault. I am a merciless, base one, like a hissing tiger, and I perform only base deeds. I am smaller than the small ones who do not know what to do. I am degraded by a foolish mind with a fickle character, and I lead a life where all deceit has taken up residence. Why was I born in this thriving world? I have not understood Your true intention, O King of the radiant dance.
commentary: This verse describes the painful self-delusion of thinking one is making spiritual progress while actually going backward. Vallalar compares himself to a hissing tiger, all aggressive instinct, and says his mind has become a home for deceit. He feels trapped by his own fickle character, unable to see God's plan for him through the fog of his own faults.

translit: aracarelām matittiṭappē rācaiyilē aracō ṭāleṉavē mikakkiḷaittēṉ aruḷaṟiyāk kaṭaiyēṉ puracamaram pōṟparuttēṉ eṭṭieṉat taḻaittēṉ puṅkeṉavum puḷieṉavum maṅkiutir kiṉṟēṉ paracumvakai terintukoḷēṉ terintāraip paṇiyēṉ pacaiaṟiyāk karuṅkalmaṉap pāvikaḷiṟ ciṟantēṉ viracunilat tēṉpiṟantēṉ niṉkaruttai aṟiyēṉ viyakkumaṇi maṉṟōṅki viḷaṅkuparam poruḷē.
translation: Driven by the great desire that all kings should respect me, I spread out extravagantly like the pipal and the banyan. I, the lowly one who does not know grace, grew fat like a palash tree and flourished like a strychnine tree. Now, like the pongam and tamarind trees, I fade and my leaves fall. I do not know how to praise You, nor do I bow to those who know. I am the foremost among sinners whose hearts are like hard black stone, knowing no tenderness. Why was I born on this teeming earth? I do not know Your intention, O Supreme Being, who shines forth, exalted in the wondrous jeweled hall!
commentary: The driving force of his life, he confesses, was the ego's desire for worldly status and respect. He uses a series of tree metaphors to describe this path: he grew big like a banyan tree and flourished like a poisonous one, but this growth was empty and now he is withering. This life of pride left his heart as hard as stone, unable to feel devotion or learn from the wise.

translit: poruḷaṟiyēṉ poruḷaṟintār pōṉṟunaṭit tiṅkē poṅkivaḻin tuṭaikiṉṟēṉ poyyakattēṉ pulaiyēṉ maruḷaṟiyāt tiruvāḷar uḷaṅkayakkat tirivēṉ vaiyuṇṭum uḻavutavā māṭeṉavē taṭittēṉ veruḷaṟiyāk koṭumaṉattēṉ viḻaṟkiṟaittuk kaḷippēṉ vīṇarkaḷil talainiṉṟēṉ vilakkaṉaittum purivēṉ teruḷaṟiyēṉ ulakiṭaināṉ ēṉpiṟantēṉ niṉatu tiruvuḷattai aṟintilēṉ teyvanaṭan tavaṉē.
translation: Though I do not know the truth, I act as if I do, overflowing and breaking apart here. I have a false heart; I am a vile, base one. I wander about, confusing the minds of the blessed who are free from delusion. I have grown thick-skinned like an ox useless for plowing, even when scolded. I have a cruel heart that knows no alarm. I take pleasure in watering weeds. I stand at the head of the worthless. I do everything that is forbidden. I have no clarity. Why was I born into this world? I have not known Your sacred will, O divine Dancer!
commentary: Vallalar confesses to being a spiritual phony, acting as if he knows the truth while being completely lost. He compares himself to a stubborn ox, too thick-skinned to be guided, and admits to taking pleasure in useless things ("watering weeds"). He has lost his inner alarm system, the conscience that warns him of wrongdoing, and so he feels totally without clarity or purpose.

translit: tavampuriyēṉ tavampurintār tamaippōla naṭittut tarukkukiṉṟēṉ uṇarcciyilāc caṭampōla iruntēṉ pavampurivēṉ kamariṉiṭaip pālkaviḻkkum kaṭaiyēṉ payaṉaṟiyā vañcamaṉap pāṟaicuman tuḻalvēṉ avampurivēṉ aṟivaṟiyēṉ aṉpaṟiyēṉ aṉpāl aiyāniṉ aṭiyaṭaintārk kaṇuttuṇaiyum utavēṉ navampuriyum ulakiṭaināṉ ēṉpiṟantēṉ niṉatu nallatiru vuḷamaṟiyēṉ ñāṉanaṭat tiṟaiyē.
translation: I perform no austerities, yet I act like those who do and strut with arrogance. I have been like an inanimate object, devoid of feeling. I commit sins. I am the base one who would spill milk into a barren crevice. I wander about, carrying the rock of a deceitful heart that knows no benefit. I do useless things, I know no wisdom, I know no love. To those who, out of love, have reached Your feet, O Father, I do not offer even an atom's worth of help. Why was I born into this world of novelty? I do not know Your good and sacred will, O Lord of the dance of wisdom!
commentary: This is a confession of spiritual hypocrisy and waste. He acts like a holy man but feels like an inanimate object, devoid of genuine feeling. Wasting grace is like spilling precious milk into a barren crack in the earth. He carries his own deceitful heart like a heavy stone, and it prevents him from feeling love or helping other seekers, even a little.

translit: iṟaiaḷavum aṟivoḻukkat ticcaiyilēṉ narakil iruntuḻaṉṟu vāṭukiṉṟōr ellārkkum iḻintēṉ poṟaiaḷavō naṉmaielām pōkkilviṭṭut tīmai purikiṉṟēṉ erikiṉṟa putuneruppiṟ koṭiyēṉ niṟaiaḷavō muṟaiaḷavō nilaiaḷavun tavirnta neṭuñcāla neñcakattēṉ nīlaviṭam pōlvēṉ kaṟaiyaḷavā ulakiṭaināṉ ēṉpiṟantēṉ niṉatu karuttaṟiyēṉ karuṇainaṭaṅ kāṭṭukiṉṟa kuruvē.
translation: I lack even the slightest desire for wisdom and discipline. I am more debased than all who suffer and languish in hell. As for patience, I have cast aside all goodness and now commit evil. I am more cruel than a newly blazing fire. My heart is a vast web of deceit that has abandoned all measure of integrity, propriety, and stability. I am like the blue poison. Why was I born into this world of immeasurable stain? I do not know Your intention, O Guru who performs the dance of compassion!
commentary: He describes a state of complete spiritual collapse, having lost even the desire for wisdom or self-discipline. His heart, he says, has become a vast web of deceit with no integrity, order or stability, making him more destructive than a fresh blaze and as deadly as the blue poison. In this state of inner chaos, he appeals to God as the ultimate teacher, the Guru who can reveal a purpose for a life that seems only to have stained the world.

translit: kāṭṭukiṉṟa uvarkkaṭalpōl kalaikaḷilum celvak kaḷippiṉilum ciṟantumikak kaḷittuniṟai kiṉṟēṉ nīṭṭukiṉṟa āpattil oruciṟitum utavēṉ neṭuntūram āḻntutavāp paṭuṅkiṇaṟu pōlvēṉ āṭṭukiṉṟa aruṭperumai oruciṟitum teriyēṉ accamilēṉ nāṇamilēṉ aṭakkamoṉṟum illēṉ kūṭṭukiṉṟa ulakiṭaināṉ ēṉpiṟantēṉ niṉatu kuṟippaṟiyēṉ maṉṟilnaṭaṅ kulavukula maṇiyē.
translation: Like the vast, salty ocean, I feel full, excelling and reveling in the arts and the intoxication of wealth. In times of drawn-out danger, I am not of the slightest help. I am like a deep pitfall of a well, useless from afar. I do not understand in the slightest the greatness of the grace that makes one dance. I have no fear, no shame, and no restraint at all. Why was I born into this world that gathers all together? I do not know Your purpose, O dynastic Gem who graces the dance in the Hall.
commentary: Learning and wealth have filled him with himself, like the salt ocean, full of water no one can drink. He helps no one in danger; he is a deep well that gives nothing. He knows nothing of the grace that moves all things, and he has no fear, no shame and no restraint. Fullness without compassion, he shows, is only emptiness.

translit: tāvu māṉeṉak kutittukkoṇ ṭōṭit taiya lārmulait taṭampaṭuṅ kaṭaiyēṉ kūvu kākkaikkuc cōṟṟilōr porukkum koṭukka nērntiṭāk koṭiyaril koṭiyēṉ ōvu ṟātuḻal īeṉap palakāl ōṭi ōṭiyē tēṭuṟum toḻilēṉ cāvu ṟāvakaik keṉceyak kaṭavēṉ tantai yēeṉait tāṅkikkoṇ ṭaruḷē.
translation: I am the lowest of men, leaping like a deer and running to fall upon the breasts of women. I am the cruelest of the cruel, never managing to give even a single grain of rice to a cawing crow. My work is that of a relentlessly buzzing fly, running here and there, searching again and again. What must I do to become deathless? O Father, please support me and bestow your grace.
commentary: Vallalar confesses a life driven by craving: leaping after pleasure like a deer, searching endlessly like a buzzing fly, never giving even a grain of rice to a crow that calls for food. Refusing food to a hungry creature is named as the height of cruelty. From this place he asks one thing: what must he do to escape death? He asks the Father to hold him.

translit: pōka mātiyai viḻaintaṉaṉ vīṇil poḻutu pōkkiṭum iḻutaiyēṉ aḻiyāt tēka mātiyaip peṟamuyaṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ ciraṅku neñcakak kuraṅkoṭum uḻalvēṉ kāka mātikaḷ aruntaōr porukkum kāṭṭa nērntiṭāk kaṭaiyaril kaṭaiyēṉ āka māticol aṟivaṟi vēṉō appa ṉēeṉai āṇṭukoṇ ṭaruḷē.
translation: I am a worthless fool who desires sensual pleasures, wasting my time in vain. I have never tried to attain an immortal body. I struggle with a monkey of a mind, scabbed in its heart. I am the lowest of the low, never managing to offer even a single morsel for crows and other creatures to eat. How could I possibly know the wisdom spoken of in the Agamas? O Father, please accept me as your own and bestow grace.
commentary: This is a raw confession of feeling spiritually bankrupt. The speaker lists his failures: chasing pleasure, having a restless "monkey mind," and neglecting the core duty of compassion by not even feeding a crow. This failure in basic kindness, he says, makes him unworthy of understanding sacred texts like the Agamas (ancient scriptures). His only hope is to throw himself on God's mercy.

translit: viḻiyait tūrkkiṉṟa vañcarai viḻaintēṉ virunti lēuṇa varuntiōr vayiṟṟuk kuḻiyait tūrkkiṉṟa koṭiyaril koṭiyēṉ kōpa veyyaṉēṉ pāpamē payiṉṟēṉ vaḻiyait tūrppavark kuḷavurait tiṭuvēṉ māya mēpuri pēyaril periyēṉ paḻiyait tūrppataṟ keṉceyak kaṭavēṉ parama ṉēeṉaip parintukoṇ ṭaruḷē.
translation: I desired deceivers who block the eye of wisdom. I am the cruelest of the cruel, gorging on food at feasts just to fill the pit of my own stomach. I am fierce with anger; I have practiced only sin. I act as an informer for those who block the roads to rob. I am the greatest among ghouls who practice deception. What must I do to erase my blame? O Supreme One, take pity on me and bestow your grace.
commentary: The confession deepens from simple neglect to active wrongdoing. The speaker admits he has chosen bad company, even served robbers as their informer, and lived a life of selfishness and anger. By calling himself the "greatest among ghouls," he expresses a deep sense of self-disgust. This extreme self-condemnation is a way of emptying out all pride to make room for grace.

translit: matatti lēapi māṉaṅkoṇ ṭuḻalvēṉ vāṭṭa mēceyum kūṭṭattil payilvēṉ itatti lēoru vārttaiyum pukalēṉ īyum moyttiṭaṟ kicaivuṟā tuṇpēṉ kutatti lēiḻi malattiṉuṅ kaṭaiyēṉ kōṭai veyyaliṉ koṭumaiyiṟ koṭiyēṉ citatti lēuṟaṟ keṉceyak kaṭavēṉ teyva mēeṉaic cērttukkoṇ ṭaruḷē.
translation: I wander about, consumed with religious pride. I associate with company that causes only affliction. I never speak a single word that is beneficial. I eat without leaving even enough for flies to swarm. I am lower than the filth that descends from the anus. I am crueler than the severity of the summer sun. What must I do to attain union in pure consciousness? O God, please gather me to you and bestow your grace.
commentary: This verse names pride in religion (matam) as a bond: he wandered about attached to his religion and kept company that only caused affliction. Vallalar does not count such attachment as virtue; he lists it beside selfish eating and cruelty. His self-portrayal then becomes extreme: so selfish he leaves nothing even for flies, lower than filth itself. This doesn’t seem like self-hatred; it is more of a desperate attempt to become nothing so that God can grant union with pure consciousness (cit).

translit: koṭiya vempulik kuṇattiṉēṉ utavāk kūvam nērntuḷēṉ pāvamē payiṉṟēṉ kaṭiya neñciṉēṉ kuṅkumam cumanta kaḻutai yēṉavap poḻutaiyē kaḻippēṉ viṭiyu muṉṉarē eḻuntiṭā tuṟaṅkum vēṭa ṉēṉmuḻu mūṭaril periyēṉ aṭiya ṉāvataṟ keṉceyak kaṭavēṉ appa ṉēeṉai āṇṭukoṇ ṭaruḷē.
translation: I have the nature of a cruel, fierce tiger. I have become like a useless, stagnant well. I have practiced only sin. I am hard-hearted. I am a donkey carrying saffron, unaware of its value. I pass my time in utter futility. I am a hunter who sleeps without rising before dawn. I am the greatest among complete fools. What must I do to become your devotee? O Father, please accept me as your own and bestow grace.
commentary: Vallalar uses a string of powerful images to describe a life wasted. The speaker is like a donkey carrying precious saffron, completely unaware of the treasure it possesses; this is a metaphor for a human being who is ignorant of their own spiritual potential. He sees himself as predatory like a tiger, stagnant like a useless well, and a fool for sleeping through his chance at enlightenment during the auspicious time of Brahmamhurta.

translit: tūṅku kiṉṟatē cukameṉa aṟintēṉ cōṟa tēpeṟum pēṟateṉ ṟuṇarntēṉ ēṅku kiṉṟatē toḻileṉap piṭittēṉ irakkiṉ ṟōrkaḷē eṉṉiṉum avarpāl vāṅku kiṉṟatē poruḷeṉa valittēṉ vañca neñciṉāl pañceṉap paṟantēṉ ōṅku kiṉṟataṟ keṉceyak kaṭavēṉ uṭaiya vāeṉai uvantukoṇṭa ruḷē.
translation: I considered sleep itself to be pleasure; I felt that getting food was the greatest attainment. I adopted pining as my profession. Even from those who begged, I insisted on taking from them as my right. With a deceitful heart, I drifted about like cotton fluff. What can I do to become exalted? O my Master, joyfully accept me and grant your grace.
commentary: Here, the confession focuses on having completely wrong priorities. The speaker has lived as if sleep and food were the highest goals of life. He describes a state of deep moral corruption where he fails to give and even takes from those who beg. This portrait of a life spent drifting aimlessly, driven by deceit and base desires, shows a state of absolute spiritual poverty from which only divine grace can offer escape.

translit: varutta nērperum pāramē cumantu vāṭum ōrpoti māṭeṉa uḻaṉṟēṉ parutta ūṉoṭu malamuṇat tiriyum paṉṟi pōṉṟuḷēṉ naṉṟiyoṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ karutti lātayal kuraittalup paṭainta kaṭaiya nāyiṉiṟ kaṭaiyaṉēṉ aruṭkup poruttaṉ āvataṟ keṉceyak kaṭavēṉ puṇṇi yāeṉaip purintukoṇ ṭaruḷē.
translation: I struggled like a pack animal, withering under a great and sorrowful burden. I am like a fat-bodied pig that roams about eating filth; I know nothing of gratitude. I am lower than the lowest dog that barks senselessly at strangers and gets kicked for it. What can I do to become worthy of grace? O Virtuous One, understand my plight and grant your grace.
commentary: The speaker uses animal imagery to show how far he feels from a truly human, let alone divine, state. He has toiled like an overburdened mule, indulged in impurity like a pig, and acted with the senselessness of a barking dog that invites its own punishment. These images describe a life lived without purpose, gratitude, or wisdom, leading to the central question: how can one who feels so unworthy ever become worthy of grace?
