translit: turukka lōkoṭuṅ karuṅkalō vayirac cūḻka lōeṉak kāḻkoḷum maṉattēṉ tarukkal āṇavak karukkalō ṭuḻalvēṉ cantai nāyeṉap pantamuṟ ṟalaivēṉ tirukke lāmpeṟu verukkeṉappukuvēṉ tīya ṉēṉperum pēyaṉēṉ uḷantāṉ urukkal ākutaṟ keṉceyak kaṭavēṉ uṭaiya vāeṉai uvantukoṇ ṭaruḷē.
translation: My heart is hard, like slag iron, cruel black stone, or diamond-core rock. I wander in the dark gloom of pride and egoism. I roam entangled in bonds, like a marketplace dog. Full of every wile, I slink in like a wildcat. I am a wicked one, a great ghoul. What can I do to make this heart of mine melt? O my Master, joyfully accept me and grant your grace.
commentary: The greatest obstacle to spiritual life is a hard heart. The images of slag iron and diamond-core rock describe a state that is closed off to feeling, compassion, and God's grace. The plea to "make this heart of mine melt" is a prayer for the emotional and spiritual softening that must happen before any true connection with the divine is possible.

translit: kāṉa mēuḻal vilaṅkiṉiṟ kaṭaiyēṉ kāma mātikaḷ kaḷaikaṇiṟ piṭittēṉ māṉa mēliṭac cātiyē matamē vāḻkkai yēeṉa vārikkoṇ ṭalaintēṉ īṉa mēporuḷ eṉakkaḷit tiruntēṉ irakkam eṉpatōr eṭṭuṇai aṟiyēṉ ñāṉa mēvutaṟ keṉceyak kaṭavēṉ nāya kāeṉai nayantukoṇ ṭaruḷē.
translation: I am lower than the animals that roam the forest. I have taken lust and other passions as my only refuge. With pride swelling, I wandered, greedily embracing caste, religion, and worldly life as everything. I rejoiced, considering base things to be precious. I do not know even a sesame seed's worth of compassion. What can I do to attain wisdom? O my Lord, desire me and grant your grace.
commentary: Worldly attachments and social identities, such as caste and religion, are presented here as traps that prevent the attainment of wisdom. Vallalar makes a clear connection: this lack of true knowledge (jñānam, or wisdom) is directly caused by a lack of compassion. Without compassion, he suggests, genuine spiritual insight is impossible.

translit: iruḷai yēoḷi eṉamatit tiruntēṉ iccai yēperu viccaieṉ ṟalantēṉ maruḷai yētaru maṉakkuraṅ kōṭum vaṉame lāñcuḻaṉ ṟiṉameṉat tirintēṉ poruḷai nāṭunaṟ punticey taṟiyēṉ potuvi lēnaṭam purikiṉṟōy uṉṟaṉ aruḷai mēvutaṟ keṉceyak kaṭavēṉ appa ṉēeṉai āṇṭukoṇ ṭaruḷē.
translation: I considered darkness itself to be light. I languished, thinking desire was the greatest knowledge. With the mind-monkey that brings delusion, I wandered through all the forests as if it were my own tribe. I have never used my good intellect to seek the ultimate Reality. O You who perform the dance in the universal expanse! What can I do to attain Your grace? O Father, take me as your own and grant your grace.
commentary: The speaker confesses to living in a state of complete delusion, mistaking darkness for light and worldly desire for true knowledge. Using the classic image of the "mind-monkey" to describe the chaotic and untamed intellect, he shows how an undisciplined mind leads one astray. His plea for grace is a plea to see clearly and begin seeking the one true Reality.
NOTES
Note 199

tamil: வெருக்கு - பூனை. ககரமெய் விரிக்கும் வழி விரித்தல். முதற்பதிப்பு.
translit: verukku - pūṉai. kakaramey virikkum vaḻi virittal. mutaṟpatippu.
translation: verukku — cat. Extension of the consonant ka where extension is permitted. First edition.

translit: maruntaṟiyēṉ maṇiaṟiyēṉ mantiramoṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ matiaṟiyēṉ vitiaṟiyēṉ vāḻkkainilai aṟiyēṉ tiruntaṟiyēṉ tiruvaruḷiṉ ceyalaṟiyēṉ aṟantāṉ ceytaṟiyēṉ maṉamaṭaṅkum tiṟattiṉilōr iṭattē iruntaṟiyēṉ aṟintōrai ēttiṭavum aṟiyēṉ entaipirāṉ maṇimaṉṟam eytaaṟi vēṉō iruntaticai colaaṟiyēṉ eṅṅaṉamnāṉ pukuvēṉ yārkkuraippēṉ eṉṉaceyvēṉ ētumaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I do not know medicine, gems, or a single mantra; I do not know wisdom, fate, or the nature of life. I do not know how to be reformed or the workings of sacred grace; I have not practiced virtue. I have not sat in one place with the skill to quiet the mind; I do not even know how to praise those who know. Will I ever know how to reach the jeweled hall of my Father, the Lord? I cannot even say in which direction it is. How will I enter? To whom can I tell this? What can I do? I know nothing at all.
commentary: The speaker catalogs a state of total spiritual bankruptcy, admitting he knows none of the traditional tools for enlightenment. He lacks knowledge of sacred chants (mantra), right action (aṟam, or virtue), and meditation. He cannot even find the location of God's presence, the 'jeweled hall' (maṇimaṉṟam). This admission of "I know nothing" is the necessary starting point for a genuine spiritual search, where all pretense is finally dropped.

translit: akaṅkārak koṭuṅkiḻaṅkai akaḻnteṟiya aṟiyēṉ aṟivaṟinta antaṇarpāl ceṟiyumneṟi aṟiyēṉ nakaṅkāṉam uṟutavarpōl nalampurintum aṟiyēṉ naccumarak kaṉipōla iccaikaṉin tuḻalvēṉ makaṅkāṇum pulavarelām vantutoḻa naṭikkum maṇimaṉṟan taṉaiaṭaiyum vaḻiyumaṟi vēṉō ikaṅkāṇat tirikiṉṟēṉ eṅṅaṉamnāṉ pukuvēṉ yārkkuraippēṉ eṉṉaceyvēṉ ētumaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I do not know how to dig up and cast out the cruel root of ego; I do not know the way to draw near to the wise sages who have realized true knowledge. I have not done good like the ascetics who dwell on mountains and in forests; I wander with my desires ripened like the fruit of a poison tree. Will I ever know the path to the jeweled hall where He dances, worshipped by all the celestials who receive the sacrificial offerings? I wander about, seeing only this world. How will I enter? To whom can I tell this? What can I do? I know nothing at all.
commentary: The "cruel root of ego" is presented as the primary obstacle that he cannot remove on his own. Vallalar compares his desires to the fruit of a poison tree: attractive on the outside but deadly within. This powerful image captures the self-destructive nature of unmanaged desire. He feels trapped, seeing only the physical world, which makes the spiritual reality of the "jeweled hall" seem impossibly far away.

translit: kaṟkumuṟai kaṟṟaṟiyēṉ kaṟpaṉakaṟ ṟaṟinta karuttartiruk kūṭṭattil kaḷittirukka aṟiyēṉ niṟkunilai niṉṟaṟiyēṉ niṉṟāriṉ naṭittēṉ neṭuṅkāmap peruṅkaṭalai nīntumvakai aṟiyēṉ ciṟkuṇamā maṇimaṉṟil tirunaṭaṉam puriyum tiruvaṭieṉ ceṉṉimicaic cērkkaaṟi vēṉō iṟkuṇañcey tuḻalkiṉṟēṉ eṅṅaṉamnāṉ pukuvēṉ yārkkuraippēṉ eṉṉaceyvēṉ ētumaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I have not learned the proper way to learn; I do not know how to rejoice in the sacred company of those wise ones who have learned what must be learned. I have not stood in the true state; I only pretend to be like those who do. I do not know how to swim across the great ocean of immense desire. Will I ever know how to place upon my head the sacred feet that perform the holy dance in the jeweled hall of consciousness-nature? I wander about, engaged in worldly conduct. How will I enter? To whom can I tell this? What can I do? I know nothing at all.
commentary: Vallalar confesses to the painful feeling of being a spiritual impostor, of only pretending to be like the truly wise. The image of a "great ocean of immense desire" vividly portrays how overwhelming and endless his worldly attachments feel. Placing the deity's sacred feet on one's head is a traditional sign of complete surrender and receiving grace, a blessing he feels utterly unworthy of.

translit: tēkamuṟu pūtanilait tiṟamciṟitum aṟiyēṉ cittānta nilaiaṟiyēṉ cittanilaiaṟiyēṉ yōkamuṟu nilaiciṟitum uṇarntaṟiyēṉ ciṟiyēṉ ulakanaṭai yiṭaikkiṭantē uḻaippāril kaṭaiyēṉ ākamuṟu tirunīṟṟiṉ oḷiviḷaṅka acaintē ampalattil āṭukiṉṟa aṭiyaiaṟi vēṉō ēkaaṉu pavamaṟiyēṉ eṅṅaṉamnāṉ pukuvēṉ yārkkuraippēṉ eṉṉaceyvēṉ ētumaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I do not know in the slightest the nature of the elements that constitute the body; I do not know the state of Siddhanta, nor do I know the state of the Siddhas. I have not experienced even a little of the state of Yoga. I am a small man, and among those who toil in worldly ways, I am the very last. Will I ever know the feet that dance in the hall, swaying, while the light of the sacred ash on His body shines forth? I do not know the experience of Oneness. How will I enter? To whom can I tell this? What can I do? I know nothing at all.
commentary: The confession of ignorance now extends to formal paths and philosophies. He admits to not knowing Siddhanta (the established doctrines), the states of Siddhas (perfected masters), or Yoga (the path of union). This is an admission of his own failure to master them, not a rejection of these paths. He feels like the most wretched person caught in worldly struggle, completely cut off from the experience of Oneness with the divine, symbolized by the sacred dance in the ampalam (hall of consciousness).

translit: vētānta nilaināṭi viraintumuyaṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ meyvakaiyum kaivakaiyum ceyvakaiyum aṟiyēṉ nātāntat tiruvīti naṭantiṭutaṟ kaṟiyēṉ nāṉāreṉ ṟaṟiyēṉeṅ kōṉāreṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ pōtāntat tirunāṭu pukaaṟiyēṉ ñāṉa pūraṇā kāyameṉum potuvaiaṟi vēṉō ētāntī yēṉcaritam eṅṅaṉamnāṉ pukuvēṉ yārkkuraippēṉ eṉṉaceyvēṉ ētumaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I have not striven diligently, seeking the state of Vedanta; I do not know the nature of truth, the practical methods, or the way to perform them. I do not know how to walk the sacred street of Nadanta; I do not know who I am, nor do I know who my King is. I do not know how to enter the sacred land of Bodhanta, will I ever know the Common Space known as the perfect expanse of wisdom-sky? With a history like this, how can I, a sinner, enter? To whom can I tell this? What can I do? I know nothing at all.
commentary: This verse brings the appeal to its climax. He admits to not knowing the highest philosophical states like Vedanta (the culmination of Vedic wisdom), Nadanta (the state beyond subtle sound), or Bodhanta (the state beyond intellect). The most devastating confession is the simplest: "I do not know who I am, nor do I know who my King is." This is the core question of all spiritual seeking, and without its answer, he feels entirely lost.

translit: kalaimuṭivu kaṇṭaṟiyēṉ karaṇamelām aṭakkum katiaṟiyēṉ katiaṟinta karuttarkaḷai aṟiyēṉ kolaipulaikaḷ viṭuttaṟiyēṉ kōpamaṟut taṟiyēṉ koṭuṅkāmak kaṭalkaṭakkum kuṟippaṟiyēṉ kuṇamām malaimicainiṉ ṟiṭaaṟiyēṉ ñāṉanaṭam puriyum maṇimaṉṟan taṉaiaṭaiyum vaḻiyumaṟi vēṉō ilaieṉumpoy ulakiṉiṭai eṅṅaṉamnāṉ pukuvēṉ yārkkuraippēṉ eṉṉaceyvēṉ ētumaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I do not know the culmination of the arts. I do not know the state in which all inner faculties are subdued. I do not know the masters who know that state. I have not abandoned killing and meat-eating. I have not cut off anger. I do not know the way to cross the ocean of cruel lust. I do not know how to stand upon the mountain of good character. So will I ever know the path to reach the jeweled hall where the dance of wisdom is performed? How can I enter this false world that is ultimately nothing? To whom can I speak? What can I do? I know nothing at all.
commentary: Here the focus shifts from what the speaker does not know to what he has not done. He has not given up killing and eating flesh (kolai, pulai); he has not cut off anger; he cannot cross the sea of cruel lust. Vallalar names killing and flesh-eating first, because no one reaches the jeweled hall of the dance of wisdom while holding to them.

translit: cātimatam camayameṉum caṅkaṭamviṭ ṭaṟiyēṉ cāttiraccē ṟāṭukiṉṟa cañcalamviṭ ṭaṟiyēṉ ātianta nilaiyaṟiyēṉ alaiaṟiyāk kaṭalpōl āṉantap perumpōkat tamarntiṭavum aṟiyēṉ nītineṟi naṭantaṟiyēṉ cōtimaṇip potuvil niruttamiṭum oruttartiruk karuttaiaṟi vēṉō ētilarcār ulakiṉiṭai eṅṅaṉamnāṉ pukuvēṉ yārkkuraippēṉ eṉṉaceyvēṉ ētumaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I have not abandoned the affliction of caste, organized religion, and creed. I have not abandoned the agitation of wading in the mire of scriptures. I do not know the state of the beginning and the end. I do not know how to abide in the great bliss of delight, like a waveless sea. I have not walked the path of justice. So will I ever know the holy intention of the One who dances in the common space of the gem of light? How can I enter this world that sides with those who are alien to the path? To whom can I speak? What can I do? I know nothing at all.
commentary: Vallalar names caste, religion and sect (cāti, matam, camayam) as afflictions, and the shastras themselves as a mire in which people wade in agitation. He has not yet left them to rest in bliss like a waveless sea. The dance takes place in the common space open to all, and these very structures are what keep people from it.

translit: cākāta talaiaṟiyēṉ vēkāta kāliṉ taramaṟiyēṉ pōkāta taṇrai aṟiyēṉ ākāya nilaiaṟiyēṉ mākāya nilaiyum aṟiyēṉmeyn neṟitaṉaiōr aṇuaḷavum aṟiyēṉ mākāta luṭaiyaperun tiruvāḷar vaḻuttum maṇimaṉṟan taṉaiaṭaiyum vaḻiyumaṟi vēṉō ēkāya ulakiṉiṭai eṅṅaṉamnāṉ pukuvēṉ yārkkuraippēṉ eṉṉaceyvēṉ ētumaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I do not know the deathless head. I do not know the quality of the un-burning air. I do not know the undiminishing cool water. I do not know the state of space, nor do I know the state of the great body. I do not know even an atom's worth of the true path. So will I ever know the path to reach the jeweled hall, praised by the greatly blessed ones who possess immense love? How can I enter this selfish world? To whom can I speak? What can I do? I know nothing at all.
commentary: Vallalar names the attainments of the deathless body: the head that does not die (cākāta talai), the breath that does not burn (vēkāta kāl), and the cool water that does not drain away (pōkāta taṇṇīr), with the states of space and of the great body. While These may be considered as symbols, they are more the marks of the body that does not die, which Vallalar sought and attained. By confessing that he knows nothing of them, not even an atom of the true path, he measures the distance between himself and those who praise the jeweled hall.

translit: tattuvameṉ vacamākat tāṉcelutta aṟiyēṉ cākāta kalvikaṟkum tarañciṟitum aṟiyēṉ attanilai cattanilai aṟiyēṉmey aṟivai aṟiyēṉmey aṟintaṭaṅkum aṟiñaraiyum aṟiyēṉ cuttaciva caṉmārkkat tiruppotuvi ṉiṭattē tūyanaṭam purikiṉṟa ñāyamaṟi vēṉō ettuṇaiyum kuṇamaṟiyēṉ eṅṅaṉamnāṉ pukuvēṉ yārkkuraippēṉ eṉṉaceyvēṉ ētumaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I do not know how to control the tattvas and make them my own. I do not know in the slightest the way to learn the deathless art. I do not know the state of meaning or the state of sound. I do not know true wisdom. I do not know the wise ones who, knowing the truth, become still. So will I ever know the principle of the One performing the pure dance in the holy common space of Suddha Siva Sanmarkkam? I have no good qualities whatsoever. How can I enter? To whom can I speak? What can I do? I know nothing at all.
commentary: The lament deepens, focusing on the speaker's failure in yogic and philosophical practice. He confesses he cannot control the tattvas (the fundamental principles of reality) or learn the "deathless art" of immortality. He feels unqualified to even understand the core of Suddha Siva Sanmarkkam (the True Path of Pure Auspiciousness), concluding with the devastating self-assessment that he has no good qualities at all.

translit: varaiapara mārkkamoṭu paramārkkam aṟiyēṉ maraṇapayam tavirttiṭuñcaṉ mārkkamatai aṟiyēṉ tiraiyaṟutaṇ kaṭalaṟiyēṉ akkaṭalaik kaṭaintē teḷḷamutam uṇavaṟiyēṉ ciṉamaṭakka aṟiyēṉ uraiuṇarvu kaṭantatiru maṇimaṉṟan taṉilē orumainaṭam purikiṉṟār perumaiaṟi vēṉō iraiyuṟupoy ulakiṉiṭai eṅṅaṉamnāṉ pukuvēṉ yārkkuraippēṉ eṉṉaceyvēṉ ētumaṟin tilaṉē.
translation: I do not know the lower paths from the higher path. I do not know the Sanmarkkam that averts the fear of death. I do not know the cool, waveless ocean. I do not know how to churn that ocean and consume the clear ambrosia. I do not know how to subdue anger. So will I ever know the greatness of the One who performs the dance of Oneness in the holy jeweled hall that is beyond speech and feeling? How can I enter this predatory, false world? To whom can I speak? What can I do? I know nothing at all.
commentary: This verse summarizes the speaker's sense of failure. He lacks basic spiritual discernment, cannot grasp the Sanmarkkam path that promises to end the fear of death, and has not had the inner experience of bliss, which he compares to churning the ocean for ambrosia. Feeling that he cannot even master a basic virtue like controlling anger, he ends in a state of near total despair.
NOTES
Note 200

translit: ēkam - mutti, īṟutokku niṉṟatu, mutaṟ patippu.
translation: ēkam: mutti (liberation); the case ending stands elided. First edition.

tamil: அடியார் வருத்தம் தனைக்கண்டு தரியார் இன்பம் அளித்திடுவார்
வடியாக் கருணைப் பெருங்கடலார் என்ற பெரியர் வார்த்தைஎலாம்
நெடியார்க் கரியாய் கொடியேன்என் ஒருவன் தனையும் நீக்கியதோ
கடியாக் கொடுமா பாதகன்முன் கண்ட பரிசுங் கண்டிலனே.
translit: aṭiyār varuttam taṉaikkaṇṭu tariyār iṉpam aḷittiṭuvār vaṭiyāk karuṇaip peruṅkaṭalār eṉṟa periyar vārttaielām neṭiyārk kariyāy koṭiyēṉeṉ oruvaṉ taṉaiyum nīkkiyatō kaṭiyāk koṭumā pātakaṉmuṉ kaṇṭa paricuṅ kaṇṭilaṉē.
translation: The great ones all say that you cannot bear to see the suffering of your devotees and grant them bliss, that you are a vast ocean of compassion that never ebbs. O You who are beyond the reach of Vishnu, have those words left out only me, this wretched one? I have not received even the grace that the cruel great sinner received of old.
commentary: The devotee begins by recalling what everyone says about God: that he is an "ocean of compassion that never ebbs" who cannot stand to see his followers suffer. He then asks, with a feeling of painful exclusion, why he alone seems to be the exception to this rule. It is a cry from someone who feels he is the one sinner left behind.

tamil: பையார் பாம்பு கொடியதெனப் பகர்வார் அதற்கும் பரிந்துமுன்னாள்
ஐயா கருணை அளித்தனைஎன் அளவில் இன்னும் அளித்திலையே
மையார் மிடற்றோய் ஆனந்த மன்றில் நடிப்போய் வல்வினையேன்
நையா நின்றேன் ஐயோநான் பாம்பிற் கொடியன் ஆனேனே.
translit: paiyār pāmpu koṭiyateṉap pakarvār ataṟkum parintumuṉṉāḷ aiyā karuṇai aḷittaṉaieṉ aḷavil iṉṉum aḷittilaiyē maiyār miṭaṟṟōy āṉanta maṉṟil naṭippōy valviṉaiyēṉ naiyā niṉṟēṉ aiyōnāṉ pāmpiṟ koṭiyaṉ āṉēṉē.
translation: People say the hooded snake is cruel, but long ago, O Lord, out of sympathy you bestowed grace even upon it. In my case, however, you still have not granted it. O You with the dark-stained throat, You who dance in the hall of bliss! I, a man of harsh karma, am wasting away. Alas, I have become more cruel than a snake!
commentary: To emphasize his feeling of unworthiness, the devotee compares himself to a venomous snake (probably refers to some story or tale). He notes that God, in his compassion, showed grace even to such a creature, yet withholds it from him. This leads to the painful conclusion that his own inner failings must make him "more cruel than a snake" in God's eyes. The reference to God's "dark-stained throat," a mark left from Siva swallowing poison to save the world, makes this withholding of compassion feel even more pointed.

tamil: பீழை புரிவான் வருந்துகின்ற பேய்க்கும் கருணை பெரிதளிப்பான்
ஊழை அகற்றும் பெருங்கருணை உடையான் என்பார் உனைஐயோ
மோழை மனத்தால் குரங்கெறிந்த விளங்கா யாகி மொத்துண்ணும்
ஏழை அடியேன் வருத்தங்கண் டிருத்தல் அழகோ எங்கோவே.
translit: pīḻai purivāṉ varuntukiṉṟa pēykkum karuṇai peritaḷippāṉ ūḻai akaṟṟum peruṅkaruṇai uṭaiyāṉ eṉpār uṉaiaiyō mōḻai maṉattāl kuraṅkeṟinta viḷaṅkā yāki mottuṇṇum ēḻai aṭiyēṉ varuttaṅkaṇ ṭiruttal aḻakō eṅkōvē.
translation: They say you are one who bestows great compassion even on the suffering demon who causes affliction; they call you the one of great compassion who removes karma. Alas! Is it fitting, O my King, for you to just watch the suffering of this poor devotee, who, with a worthless mind, is being battered like an unripe wood-apple struck by a monkey?
commentary: God is said to show compassion even to destructive demons, yet seems to ignore Vallalar's suffering. He compares himself to an unripe fruit being mindlessly battered by a monkey, a powerful image of feeling helpless and tormented while God simply watches. This feeling of being seen but not helped is the source of his anguish.

tamil: மருணா டுலகில் கொலைபுரிவார் மனமே கரையாக் கல்என்று
பொருணா டியநின் திருவாக்கே புகல அறிந்தேன் என்னளவில்
கருணா நிதிநின் திருவுளமுங் கல்என் றுரைக்க அறிந்திலனே
இருணா டியஇச் சிறியேனுக் கின்னும் இரங்கா திருந்தாயே.
translit: maruṇā ṭulakil kolaipurivār maṉamē karaiyāk kaleṉṟu poruṇā ṭiyaniṉ tiruvākkē pukala aṟintēṉ eṉṉaḷavil karuṇā nitiniṉ tiruvuḷamuṅ kaleṉ ṟuraikka aṟintilaṉē iruṇā ṭiya:ic ciṟiyēṉuk kiṉṉum iraṅkā tiruntāyē.
translation: From your own sacred words, which seek the true meaning of things, I learned it proclaimed that the minds of those who commit murder in this world of delusion are like unmelting stone. But I never knew I would have to say that your divine will, O treasury of compassion, is also stone. You still remain without taking pity on this lowly one, steeped in darkness.
commentary: In a moment of deep pain, Vallalar turns God's own teaching back on him. He knows the scriptures say a murderer's heart is like stone. But now, as he suffers without any sign of grace, he feels forced to say that God's own heart has become stone. It is a shocking reversal where the devotee challenges the "treasury of compassion" for being so silent.

tamil: முன்னுங் கொடுமை பலபுரிந்து முடுகிப் பின்னுங் கொடுமைசெய
உன்னுங் கொடியர் தமக்கும்அருள் உதவுங் கருணை உடையானே
மன்னும் பதமே துணைஎன்று மதித்து வருந்தும் சிறியேனுக்
கின்னுங் கருணை புரிந்திலைநான் என்ன கொடுமை செய்தேனோ.
translit: muṉṉuṅ koṭumai palapurintu muṭukip piṉṉuṅ koṭumaiceya uṉṉuṅ koṭiyar tamakkumaruḷ utavuṅ karuṇai uṭaiyāṉē maṉṉum patamē tuṇaieṉṟu matittu varuntum ciṟiyēṉuk kiṉṉuṅ karuṇai purintilaināṉ eṉṉa koṭumai ceytēṉō.
translation: O You who possess the compassion to grant grace even to those cruel people who, having committed many cruelties before, hasten to commit even more! You have still not shown compassion to this lowly one, who suffers, considering your eternal feet my only support. What cruelty could I have possibly done?
commentary: Vallalar is bewildered by a perceived divine injustice. God is known to show mercy even to those who are deliberately and repeatedly cruel. Yet Vallalar, who has placed all his trust in God's feet as his only refuge, receives nothing. He is left to ask the most painful question of all: "What could I have possibly done to deserve this?"

tamil: அங்கே அடியர் தமக்கெல்லாம் அருளார் அமுதம் அளித்தையோ
இங்கே சிறியேன் ஒருவனுக்கும் இடர்தான் அளிக்க இசைந்தாயேல்
எங்கே புகுவேன் என்செய்வேன் எவர்என் முகம்பார்த் திடுவாரே.
translit: aṅkē aṭiyar tamakkellām aruḷār amutam aḷittaiyō iṅkē ciṟiyēṉ oruvaṉukkum iṭartāṉ aḷikka icaintāyēl ceṅkēḻ itaḻic caṭaikkaṉiyēcivamē aṭimaic ciṟunāyēṉ eṅkē pukuvēṉ eṉceyvēṉ evareṉ mukampārt tiṭuvārē.
translation: There, you gave grace-filled nectar to all your devotees. Here, you have consented to give only hardship to me, this insignificant one. O ripe Fruit on the matted hair adorned with golden konrai flowers! O Sivam! I am just a small dog of a slave. Where can I go for refuge? What can I do? Who will look upon my face?
commentary: This is a cry from the depths of abandonment. While other devotees receive the nectar of grace, Vallalar feels he has been singled out to receive only hardship. Calling himself a "small dog of a slave," a term of extreme humility, he asks where he can possibly go now. If even the ultimate source of grace, Sivam (The Auspicious One), has turned away, who is left to even look upon his face? It is the sound of absolute desolation.

tamil: அளியே அன்பர் அன்பேநல் லமுதே சுத்த அறிவான
வெளியே வெளியில் இன்பநடம் புரியும் அரசே விதிஒன்றும்
தெளியேன் தீங்கு பிறர்செயினும் தீங்கு நினையாத் திருவுளந்தான்
எளியேன் அளவில் நினைக்கஒருப் படுமோ கருணை எந்தாயே.
translit: aḷiyē aṉpar aṉpēnal lamutē cutta aṟivāṉa veḷiyē veḷiyil iṉpanaṭam puriyum aracē vitioṉṟum teḷiyēṉ tīṅku piṟarceyiṉum tīṅku niṉaiyāt tiruvuḷantāṉ eḷiyēṉ aḷavil niṉaikkaorup paṭumō karuṇai entāyē.
translation: O my Love! O Love of your devotees! O good nectar! O King who performs the dance of bliss in the expanse of pure consciousness! I do not understand fate's decree at all. Your sacred mind does not contemplate harm even when others inflict it. Will that mind, then, consent to think of harming me, a helpless man? O my compassionate Father!
commentary: The speaker appeals to God's essential nature as pure love and consciousness, which is incapable of even thinking of harm. The argument is simple: if your very being is compassion, how could you ever consent to make me, a helpless person, suffer? It is a logical and emotional appeal, questioning how an all-good being could be the source of his pain.

tamil: தீது நினைக்கும் பாவிகட்கும் செய்தாய் கருணை எனத்தெளிந்து
வாது நினைக்கும் மனக்கடையேன் மகிழ்வுற் றிருந்தேன் என்னளவில்
சூது நினைப்பாய் எனில்யார்க்குச் சொல்வேன் யாரைத் துணைகொள்வேன்
ஏது நினைப்பேன் ஐயோநான் பாவி உடம்பேன் எடுத்தேனே.
translit: tītu niṉaikkum pāvikaṭkum ceytāy karuṇai eṉatteḷintu vātu niṉaikkum maṉakkaṭaiyēṉ makiḻvuṟ ṟiruntēṉ eṉṉaḷavil cūtu niṉaippāy eṉilyārkkuc colvēṉ yārait tuṇaikoḷvēṉ ētu niṉaippēṉ aiyōnāṉ pāvi uṭampēṉ eṭuttēṉē.
translation: Realizing that you showed compassion even to sinners who think evil thoughts, I, the lowliest of beings with a contentious mind, was filled with joy. If you now intend deceit in my case, to whom will I speak? Whom will I take as my support? What will I think? Alas, why did I, a sinner, take on this body?
commentary: A fragile hope, built on seeing God's mercy to sinners, has now shattered into a feeling of betrayal. The speaker worries that God might be intentionally deceptive, turning the promise of grace into a cruel game. This fear plunges the devotee into a crisis, questioning the very purpose of his life and embodiment in the face of what feels like divine deceit.

tamil: பொதுவென் றறிந்தும் இரங்காத சிலர்க்கும் கருணை புரிவதன்றிக்
கழுதுவென் றழுங்க நினையாநின் கருணை உளந்தான் அறிவென்ப
திதுவென் றறியா எனைவருத்த எந்த வகையால் துணிந்ததுவோ
எதுவென் றறிவேன் என்புரிவேன் ஐயோ புழுவில் இழிந்தேனே.
translit: potuveṉ ṟaṟintum iraṅkāta cilarkkum karuṇai purivataṉṟik kaḻutuveṉ ṟaḻuṅka niṉaiyāniṉ karuṇai uḷantāṉ aṟiveṉpa tituveṉ ṟaṟiyā eṉaivarutta enta vakaiyāl tuṇintatuvō etuveṉ ṟaṟivēṉ eṉpurivēṉ aiyō puḻuvil iḻintēṉē.
translation: Your compassionate mind shows mercy even to those who, knowing you are impartial, show no pity; it does not even think of making a demon shrink in fear. By what means, then, did it resolve to torment me, who does not even know what knowledge is? What am I to know? What am I to do? Alas, I have become lower than a worm.
commentary: The speaker's self-worth collapses, feeling "lower than a worm." He reasons that God's compassion is so vast it extends even to those without pity, so there is no logical reason for it to fail him. The suffering feels like a violation of the divine character itself, leaving the speaker bewildered and without recourse.

tamil: வெடிக்கப் பார்த்து நிற்கின்ற வெய்யர் தமையும் வினைத்துயர்கள்
பிடிக்கப் பார்க்கத் துணியாத பெருமான் நினது திருவுளந்தான்
நடிக்கப் பார்க்கும் உலகத்தே சிறியேன் மனது நவையாலே
துடிக்கப் பார்த்திங் கிருந்ததுகாண் ஐயோ இதற்குந் துணிந்ததுவோ.
translit: veṭikkap pārttu niṟkiṉṟa veyyar tamaiyum viṉaittuyarkaḷ piṭikkap pārkkat tuṇiyāta perumāṉ niṉatu tiruvuḷantāṉ naṭikkap pārkkum ulakattē ciṟiyēṉ maṉatu navaiyālē tuṭikkap pārttiṅ kiruntatukāṇ aiyō itaṟkun tuṇintatuvō.
translation: O Great One, who would not dare to let the sorrows of karma seize even the cruel who stand by, waiting to watch things shatter! In this world that watches a performance, your sacred mind has stood here and watched my lowly mind writhe in agony from its flaws. Look! Alas, did it dare to do this too?
commentary: This verse uses a powerful image: God, who protects even the wicked from their karma, seems to stand by and watch the speaker's mind "writhe in agony." The devotee feels as if his suffering is a spectacle for a detached divine audience. This is the ultimate cry of abandonment, expressing shock that the source of all compassion could witness such pain and do nothing.

tamil: கல்லுங் கனியத் திருநோக்கம் புரியும் கருணைக் கடலேநான்
அல்லும் பகலுந் திருக்குறிப்பை எதிர்பார்த் திங்கே அயர்கின்றேன்
கொல்லுங் கொடியார்க் குதவுகின்ற குறும்புத் தேவர் மனம்போலச்
சொல்லும் இரங்கா வன்மைகற்க எங்கே ஐயோ துணிந்தாயோ.
translit: kalluṅ kaṉiyat tirunōkkam puriyum karuṇaik kaṭalēnāṉ allum pakalun tirukkuṟippai etirpārt tiṅkē ayarkiṉṟēṉ kolluṅ koṭiyārk kutavukiṉṟa kuṟumput tēvar maṉampōlac collum iraṅkā vaṉmaikaṟka eṅkē aiyō tuṇintāyō.
translation: O Ocean of Grace, whose blessed gaze makes even stone soften, I wait here day and night for your holy sign, growing weary. Alas, where have you decided to learn such pitiless hardness, like the hearts of mischievous gods who help cruel killers?
commentary: Vallalar's appeal grows more intense as he directly challenges God's nature. He contrasts God's legendary power to melt stone with his current hard-heartedness. By asking where God learned to be so pitiless, he implies that this behavior is unnatural for the divine. This is the language of deep intimacy, where the devotee can question God with the raw honesty of a broken heart.

tamil: படிமேல் ஆசை பலவைத்துப் பணியும் அவர்க்கும் பரிந்துசுகக்
கொடிமேல் உறச்செய் தருள்கின்றாய் என்பால் இரக்கங் கொண்டிலையே
பொடிமேல் அணிநின் அருட்கிதுதான் அழகோ பொதுவில் நடிக்கும்உன்றன்
அடிமேல் அசை அல்லால்வே றாசை ஐயோ அறியேனே.
translit: paṭimēl ācai palavaittup paṇiyum avarkkum parintucukak koṭimēl uṟaccey taruḷkiṉṟāy eṉpāl irakkaṅ koṇṭilaiyē poṭimēl aṇiniṉ aruṭkitutāṉ aḻakō potuvil naṭikkumuṉṟaṉ aṭimēl acai allālvē ṟācai aiyō aṟiyēṉē.
translation: You show compassion even to those who bow to you with many worldly desires, graciously causing them to flourish like a banner on high. Yet you have had no pity on me. You who wear sacred ash, is this becoming of your grace? You who dance in the common space, alas, I know no desire other than the desire for your feet.
commentary: This verse highlights a feeling of unfairness. God grants blessings even to those whose devotion is mixed with selfish material desires, yet seems to ignore Vallalar, who wants nothing but God. He appeals to God's own honor, asking if it is right for such perfect grace to be withheld from a soul whose only desire is for the divine.

tamil: நாயேன் உலகில் அறிவுவந்த நாள்தொட் டிந்த நாள்வரையும்
ஏயேன் பிறிதி லுன்குறிப்பே எதிர்பார்த் திருந்தேன் என்னுடைய
தாயே பொதுவில் நடம்புரிஎந் தாயே தயவு தாராயேல்
மாயேன் ஐயோ எதுகொண்டு வாழ்ந்திங் கிருக்கத் துணிவேனே.
translit: nāyēṉ ulakil aṟivuvanta nāḷtoṭ ṭinta nāḷvaraiyum ēyēṉ piṟiti luṉkuṟippē etirpārt tiruntēṉ eṉṉuṭaiya tāyē potuvil naṭampurien tāyē tayavu tārāyēl māyēṉ aiyō etukoṇṭu vāḻntiṅ kirukkat tuṇivēṉē.
translation: I, this dog, from the day I gained awareness in this world until this very day, have done nothing else but wait, expecting your sign. My Mother! My Father who performs the dance in the common space! If you do not grant your compassion, I will not perish. Alas, with what support could I then resolve to go on living here?
commentary: The plea becomes a raw, personal witness. Vallalar states that his entire conscious life has been spent waiting for a sign of grace. The line "I will not perish" is a cry of despair. Living on without God's compassion would be a fate worse than death, an empty survival devoid of meaning.

tamil: நயத்தால் உனது திருவருளை நண்ணாக் கொடியேன் நாய் உடம்பை
உயத்தான் வையேன் மடித்திடுவேன் மடித்தாற் பின்னர் உலகத்தே
வயத்தால் எந்த உடம்புறுமோ என்ன வருமோ என்கின்ற
பயத்தால் ஐயோ இவ்வுடம்பைச் சுமக்கின் றேன்எம் பரஞ்சுடரே.
translit: nayattāl uṉatu tiruvaruḷai naṇṇāk koṭiyēṉ nāy uṭampai uyattāṉ vaiyēṉ maṭittiṭuvēṉ maṭittāṟ piṉṉar ulakattē vayattāl enta uṭampuṟumō eṉṉa varumō eṉkiṉṟa payattāl aiyō ivvuṭampaic cumakkiṉ ṟēṉem parañcuṭarē.
translation: I, the wicked one who has not obtained your sacred grace through loving devotion, would not keep this dog's body alive; I would destroy it. But then, in this world, by the force of karma, I fear what body I might get and what might befall me. It is because of this fear, alas, that I continue to bear this body, O my Supreme Flame.
commentary: Vallalar explains why he doesn't end his own life, despite his agony. He is not afraid of death itself but of karma, the force that determines future births. He fears that by dying now, he might be reborn in a form or situation even more distant from God. Perhaps as animal or other lower body forms. His current suffering is something he endures only because the alternative might be spiritually worse. Suicide is not the solution, but the worsening of the problem. By losing the precious human body, one can no longer help other beings, so it’s considered a sin and not rewarded, no matter how much pain a jeevan is going through.

tamil: இன்ப மடுத்துன் அடியர்எலாம் இழியா தேறி யிருக்கின்றார்
வன்ப ரிடத்தே பலகாற்சென் றவரோ டுறவு வழங்கிஉன்றன்
அன்பர் உறவை விடுத்துலகில் ஆடிப் பாடி அடுத்தவினைத்
துன்ப முடுகிச் சுடச்சுடவுஞ் சோறுண் டிருக்கத் துணிந்தேனே.
translit: iṉpa maṭuttuṉ aṭiyarelām iḻiyā tēṟi yirukkiṉṟār vaṉpa riṭattē palakāṟceṉ ṟavarō ṭuṟavu vaḻaṅkiuṉṟaṉ aṉpar uṟavai viṭuttulakil āṭip pāṭi aṭuttaviṉait tuṉpa muṭukic cuṭaccuṭavuñ cōṟuṇ ṭirukkat tuṇintēṉē.
translation: All your devotees, drawing near to bliss, are ascending without falling back. But I went many times to hard-hearted people, cultivating relationships with them and abandoning the company of your true lovers. I danced and sang in the world, and even as the suffering of my accumulated karma rushes to burn me again and again, I have resolved to just keep eating my food and stay here.
commentary: He contrasts his own spiritual stagnation with the progress of other devotees. While they ascend toward bliss, he feels he made the wrong choices, seeking out worldly company instead of the companionship of God's lovers. Now, even as the painful consequences of his past actions burn him, he finds himself in a state of weary resignation, just mechanically eating and existing without spiritual joy. It is a stark admission of feeling left behind.

tamil: எந்நாள் கருணைத் தனிமுதல்நீ என்பால் இரங்கி அருளுதலோ
அந்நாள் இந்நாள் இந்நாள்என் றெண்ணி எண்ணி அலமந்தேன்
சென்னாள் களில்ஓர் நன்னாளுந் திருநா ளான திலைஐயோ
முன்னாள் என்னை ஆட்கொண்டாய் என்ன நாணம் முடுகுவதே.
translit: ennāḷ karuṇait taṉimutalnī eṉpāl iraṅki aruḷutalō annāḷ innāḷ innāḷeṉ ṟeṇṇi eṇṇi alamantēṉ ceṉṉāḷ kaḷilōr naṉṉāḷun tirunā ḷāṉa tilaiaiyō muṉṉāḷ eṉṉai āṭkoṇṭāy eṉṉa nāṇam muṭukuvatē.
translation: Thinking, "That day is today, today," I have suffered endlessly, wondering when you, the singular source of compassion, will take pity and bestow your grace on me. Alas, among the days that have passed, not one good day became that sacred day. You took me as your own long ago; why this reluctance now?
commentary: The pain of waiting is the central theme here. Every single day, Vallalar has hoped for the arrival of God's grace, only to be disappointed. This longing is made more acute by his memory of a past moment when he felt accepted by God. He is asking a question familiar to anyone who has felt a spiritual connection that later seems to fade: "You claimed me once; why do you hesitate now?" This is perhaps a compassionate trick of the divine, further increasing the desire for union of the devotee by its felt, apparent absence.

tamil: எந்த வகைசெய் திடிற்கருணை எந்தாய் நீதான் இரங்குவையோ
அந்த வகையை நான்அறியேன் அறிவிப் பாரும் எனக்கில்லை
இந்த வகைஇங் கையோநான் இருந்தால் பின்னர் என்செய்வேன்
பந்த வகைஅற் றவர்உளத்தே நடிக்கும் உண்மைப் பரம்பொருளே203.
translit: enta vakaicey tiṭiṟkaruṇai entāy nītāṉ iraṅkuvaiyō anta vakaiyai nāṉaṟiyēṉ aṟivip pārum eṉakkillai inta vakaiiṅ kaiyōnāṉ iruntāl piṉṉar eṉceyvēṉ panta vakaiaṟ ṟavaruḷattē naṭikkum uṇmaip paramporuḷē.
translation: O true Supreme Being, who dances in the hearts of those free from all kinds of attachments! I do not know what I must do for you, my compassionate Father, to take pity on me, and there is no one to inform me. If I remain here in this state, alas, what will I do then?
commentary: This is a cry of desperate confusion. Vallalar knows that God dwells in the hearts of those who are free from worldly attachments, but he feels he has not reached that state. More painfully, he feels he has no map and no guide; he simply does not know what specific actions or inner changes are needed to win God's favor. It is the lament of someone who is willing to do the work but does not know what the work is.

tamil: அடுக்குந் தொண்டர் தமக்கெல்லாம் அருளீந் திங்கே என்னளவில்
கொடுக்குந் தன்மை தனைஒளித்தால் ஒளிக்கப் படுமோ குணக்குன்றே
தடுக்குந் தடையும் வேறில்லை தமியேன் தனைஇத் தாழ்வகற்றி
எடுக்குந் துணையும் பிறிதில்லை ஐயோ இன்னும் இரங்கிலையே.
translit: aṭukkun toṇṭar tamakkellām aruḷīn tiṅkē eṉṉaḷavil koṭukkun taṉmai taṉaioḷittāl oḷikkap paṭumō kuṇakkuṉṟē taṭukkun taṭaiyum vēṟillai tamiyēṉ taṉaiit tāḻvakaṟṟi eṭukkun tuṇaiyum piṟitillai aiyō iṉṉum iraṅkilaiyē.
translation: O mountain of virtue, you have bestowed grace upon all worthy devotees. In my case, if you try to hide your nature of giving, can it truly be hidden? There is no other obstacle stopping you, and to lift this lonely one from this abject state, there is no other support. Alas, you still have not taken pity.
commentary: Vallalar makes a final, intimate appeal based on God's own character. He argues that God's fundamental nature is to be a "mountain of virtue" whose essence is to give grace. Trying to conceal this generosity would be a contradiction, like the sun trying to hide its light. Since he has no other help and there are no external obstacles, the only reason for his suffering is God's own choice to not yet show pity.

tamil: எல்லாம் உடையாய் நின்செயலே எல்லாம் என்றால் என்செயல்கள்
எல்லாம் நினது செயல்அன்றோ என்னே என்னைப் புறந்தள்ளல்
வல்லாய் என்னைப் புறம்விடுத்தால் புறத்தும் உன்றன் மயம்அன்றே
நல்லார் எங்கும் சிவமயம்என் றுரைப்பார் எங்கள் நாயகனே.
translit: ellām uṭaiyāy niṉceyalē ellām eṉṟāl eṉceyalkaḷ ellām niṉatu ceyalaṉṟō eṉṉē eṉṉaip puṟantaḷḷal vallāy eṉṉaip puṟamviṭuttāl puṟattum uṉṟaṉ mayamaṉṟē nallār eṅkum civamayameṉ ṟuraippār eṅkaḷ nāyakaṉē.
translation: O you who possess everything, if all actions are your actions, are not all my actions yours as well? Why then do you push me aside? O all-powerful one, if you cast me out, is not the "out" also pervaded by you? Our Master, the virtuous say that "Everywhere is the fullness of Siva."
commentary: A powerful philosophical point is made in the midst of this plea. If God is the ultimate cause of everything, then even the speaker's flaws are part of God's action. Pushing the devotee “outside” is therefore meaningless, since God pervades even the "outside." The line "Everywhere is the fullness of Siva (Sivamayam)" declares that no place exists apart from God.

tamil: கூடுங் கருணைத் திருக்குறிப்பை இற்றைப் பொழுதே குறிப்பித்து
வாடுஞ் சிறியேன் வாட்டம்எலாந் தீர்த்து வாழ்வித் திடல்வேண்டும்
பாடும் புகழோய் நினைஅல்லால் துணைவே றில்லைப் பரவெளியில்
ஆடுஞ் செல்வத் திருவடிமேல் ஆணை முக்கால் ஆணையதே.
translit: kūṭuṅ karuṇait tirukkuṟippai iṟṟaip poḻutē kuṟippittu vāṭuñ ciṟiyēṉ vāṭṭamelān tīrttu vāḻvit tiṭalvēṇṭum pāṭum pukaḻōy niṉaiallāl tuṇaivē ṟillaip paraveḷiyil āṭuñ celvat tiruvaṭimēl āṇai mukkāl āṇaiyatē.
translation: This very day, you must show me the sacred sign of your fitting compassion, end all the suffering of this withering, humble one, and grant me life. O you of sung praises, I have no other support but you. Upon your bounteous, sacred feet that dance in the supreme expanse, I swear. I swear it three times.
commentary: The urgency becomes a demand. The speaker insists God must show a sign of compassion today. Swearing a triple oath on God's own feet reveals the depth of a soul's desperation and faith, a last resort when there is no other support in the universe.
NOTES
Note 201

tamil: செங்கேழ் வண்ணத் தனிக்கனியே - முதற்பதிப்பு, பொ. சு. பி. இரா. பாடம்.
translit: ceṅkēḻ vaṇṇat taṉikkaṉiyē - mutaṟpatippu, po. cu. pi. irā. pāṭam.
translation: ceṅkēḻ vaṇṇat taṉikkaṉiyē — reading of the first edition and of the Po. Su. and P. Irā. editions.
Note 202

translit: eṉceykēṉ - ca mu ka. patippu.
translation: eṉceykēṉ — reading of the S. Mu. Ka. edition.
Note 203

translit: parañcuṭarē - paṭivēṟupāṭu. ā pā.
translation: parañcuṭarē — variant reading. Ā. Pā. edition.

tamil: போகமே விழைந்தேன் புலைமனச் சிறியேன் பூப்பினும் புணர்ந்தவெம் பொறியேன்
ஏகமே பொருள்என் றறிந்திலேன் பொருளின் இச்சையால் எருதுநோ வறியாக்
translit: pōkamē viḻaintēṉ pulaimaṉac ciṟiyēṉ pūppiṉum puṇarntavem poṟiyēṉ ēkamē poruḷeṉ ṟaṟintilēṉ poruḷiṉ iccaiyāl erutunō vaṟiyāk kākamēeṉappōyppiṟar tamaivaruttikkaḷittapātakattoḻiṟkaṭaiyēṉ mōkamēuṭaiyēṉ eṉṉiṉumentāy muṉintiṭēlkāttaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: I desired only sensual pleasure, a petty person with a base mind. My cruel senses have united with women even during their monthly flow. I did not know that the Supreme Being is One. Driven by desire for things, like a crow that does not know an ox's pain, I went and tormented others and rejoiced. I am the lowest of those who perform sinful deeds, possessing only infatuation. Even so, my Parent, do not be angry; protect and grace me.
commentary: The poem opens with an unflinching confession: lust, a base mind, ignorance that God is One, and cruelty toward others. He compares himself to a crow pecking at an ox's sore, blind to its pain, and says he tormented others and rejoiced. He hides nothing. Even so, he asks the Parent not to be angry, but to protect him and grant grace.

tamil: பூப்பினும் பலகால் மடந்தையர் தமைப்போய்ப்புணர்ந்தவெம் புலையனேன் விடஞ்சார்
பாப்பினுங் கொடியர் உறவையே விழைந்த பள்ளனேன் கள்ளனேன் நெருக்கும்
கூப்பினுங்கூப்பாக் கொடுங்கையேன் எனினும் கோபியேல் காத்தருள் எனையே.
translit: pūppiṉum palakāl maṭantaiyar tamaippōyppuṇarntavem pulaiyaṉēṉ viṭañcār pāppiṉuṅ koṭiyar uṟavaiyē viḻainta paḷḷaṉēṉ kaḷḷaṉēṉ nerukkum āppiṉum valiyēṉ aṟattoḻil puriyēṉaṉpiṉālaṭuttavarkaraṅkaḷ kūppiṉuṅkūppāk koṭuṅkaiyēṉ eṉiṉum kōpiyēl kāttaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: A cruel, base man, I went and united with women many times, even during their menses. I am a base man, a thief, who desired the company of people more venomous than a poison snake. I am harder than a driven wedge. I performed no righteous deeds. I am a cruel-handed man who would not even join my hands in respect when others approached me with love and folded their own. Even so, do not be angry; protect and grace me.
commentary: The confession is unsparing: lust, the company of people more venomous than snakes, a heart harder than a wedge, no righteous deeds. He would not even join his hands when others greeted him with folded hands in love. Yet the verse ends in a plea: do not be angry, protect me. Grace is asked for precisely because it is not deserved.

tamil: விழுத்தலை நெறியை விரும்பிலேன் கரும்பின் மிகஇனிக் கின்றநின் புகழ்கள்
வழுத்தலை அறியேன் மக்களே மனையே வாழ்க்கையே துணைஎனமதித்துக்
கொழுத்தலை மனத்துப் புழுத்தலைப் புலையேன் கொக்கனேன் செக்கினைப் பலகால்
இழுத்தலை எருதேன் உழத்தலே உடையேன் என்னினும் காத்தருள் எனையே.
translit: viḻuttalai neṟiyai virumpilēṉ karumpiṉ mika:iṉik kiṉṟaniṉ pukaḻkaḷ vaḻuttalai aṟiyēṉ makkaḷē maṉaiyē vāḻkkaiyē tuṇaieṉamatittuk koḻuttalai maṉattup puḻuttalaip pulaiyēṉ kokkaṉēṉ cekkiṉaip palakāl iḻuttalai erutēṉ uḻattalē uṭaiyēṉ eṉṉiṉum kāttaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: I did not desire the foremost path. I do not know how to praise Your glories, which are sweeter than sugarcane. I considered children, wife, and worldly life as my only support. I am a base man with a worm-eaten head and an arrogant mind. I am like a hypocritical crane, like an ox that has pulled the oil press many times. I possess only toil and suffering. Even so, protect and grace me.
commentary: Vallalar did not seek the highest path and did not know how to praise God. He took wife, children and household as his only support, and toiled round and round like an ox at the oil press. The image is of effort without arrival: a whole life of labour that goes nowhere. Even so, he asks God to protect him and grant grace.

tamil: புலைவிலைக் கடையில் தலைகுனித் தலைந்து பொறுக்கிய சுணங்கனேன் புரத்தில்
தலைவிலை பிடித்துக் கடைவிலை படித்த தயவிலாச் சழக்கனேன் சழக்கர்
உலைவிலை எனவே வியக்கவெந் தொழிலில் உழன்றுழன் றழன்றதோர் உளத்தேன்
இலைவிலை எனக்கென் றகங்கரித் திருந்தேன் என்னினும் காத்தருள் எனையே.
translit: pulaivilaik kaṭaiyil talaikuṉit talaintu poṟukkiya cuṇaṅkaṉēṉ purattil talaivilai piṭittuk kaṭaivilai paṭitta tayavilāc caḻakkaṉēṉ caḻakkar ulaivilai eṉavē viyakkaven toḻilil uḻaṉṟuḻaṉ ṟaḻaṉṟatōr uḷattēṉ ilaivilai eṉakkeṉ ṟakaṅkarit tiruntēṉ eṉṉiṉum kāttaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: I am like a dog that hangs its head, wandering and scavenging in a butcher's shop. I am a merciless rogue, a heartless cheat in business, making even other rogues marvel at my ruinous practices. My mind is scorched from toiling again and again in cruel deeds. I lived in arrogance, thinking myself beyond compare. Even so, protect and grace me.
commentary: This is a raw confession of a life lived badly. The self-comparison to a scavenging dog, a cruel cheat, and an arrogant man shows a deep sense of unworthiness, yet it ends with a plea for grace, suggesting no sin is too great to be forgiven.

tamil: கொட்டிலை அடையாப் பட்டிமா டனையேன் கொட்டைகள் பரப்பிமேல் வனைந்த
கட்டிலை விரும்பி அடிக்கடி படுத்த கடையனேன் கங்குலும் பகலும்
அட்டிலை அடுத்த பூஞையேன் உணவை அறவுண்டு குப்பைமேற் போட்ட
நெட்டிலை அனையேன் என்னினும் வேறு நினைத்திடேல் காத்தருள் எனையே.
translit: koṭṭilai aṭaiyāp paṭṭimā ṭaṉaiyēṉ koṭṭaikaḷ parappimēl vaṉainta kaṭṭilai virumpi aṭikkaṭi paṭutta kaṭaiyaṉēṉ kaṅkulum pakalum aṭṭilai aṭutta pūñaiyēṉ uṇavai aṟavuṇṭu kuppaimēṟ pōṭṭa neṭṭilai aṉaiyēṉ eṉṉiṉum vēṟu niṉaittiṭēl kāttaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: I am like a stray bullock that does not return to its pen. I am the lowest of beings, who desired a woven cot and frequently lay upon it. Day and night, I am like a cat lingering by the kitchen. Having eaten my fill, I am like the long leaf-plate thrown onto the rubbish heap. Even so, do not think of me as separate; protect and grace me.
commentary: The feeling of being worthless is expressed through a series of humble comparisons: a stray animal, a lazy cat, a piece of trash. The plea "do not think of me as separate" is a powerful request for unity with God, even from this state of abjection.

tamil: நேரிழை யவர்தம் புணர்முலை நெருக்கில் நெருக்கிய மனத்தினேன் வீணில்
போரிழை வெறியர் புகழ்பெறு வெறியேன் புனைகலை இலர்க்கொரு கலையில்
ஓரிழை எனினும் கொடுத்திலேன் நீள உடுத்துடுத் தூர்தொறுந் திரிந்தேன்
ஏரிழை விழைந்து பூண்டுளங் களித்தேன் என்னினும் காத்தருள்எனையே.
translit: nēriḻai yavartam puṇarmulai nerukkil nerukkiya maṉattiṉēṉ vīṇil pōriḻai veṟiyar pukaḻpeṟu veṟiyēṉ puṉaikalai ilarkkoru kalaiyil ōriḻai eṉiṉum koṭuttilēṉ nīḷa uṭuttuṭut tūrtoṟun tirintēṉ ēriḻai viḻaintu pūṇṭuḷaṅ kaḷittēṉ eṉṉiṉum kāttaruḷeṉaiyē.
translation: My mind was fixated on the press of the breasts of bejeweled women. I was a madman who praised other madmen famed for their pointless conflicts. To those who had no clothes to wear, I did not give even a single thread from my garments, yet I wandered from town to town dressed in long robes. I desired, wore, and delighted in beautiful ornaments. Even so, protect me with Your grace.
commentary: This verse confronts sins of desire and materialism. It confesses to a mind consumed by lust, a foolish pride that seeks honor among other fools, and a selfish attachment to fine clothes while ignoring the needs of the poor.

tamil: குளத்திலே குளிப்பார் குளிக்கவெஞ் சிறுநீர்க் குழியிலே குளித்தவெங் கொடியேன்
வளத்திலே பொசித்துத் தளத்திலே படுக்க மனங்கொணட சிறியேனன் மாயைக்
களத்திலே பயின்ற உளத்திலே பெரியன் என்னினும் காத்தருள் எனையே.
translit: aḷattilē paṭinta turumpiṉum kaṭaiyēṉacaṭaṉēṉ aṟivilēṉulakil kuḷattilē kuḷippār kuḷikkaveñ ciṟunīrk kuḻiyilē kuḷittaveṅ koṭiyēṉ vaḷattilē pocittut taḷattilē paṭukka maṉaṅkoṇaṭa ciṟiyēṉaṉ māyaik kaḷattilē payiṉṟa uḷattilē periyaṉ eṉṉiṉum kāttaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: I am lower than a blade of straw mired in mud; I am a fool, I have no wisdom. While others in the world bathe in ponds, I, the cruel one, bathed in a foul pit of urine. I am a petty man whose mind was set on eating rich food and sleeping on a soft bed. I am great-minded only in the arena of illusion, where I am well-practiced. Even so, protect me with Your grace.
commentary: The sense of spiritual impurity here is extreme, using the shocking image of choosing to bathe in a foul pit while others use clean water. This symbolizes a preference for sin over purity. The confession of being skilled only in the "arena of illusion" (māyai, the deceptive power that makes the unreal seem real) shows a deep awareness of having wasted one's life on fleeting worldly comforts.

tamil: தொழுதெலாம் வல்ல கடவுளே நின்னைத் துதித்திலேன் தூய்மைஒன் றறியேன்
கழுதெலாம் அனையேன் இழுதெலாம் உணவில் கலந்துணக் கருதிய கருத்தேன்
பழுதெலாம் புரிந்து பொழுதெலாம் கழித்த பாவியேன் தீமைகள் சிறிதும்
எழுதலாம் படித்தன் றெனமிக உடையேன் என்னினும் காத்தருள் எனையே.
translit: toḻutelām valla kaṭavuḷē niṉṉait tutittilēṉ tūymaioṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ kaḻutelām aṉaiyēṉ iḻutelām uṇavil kalantuṇak karutiya karuttēṉ paḻutelām purintu poḻutelām kaḻitta pāviyēṉ tīmaikaḷ ciṟitum eḻutalām paṭittaṉ ṟeṉamika uṭaiyēṉ eṉṉiṉum kāttaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: O God, worshipped by all and all-powerful, I did not praise You. I know nothing of purity. I am like a ghoul. My mind was set on mixing every kind of ghee into my food to eat it. I am a sinner who spent all my time committing every fault. The evils I possess are so many that not even a fraction of them could be written down. Even so, protect me with Your grace.
commentary: A life of spiritual neglect is confessed here: failing to praise God, knowing nothing of purity, and being like a ghoul. The verse highlights gluttony and a life so full of faults they cannot even be written down. It is an admission of complete failure, from which only God's grace can offer rescue.

tamil: வட்டியே பெருக்கிக் கொட்டியே ஏழை மனைகவர் கருத்தினேன் ஓட்டைச்
சட்டியே எனினும் பிறர்கொளத் தரியேன் தயவிலேன் சூதெலாம் அடைத்த
பெட்டியே நிகர்த்த மனத்தினேன் உலகில் பெரியவர் மனம்வெறுக் கச்செய்
எட்டியே மண்ணாங் கட்டியே அனையேன் என்னினும் காத்தருள் எனையே.
translit: vaṭṭiyē perukkik koṭṭiyē ēḻai maṉaikavar karuttiṉēṉ ōṭṭaic caṭṭiyē eṉiṉum piṟarkoḷat tariyēṉ tayavilēṉ cūtelām aṭaitta peṭṭiyē nikartta maṉattiṉēṉ ulakil periyavar maṉamveṟuk kaccey eṭṭiyē maṇṇāṅ kaṭṭiyē aṉaiyēṉ eṉṉiṉum kāttaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: My mind was set on seizing the homes of the poor by compounding their interest and heaping up their debt. I could not bear for others to take what was mine, even if it were just a broken pot. I have no compassion. My mind is like a box crammed with every kind of deceit. I am like a poisonous etty tree that disgusts the world's great ones; I am like a mere clod of earth. Even so, protect me with Your grace.
commentary: This verse confronts the social sin of greed. It is a confession of exploiting the poor through predatory loans and of a miserliness so deep that even a broken pot is hoarded. The self is described as a poisonous tree that repels good people, a person who feels they have become a source of poison in the world.

tamil: உடுத்திலேம் சிறிதும் உண்டிலேம் எனவந் தோதிய வறிஞருக் கேதும்
கொடுத்திலேன் கொடுக்கும் குறிப்பிலேன் உலகில் குணம்பெரி துடையநல் லோரை
அடுத்திலேன் அடுத்தற்காசையும் இல்லேன் அவனிமேல் நல்லவன் எனப்பேர்
எடுத்திலேன் எனினும் தெய்வமே துணைஎன் றிருக்கின்றேன் காத்தருள் எனையே.
translit: uṭuttilēm ciṟitum uṇṭilēm eṉavan tōtiya vaṟiñaruk kētum koṭuttilēṉ koṭukkum kuṟippilēṉ ulakil kuṇamperi tuṭaiyanal lōrai aṭuttilēṉ aṭuttaṟkācaiyum illēṉ avaṉimēl nallavaṉ eṉappēr eṭuttilēṉ eṉiṉum teyvamē tuṇaieṉ ṟirukkiṉṟēṉ kāttaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: To the poor who came saying, “We have nothing to wear and nothing to eat,” I gave nothing; I had no intention of giving. I did not seek the company of good people in this world who possess great character, nor did I desire to. Even though I have not earned the name “a good man” on this earth, I live on with the thought that God alone is my refuge. Protect me with Your grace.
commentary: Here, the confession focuses on failures of compassion, specifically the refusal to help the poor. By admitting he neither gave to the needy nor sought the company of the good, the speaker paints a picture of complete spiritual isolation. Yet in that isolation, he finds his one remaining connection: a desperate, unearned reliance on God as his only refuge. This total dependence is the foundation of his plea for grace.

tamil: தாலவாழ்க் கையிலே சார்ந்தவர் எல்லாம் தக்கமுப் போதினும் தனித்தே
சீலமார் பூசைக் கடன்முடிக் கின்றார் சிறியனேன் தவஞ்செய்வான் போலே
ஞாலமே லவர்க்குக் காட்டிநான் தனித்தே நவிலும்இந் நாய்வயிற் றினுக்கே
காலையா தியமுப் போதினும் சோற்றுக் கடன்முடித் திருந்தனன் எந்தாய்.
translit: tālavāḻk kaiyilē cārntavar ellām takkamup pōtiṉum taṉittē cīlamār pūcaik kaṭaṉmuṭik kiṉṟār ciṟiyaṉēṉ tavañceyvāṉ pōlē ñālamē lavarkkuk kāṭṭināṉ taṉittē navilumin nāyvayiṟ ṟiṉukkē kālaiyā tiyamup pōtiṉum cōṟṟuk kaṭaṉmuṭit tiruntaṉaṉ entāy.
translation: All who are engaged in this worldly life dutifully complete their noble worship rituals alone at the three proper times. I, this lowly one, show the world that I am like someone performing austerities. But in private, for this demanding dog-stomach of mine, I have only been completing the duty of providing it rice at the three times, starting with the morning. O my Father!
commentary: Vallalar begins with a painful contrast: while others perform genuine worship three times a day, his only thrice-daily ritual is feeding his stomach. He exposes his own hypocrisy, appearing to be an ascetic while secretly serving his body's "dog-stomach." This frames the desire for food not as a simple indulgence, but as a false religion that replaces the worship of God.

tamil: சோற்றிலே விருப்பஞ் சூழ்ந்திடில் ஒருவன் துன்னுநல் தவம்எலாஞ் சுருங்கி
ஆற்றிலே கரைத்த புளிஎனப் போம்என் றறிஞர்கள் உரைத்திடல் சிறிதும்
போற்றிலேன் உன்னைப் போற்றிலேன் சுவையில் பொருந்திய காரசா ரஞ்சேர்
சாற்றிலே கலந்த சோற்றிலே ஆசை தங்கினேன் என்செய்வேன் எந்தாய்.
translit: cōṟṟilē viruppañ cūḻntiṭil oruvaṉ tuṉṉunal tavamelāñ curuṅki āṟṟilē karaitta puḷieṉap pōmeṉ ṟaṟiñarkaḷ uraittiṭal ciṟitum pōṟṟilēṉ uṉṉaip pōṟṟilēṉ cuvaiyil poruntiya kāracā rañcēr cāṟṟilē kalanta cōṟṟilē ācai taṅkiṉēṉ eṉceyvēṉ entāy.
translation: The wise say that if desire for rice envelops a person, all of their accumulated good austerities will diminish and disappear like tamarind dissolved in a river. I did not heed their words in the slightest. I did not praise You. My desire has become fixed on rice mixed with a flavorful, spicy, and savory curry. What can I do, O my Father?
commentary: The obsession with food is presented as a spiritual catastrophe that can completely undo years of effort in an instant. Vallalar uses a vivid image: good deeds and austerities dissolving uselessly, like tamarind in a river, when faced with overwhelming desire. He confesses that despite knowing this truth, he is helplessly captivated by the taste of rich, savory food.

tamil: விருப்பிலேன் போலக் காட்டினேன் அன்றி விளைவிலா தூண்எலாம் மறுத்த
கருப்பிலே எனினும் கஞ்சியா திகளைக் கருத்துவந் துண்ணுதற் கமையேன்
நெருப்பிலே உருக்கு நெய்யிலே சிறிதும் நீரிடாத் தயிரிலே நெகிழ்ந்த
பருப்பிலே சோற்றுப் பொருப்பிலே ஆசை பற்றினேன் என்செய்வேன் எந்தாய்.
translit: viruppilēṉ pōlak kāṭṭiṉēṉ aṉṟi viḷaivilā tūṇelām maṟutta karuppilē eṉiṉum kañciyā tikaḷaik karuttuvan tuṇṇutaṟ kamaiyēṉ neruppilē urukku neyyilē ciṟitum nīriṭāt tayirilē nekiḻnta paruppilē cōṟṟup poruppilē ācai paṟṟiṉēṉ eṉceyvēṉ entāy.
translation: I put on a show as if I had no desire. Yet even in a famine, when failed harvests have taken away all food, I would not be content to eat simple things like rice gruel. I have latched onto a desire for ghee melted on fire, for yogurt with not a drop of water in it, for tender dhal, and for a mountain of rice. What can I do, O my Father?
commentary: The struggle is with gluttony and with the desire for luxury and excess. The speaker confesses his hypocrisy, pretending to be indifferent while inwardly craving the richest foods: pure ghee, thick yogurt, and a "mountain of rice." His inability to be satisfied with simple porridge (kañci) reveals how deeply the attachment to sensory pleasure has taken root, making true detachment feel impossible.

tamil: உறியிலே தயிரைத் திருடிஉண் டனன்என் றொருவனை உரைப்பதோர் வியப்போ
குறியிலே அமைத்த உணவெலாம் திருடிக் கொண்டுபோய் உண்டனன் பருப்புக்
கறியிலே பொரித்த கறியிலே கூட்டுக் கறியிலே கலந்தபே ராசை
வெறியிலே உனையும் மறந்தனன் வயிறு வீங்கிட உண்டனன் எந்தாய்.
translit: uṟiyilē tayirait tiruṭiuṇ ṭaṉaṉeṉ ṟoruvaṉai uraippatōr viyappō kuṟiyilē amaitta uṇavelām tiruṭik koṇṭupōy uṇṭaṉaṉ paruppuk kaṟiyilē poritta kaṟiyilē kūṭṭuk kaṟiyilē kalantapē rācai veṟiyilē uṉaiyum maṟantaṉaṉ vayiṟu vīṅkiṭa uṇṭaṉaṉ entāy.
translation: Is it any wonder to speak of the one who stole and ate the yogurt from the hanging pot? I have stolen and eaten all the food that was set aside for offering. In the frenzy of my great desire for dhal curry, fried curry, and mixed-vegetable curry, I forgot even You. I ate until my stomach swelled, O my Father.
commentary: He compares his own greed to the famous stories of the child god Krishna stealing butter and yogurt. But where Krishna's theft was a divine game, Vallalar sees his own act as base and shameful. He confesses to the sacrilege of stealing food meant for a religious offering, a low point where his obsession made him forget God entirely.

tamil: கீரையே விரும்பேன் பருப்பொடு கலந்த கீரையே விரும்பினேன் வெறுந்தண்
நீரையே விரும்பேன் தெங்கிளங் காயின் நீரையே விரும்பினேன் உணவில்
ஆரையே எனக்கு நிகர்எனப் புகல்வேன் அய்யகோ அடிச்சிறு நாயேன்
பேரையே உரைக்கில் தவம்எலாம் ஓட்டம் பிடிக்குமே என்செய்வேன் எந்தாய்.
translit: kīraiyē virumpēṉ paruppoṭu kalanta kīraiyē virumpiṉēṉ veṟuntaṇ nīraiyē virumpēṉ teṅkiḷaṅ kāyiṉ nīraiyē virumpiṉēṉ uṇavil āraiyē eṉakku nikareṉap pukalvēṉ ayyakō aṭicciṟu nāyēṉ pēraiyē uraikkil tavamelām ōṭṭam piṭikkumē eṉceyvēṉ entāy.
translation: I do not desire greens alone; I desire greens mixed with dhal. I do not desire just plain cold water; I desire the water from a tender coconut. When it comes to food, who can I say is my equal? Alas! If the very name of this lowly little dog were uttered, all austerity would take flight. What can I do, O my Father?
commentary: This verse shows how refined his cravings are. Plain food will not do; he wants particular, pleasing combinations of it. His self-reproach is absolute: he calls himself a lowly dog and claims that just speaking his name is enough to ruin anyone's spiritual efforts.

tamil: பாலிலே கலந்த சோறெனில் விரைந்தே பத்தியால் ஒருபெரு வயிற்றுச்
சாலிலே அடைக்கத் தடைபடேன் வாழை தகுபலா மாமுதற் பழத்தின்
தோலிலே எனினும் கிள்ளிஓர் சிறிதும் சூழ்ந்தவர்க் கீந்திடத் துணியேன்
வாலிலேன் இருக்கில் வனத்திலே இருக்க வாய்ப்புளேன் என்செய்வேன் எந்தாய்.
translit: pālilē kalanta cōṟeṉil viraintē pattiyāl oruperu vayiṟṟuc cālilē aṭaikkat taṭaipaṭēṉ vāḻai takupalā māmutaṟ paḻattiṉ tōlilē eṉiṉum kiḷḷiōr ciṟitum cūḻntavark kīntiṭat tuṇiyēṉ vālilēṉ irukkil vaṉattilē irukka vāyppuḷēṉ eṉceyvēṉ entāy.
translation: If it is rice mixed with milk, I rush with devotion to stuff it into the great sack of my stomach without hesitation. Even if it is a tiny piece pinched from the peel of a banana, jackfruit, or mango, I do not dare give it to those around me. I am a beast, fit only to live in the forest. What shall I do, my Lord?
commentary: Greed has made him selfish. He eagerly devours rich food but cannot bring himself to share even a scrap with others. This lack of compassion and generosity, born from gluttony, leads him to conclude he is like a wild animal, unfit for human society.

tamil: உடம்பொரு வயிறாய்ச் சருக்கரை கலந்த உண்டியே உண்டனன் பலகால்
கடம்பெறு புளிச்சோ றுண்டுளே களித்தேன் கட்டிநல் தயிரிலே கலந்த
தடம்பெறு சோற்றில் தருக்கினேன் எலுமிச் சம்பழச் சோற்றிலே தடித்தேன்
திடம்பெறும் மற்றைச் சித்திரச் சோற்றில் செருக்கினேன் என்செய்வேன் எந்தாய்.
translit: uṭamporu vayiṟāyc carukkarai kalanta uṇṭiyē uṇṭaṉaṉ palakāl kaṭampeṟu puḷiccō ṟuṇṭuḷē kaḷittēṉ kaṭṭinal tayirilē kalanta taṭampeṟu cōṟṟil tarukkiṉēṉ elumic campaḻac cōṟṟilē taṭittēṉ tiṭampeṟum maṟṟaic cittirac cōṟṟil cerukkiṉēṉ eṉceyvēṉ entāy.
translation: My whole body became a stomach. Many times, I have eaten food mixed with sugar. I reveled in eating fragrant tamarind rice. I grew arrogant from vast portions of rice mixed in thick, good curd. I grew fat on lemon rice; I became conceited from other rich variety rices. What shall I do, my Lord?
commentary: The final stage of this obsession is a total corruption of body and spirit. He says his body has become nothing more than a stomach, and the pleasure of eating has made him arrogant and conceited. Far from leading to humility, his indulgence in rich and varied foods has only inflated his ego, creating a spiritual dead end.

tamil: மிளகுமேன் மேலும் சேர்த்தபல் உணவில் விருப்பெலாம் வைத்தனன்உதவாச்
சுளகினும் கடையேன் பருப்பிலே அமைத்த துவையலே சுவர்க்கம்என் றுண்டேன்
இளகிலா மனத்தேன் இனியபச் சடிசில் எவற்றிலும் இச்சைவைத் திசைத்தேன்
குளகுணும் விலங்கின் இலைக்கறிக் காசை கொண்டனன் என்செய்வேன்எந்தாய்.
translit: miḷakumēṉ mēlum cērttapal uṇavil viruppelām vaittaṉaṉutavāc cuḷakiṉum kaṭaiyēṉ paruppilē amaitta tuvaiyalē cuvarkkameṉ ṟuṇṭēṉ iḷakilā maṉattēṉ iṉiyapac caṭicil evaṟṟilum iccaivait ticaittēṉ kuḷakuṇum vilaṅkiṉ ilaikkaṟik kācai koṇṭaṉaṉ eṉceyvēṉentāy.
translation: I set all my desire on various foods with more and more pepper added. I, who am lower than a useless winnowing fan, ate dhal chutney as if it were heaven. I, the hard-hearted one, lusted after and praised every kind of sweet pachadi Like a leaf-eating animal, I craved leafy green curries. What shall I do, my Lord?
commentary: Vallalar states a scenario of gluttony. Adding more spices like more pepper to dishes, enjoying lentil chutney as if it was the highest heaven (but it’s not). Desired for every kind of sweet pachadi (traditional South Indian side dish). Like an herbivore animal, he craved for leafy green dishes.

tamil: தண்டுகாய் கிழங்கு பூமுதல் ஒன்றும் தவறவிட் டிடுவதற் கமையேன்
கொண்டுபோய் வயிற்றுக் குழிஎலாம் நிரம்பக் கொட்டினேன் குணமிலாக் கொடியேன்
வண்டுபோல் விரைந்து வயல்எலாம் நிரம்ப மலங்கொட்டஓடிய புலையேன்
பண்டுபோல் பசித்தூண் வருவழி பார்த்த பாவியேன் என்செய்வேன் எந்தாய்.
translit: taṇṭukāy kiḻaṅku pūmutal oṉṟum tavaṟaviṭ ṭiṭuvataṟ kamaiyēṉ koṇṭupōy vayiṟṟuk kuḻielām nirampak koṭṭiṉēṉ kuṇamilāk koṭiyēṉ vaṇṭupōl viraintu vayalelām nirampa malaṅkoṭṭaōṭiya pulaiyēṉ paṇṭupōl pacittūṇ varuvaḻi pārtta pāviyēṉ eṉceyvēṉ entāy.
translation: Stems, unripe fruits, tubers, flowers: I could not bear to let a single one get away. I, the wicked one with no good qualities, dumped them in until the entire pit of my stomach was full. I am a base one who rushed like a beetle to fill the fields with my excrement. I am a sinner who, as always, watched the road, waiting for my next meal to arrive. What shall I do, my Lord?
commentary: Vallalar expresses intense remorse over an insatiable, undiscerning appetite. By comparing themselves to a beetle, they highlight the futility and baseness of indulgence, equating the mindless hoarding of food to the expulsion of it as excrement. The verse captures the tragedy of a mind entirely consumed by its next meal, completely blocking the seeker to higher spiritual nourishment.

tamil: உறுத்தலே முதலா உற்றபல் உணவை ஒருமல வயிற்றுப்பை உள்ளே
துறுத்தலே எனக்குத் தொழில்எனத் துணிந்தேன் துணிந்தரைக்கணத்தும்வன் பசியைப்
translit: vaṟuttalē poṭittu malarttalē puraṭṭivaittalē tuvaṭṭalilcuvaikaḷ uṟuttalē mutalā uṟṟapal uṇavai orumala vayiṟṟuppai uḷḷē tuṟuttalē eṉakkut toḻileṉat tuṇintēṉ tuṇintaraikkaṇattumvaṉ paciyaip poṟuttalēaṟiyēṉ malappulaikkūṭṭaippoṟuttaṉaṉeṉceyvēṉentāy.
translation: I decided my only work was to stuff various foods into the single bag of my filth-filled stomach: foods with stimulating flavors from being fried, powdered, puffed, stirred, and sautéed. I cannot endure fierce hunger for even half a moment, yet I have borne this body, this cage of filth and baseness. What shall I do, my Lord?
commentary: This verse highlights the mind’s enslavement to sensory pleasure, specifically the obsessive curation of culinary variety and preparation. Ramalinga points out the bitter irony of human priorities: dedicating meticulous care and effort to stimulate the palate, only to stuff it into a body that is fundamentally a transient "cage of filth." It is a lamentation on the inability to tolerate even brief hunger for the sake of spiritual discipline, revealing how easily the soul becomes a servant to the stomach.

tamil: பருப்பிடி யரிவா லிடிகளா திகளால் பண்ணிய பண்ணிகா ரங்கள்
உருப்பிடி நிரம்ப வரவர எல்லாம் ஒருபெரு வயிற்றிலே அடைத்தேன்
கருப்பிடி உலகின் எருப்பிடி அனைய கடையரில் கடையனேன் உதவாத்
துருப்பிடி இருப்புத் துண்டுபோல் கிடந்து தூங்கினேன் என்செய்வேன் எந்தாய்.
translit: paruppiṭi yarivā liṭikaḷā tikaḷāl paṇṇiya paṇṇikā raṅkaḷ uruppiṭi nirampa varavara ellām oruperu vayiṟṟilē aṭaittēṉ karuppiṭi ulakiṉ eruppiṭi aṉaiya kaṭaiyaril kaṭaiyaṉēṉ utavāt turuppiṭi irupput tuṇṭupōl kiṭantu tūṅkiṉēṉ eṉceyvēṉ entāy.
translation: I stuffed into one huge stomach all the prepared delicacies made from mashed dal, rice flour, and ground items as they arrived in abundance. I, the lowest of the low, am like a ball of dung in this imagined world. I lay and slept like a useless, rusted piece of iron. What shall I do, my father?
commentary: The overarching theme here is the deep spiritual lethargy that follows physical overindulgence. The heavy, rich foods lead directly to a state of total inertia. The striking metaphor of a "useless, rusted piece of iron" vividly illustrates a life devoid of spiritual vitality or purpose—a soul that has allowed itself to corrode and paralyze under the weight of sheer physical consumption.

tamil: அடிக்கடி நுண்மை விழைந்துபோய் அவைகள் அடுக்கிய இடந்தொறும் அலைந்தே
தடிக்கடி நாய்போல் நுகர்ந்துவாய் சுவைத்துத் தவம்புரிந் தான்என நடித்தேன்
பொடிக்கடி நாசித் துளையிலே புகுத்திப் பொங்கினேன் அய்யகோ எனது
translit: aṭikkaṭi nuṇmai viḻaintupōy avaikaḷ aṭukkiya iṭantoṟum alaintē taṭikkaṭi nāypōl nukarntuvāy cuvaittut tavampurin tāṉeṉa naṭittēṉ poṭikkaṭi nācit tuḷaiyilē pukuttip poṅkiṉēṉ ayyakō eṉatu muṭikkaṭipuṉaiyamuyaṉṟilēṉ aṟivilmūṭaṉēṉeṉceyvēṉentāy.
translation: Frequently craving subtle pleasures, I wandered to every place they were gathered. I sniffed and savored them like a beaten dog, all while acting as though I were performing austerities. I shoved pinches of snuff into my nostrils and puffed myself up with pride. Alas, I did not strive to adorn my head with Your feet. I am a fool without wisdom. What shall I do, my father?
commentary: This verse boldly calls out spiritual hypocrisy and the distraction of petty sensory highs. The speaker confesses to wearing the outward mask of an ascetic while secretly chasing trivial stimulations, like sniffing snuff. The ultimate tragedy expressed here is lost opportunity: trading the true prize, God's feet upon his head, for cheap and fleeting habits of the body.

tamil: உண்டியே விழைந்தேன் எனினும்என் தன்னை உடையவா அடியனேன் உனையே
அண்டியே இருந்தேன் இருக்கின்றேன் இருப்பேன் அப்பநின் ஆணைநின் தனக்கே
தொண்டுறா தவர்கைச் சோற்றினை விரும்பேன் தூயனே துணைநினை அல்லால்
கண்டிலேன் என்னைக் காப்பதுன் கடன்காண் கைவிடேல் கைவிடேல் எந்தாய்.
translit: uṇṭiyē viḻaintēṉ eṉiṉumeṉ taṉṉai uṭaiyavā aṭiyaṉēṉ uṉaiyē aṇṭiyē iruntēṉ irukkiṉṟēṉ iruppēṉ appaniṉ āṇainiṉ taṉakkē toṇṭuṟā tavarkaic cōṟṟiṉai virumpēṉ tūyaṉē tuṇainiṉai allāl kaṇṭilēṉ eṉṉaik kāppatuṉ kaṭaṉkāṇ kaiviṭēl kaiviṭēl entāy.
translation: O you who possess me, although I have craved only food, I, your slave, have sought refuge in you, am seeking refuge in you, and will always seek refuge in you. Father, I swear by you: I will not desire food from the hands of those who do not serve you. O pure one! I see no support other than you. Know that protecting me is your duty. Do not abandon me, do not abandon me, my father.
commentary: Absolute devotion to God extends even to the most basic act of eating. The devotee pledges not to accept food from anyone who does not serve God, placing his survival entirely in divine hands. This isn't just a preference; it is a declaration of total dependence and a test of faith, framing protection as God's undeniable duty.

translit: ceyvakai aṟiyēṉ maṉṟuḷmā maṇiniṉ tiruvuḷak kuṟippaiyum teriyēṉ uyvakai aṟiyēṉ uṇarvilēṉ antō uṟukaṇmēl uṟuṅkoleṉ ṟulaintēṉ meyvakai aṭaiyēṉ vēṟevark kuraippēṉ viṉaiyaṉēṉ eṉceya viraikēṉ poyvakai uṭaiyēṉ eṅṅaṉam pukuvēṉ pulaiyaṉēṉ pukalaṟi yēṉē.
translation: I do not know what to do. O great Gem in the Hall, I do not understand the signs of Your sacred will. I do not know the way to salvation. I am without understanding. Alas, I agonized, wondering if suffering would pile upon suffering. I have not attained the way of Truth. To whom else can I speak? I, who am bound by karma, what shall I do? Where can I hasten? I am full of falsehood. How will I ever enter? I, a base, lowly one, know of no refuge.
commentary: The spiritual path often begins with a deep sense of being lost. Here, the devotee feels completely helpless, ignorant of God's will, and trapped by his own failings. This is the raw cry of a soul that has exhausted its own resources and has nowhere left to turn.

translit: aṟivilēṉ aṟintārk kaṭippaṇi puriyēṉ accamum avalamum uṭaiyēṉ ceṟivilēṉ potuvām teyvamnī niṉatu tiruvuḷat teṉainiṉai yāyēl eṟivilēṉ ciṟiyēṉ eṅṅaṉam pukuvēṉ eṉceyvēṉ yārtuṇai eṉpēṉ piṟivilēṉ pirintāl uyirtarik kalaṉeṉ piḻaipoṟut taruḷvatuṉ kaṭaṉē.
translation: I am without knowledge. I do not perform service at the feet of the wise. I am filled with fear and sorrow. I lack devotion. You are the universal God. If You do not think of me in Your sacred will, how will I, who am worthless and lowly, ever enter? What will I do? Whom will I call my support? I cannot be separated from You; if separated, I cannot sustain my life. It is Your duty to forgive my faults and bestow grace.
commentary: A powerful shift occurs when the devotee, having admitted his own powerlessness, places the responsibility for his salvation entirely on God. He argues that since his very life depends on staying connected to God, it becomes God's duty to forgive and grant grace.

translit: uṉkaṭaṉ aṭiyēṟ karuḷaleṉ ṟuṇarntēṉ uṭalporuḷ āviyum uṉakkē piṉkaṭaṉ iṉṟik koṭuttaṉaṉ koṭutta piṉṉumnāṉ taḷarutal aḻakō eṉkaṭaṉ purivēṉ yārkkeṭut turaippēṉ eṉceyvēṉ yārtuṇai eṉpēṉ muṉkaṭaṉ paṭṭār pōlmaṉam kalaṅki muṟitalōr kaṇamtari yēṉē.
translation: I have realized that Your duty is to bestow grace upon me, Your slave. I have given my body, possessions, and life to You with no remaining obligation. After giving them, is it proper for me to languish? What duty shall I perform? To whom can I speak of this? What shall I do? Whom will I call my support? With my mind agitated like one who has incurred a prior debt, I cannot bear being broken for even a moment.
commentary: Having surrendered his body, possessions, and life to God, the devotee now questions why he is still left to suffer. The surrender is seen as a completed transaction, making God responsible for his well-being. To be left languishing feels like a breach of this sacred pact.

translit: tarittiṭēṉ ciṟitum tarittiṭēṉ eṉatu taḷarcciyum tuṉpamum tavirttē terittiṭal aṉaittum terittiṭal vēṇṭum terittiṭāy eṉiliṭar eṉaittāṉ erittiṭum antō eṉceyvēṉ eṅkē eytukēṉ yārtuṇai eṉpēṉ tirittaneñ cakattēṉ carittiram aṉaittum tiruvuḷam terintatu tāṉē.
translation: I cannot bear it, I cannot bear it in the least. You must remove my weariness and suffering. You must make everything known to me. If You do not reveal it, this affliction will burn me. Alas! What will I do? Where will I go? Whom will I call my support? The entire history of me, one with a deceitful heart, is known to Your sacred will, is it not?
commentary: The pain of being separated from God is an active, burning torment that feels unsurvivable. The devotee appeals to God's omniscience, pointing out that God already knows his entire history of failings, which makes the divine silence all the more agonizing.

translit: tāṉeṉaip puṇarum taruṇamī teṉavē cattiyam uṇarntaṉaṉ taṉittē tēṉuṟak karuti irukkiṉṟēṉ ituniṉ tiruvuḷam terintaten tāyē āṉeṉak kūvi aṇaintiṭal vēṇṭum araikkaṇam āyiṉum tāḻkkil nāṉirup paṟiyēṉ tirucciṟṟam palattē naṭampuri ñāṉanā ṭakaṉē.
translation: I have realized the truth that "This is the moment He will unite with me." I remain alone, intent on attaining that honey. This is known to Your sacred will, O my Mother. You must call out to me as a cow calls its calf and embrace me. If You delay even for half a moment, I will not survive. O Performer of the wisdom-play in Thiru Chitrambalam!
commentary: A moment of absolute certainty cuts through the despair: the time for union is now. It is a deeply felt truth. The plea remains just as desperate, because any delay, however small, is unbearable. The image of a mother cow calling its calf expresses the tender, immediate, and loving response he craves from God, the dancer in Thiru Chitrambalam (the sacred hall of consciousness).

translit: ñāṉamum ataṉāl aṭaiaṉu pavamum nāyiṉēṉ uṇarntiṭa uṇartti īṉamum iṭarum tavirttaṉai annāḷ intanāḷ aṭiyaṉēṉ iṅkē ūṉamoṉ ṟillōy niṉṟaṉaik kūvi uḻaikkiṉṟēṉ oruciṟi teṉiṉum ēṉeṉa viṉavā tiruttalum aḻakō iṟaiyumnāṉ tarikkalaṉ iṉiyē.
translation: You made me, who am like a dog, understand wisdom and the experience gained through it, and on that day, you averted my degradation and affliction. Today, I, your devotee, am here, O Flawless One, calling out to you and struggling. Is it right for you not to ask me, even a little, "What is it?" From this moment, I can no longer bear this, not even for an instant.
commentary: The poet reminds God of a past intervention, when divine grace saved him from degradation and gave him a taste of wisdom. Now, finding himself struggling again, he makes a heartfelt complaint: after showing such favor before, how can God now ignore his cries for help? This questioning is a form of intimate, challenging prayer, appealing to God's own sense of fairness and compassion.

translit: iṉiyanaṟ ṟāyiṉ iṉiyaeṉ aracē eṉṉiru kaṇṇiṉuṇ maṇiyē kaṉieṉa iṉikkum karuṇaiyā ramutē kaṉakaam palattuṟum kaḷippē tuṉiuṟu maṉamum cōmpuṟum uṇarvum cōrvuṟu mukamumkoṇ ṭaṭiyēṉ taṉiuḷaṅ kalaṅkal aḻakatō eṉaittāṉ tantanaṟ ṟantainī alaiyō.
translation: O my King, sweeter than a good mother, O apple of my eye, O ambrosia of grace that is sweet like ripened fruit, O bliss dwelling in the golden hall! With a grieving mind, a languid consciousness, and a weary face, I am your devotee. Is it right for my solitary heart to be in turmoil? Are you not the good father who gave me myself?
commentary: In a torrent of loving names, King, Mother, apple of my eye, the poet expresses his deep affection for God. He then contrasts this divine sweetness with his own inner state of grief and weariness. He asks a pointed question: is it right for the child of such a loving Father to be left in turmoil?

translit: tantaiyum tāyum kuruvumyāṉ pōṟṟum cāmiyum pūmiyum poruḷum contanal vāḻvum nēyamum tuṇaiyum cuṟṟamum muṟṟumnī eṉṟē cintaiyuṟ ṟiṅkē irukkiṉṟēṉ ituniṉ tiruvuḷam terintatē entāy nintaicey ulakil yāṉuḷam kalaṅkal nītiyō niṉaruṭ kaḻakō.
translation: You are my father and mother, my guru, the God I praise, my land and wealth, my own good life, love, companion, my relatives, and everything else. I remain here with this conviction in my mind. Your sacred will knows this, my Father! In this world of censure, is it justice for my heart to be in turmoil? Is this right for the beauty of your assembly of grace?
commentary: The poet declares that God is the sum total of his existence: parent, guru (spiritual teacher), wealth, love, and all worldly relations. Having surrendered everything to this single conviction, he questions the justice of being left in anguish, especially while living in a critical and uncomprehending world.

translit: aḻakaṉē ñāṉa amutaṉē eṉṟaṉ appaṉē ampalat taracē kuḻakaṉē iṉpak koṭiuḷam kaḷikkum koḻunaṉē cuttacaṉ mārkkak kaḻakanēr niṉṟa karuṇaimā nitiyē kaṭavuḷē kaṭavuḷē eṉanāṉ paḻakanērn tiṭṭēṉ iṉṉumiv vulakil paḻaṅkaṇāl aḻuṅkutal aḻakō.
translation: O Beautiful One, O Ambrosia of wisdom, my Father, King of the sacred hall! O Youthful One, O Husband in whom the heart of the creeper of bliss rejoices! O great treasury of grace who stands manifest in the assembly of the Suddha Sanmarkkam! I have accustomed myself to calling out, "O God! O God!" Is it beautiful for me still to suffer from old afflictions in this world?
commentary: Addressing God with a series of loving and intimate titles, the poet states his case. He has made a habit of devotion, constantly calling on God, and he recognizes the divine presence in the Suddha Sanmarkkam (The True Path of Purity). After all this, he asks, is it fitting that he should still be tormented by the ordinary sufferings of the world?

translit: paḻampiḻi maturap pāṭṭala eṉiṉum pattarum pittarum pitaṟṟum kiḻamperum pāṭṭum kēṭpatuṉ uḷḷak kiḷarccieṉ ṟaṟintanāḷ mutalāy vaḻaṅkuniṉ pukaḻē pāṭuṟu kiṉṟēṉ maṟṟoru paṟṟumiṅ kaṟiyēṉ caḻaṅkuṭai ulakil taḷarutal aḻakō tantaiyun tāyumnī alaiyō.
translation: Even though my songs are not as sweet as the juice of pressed fruit, hearing the great, unpolished songs babbled by devotees and madmen is your heart's delight. From the day I learned this, I sing only of your renowned glory. I know no other attachment here. In this treacherous world, is it right for me to falter? Are you not my father and my mother?
commentary: This verse expresses deep humility. Vallalar acknowledges his own praise might be simple or "unpolished," but he takes comfort in the belief that God values sincerity over artistry. Because he has learned that God delights in the heartfelt cries of devotees, he has dedicated himself completely to this single act of praise. He then brings the question back to his central plea: if he has abandoned all other attachments for God, is it right for him to be left to struggle alone?

translit: tāyumeṉ orumait tantaiyum ñāṉa capaiyilē taṉinaṭam puriyum tūyaniṉ pātat tuṇaieṉap piṭittēṉ tūkkamum cōmpalum tuyarum māyaiyum viṉaiyum maṟaippumā ṇavamum vaḷaitteṉaip piṭittiṭal vaḻakkō nāyiṉēṉ iṉiōr kaṇantarip paṟiyēṉ nalaruṭ cōtitan taruḷē.
translation: You are my mother and my one father, performing the unique dance in the Hall of Wisdom. I have grasped Your pure twin feet as my refuge. Is it right that sleepiness, laziness, sorrow, illusion, karma, concealment, and egoism surround and seize me? I, who am like a dog, can no longer endure for even a moment. Grant me the good grace-light.
commentary: The obstacles listed are internal states that cloud the soul: laziness, sorrow, illusion, the consequences of past actions (karma), and egoism. By holding onto God's feet, the traditional symbol of total surrender, Vallalar places the responsibility for his liberation on God. He presents his spiritual struggles as an injustice and makes an urgent plea for the "grace-light," the divine intervention that alone can dissolve these inner hindrances. The reference to the Gnana Sabai (Hall of Wisdom) locates this divine dance of creation and dissolution within the space of pure consciousness.

translit: cōtiyēl eṉainī cōtaṉai toṭaṅkil cūḻuyir viṭattoṭaṅ kuvaṉnāṉ nītiyē niṟainiṉ tiruvaruḷ aṟiya nikaḻttiṉēṉ niccayam ituvē ōtiyē uṇartaṟ karumperum poruḷē uyirkkuyir ākiya oḷiyē ātiyē naṭuvē antamē āti naṭuantam illatōr aṟivē.
translation: Do not test me! If You begin to test me, I will begin to give up this life. O embodiment of Justice! I have stated this with certainty for Your holy grace to know. O great substance, so difficult to realize through study! O light that is the life of life! O beginning, middle, and end! O awareness that has no beginning, middle, or end!
commentary: This is a moment of raw, almost shocking desperation. Vallalar declares that he cannot bear any more "tests" and threatens to abandon his life, framing it as a certainty for God to know. This is the cry of a soul at its limit.
