translit: iṉippirin tiṟaiyum irukkalēṉ pirivai eṇṇiṉum aiyavō mayaṅkip paṉippileṉ uṭampum uyirumuḷ uṇarvum paratavip pataiaṟin tilaiyō taṉippaṭu ñāṉa veḷiyilē iṉpat taṉinaṭam puritaṉit talaivā kaṉippayaṉ tarutaṟ kitutaku taruṇam kalantaruḷ kalantaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: I can no longer bear even a moment of separation. Oh Lord, the very thought of separation makes me faint. Do you not know that my body, my life, and my inner consciousness tremble and thrash in agony? O peerless Lord who performs the unique dance of bliss in the singular expanse of wisdom! This is the right moment to give the ripened fruit. Merge with me in grace, merge with me in grace.
commentary: For the enlightened soul, separation from God is a visceral, unbearable pain. Vallalar describes how his entire being, from his physical body to his innermost consciousness, is thrown into turmoil by even the thought of being apart from the divine. The plea is urgent: the soul is ripe for union, and the time for God to grant this merging is now.

translit: pirintiṉic ciṟitum tarikkalēṉ pirivaip pēciṉum neyviṭun tīppōl erintuḷaṅ kalaṅkimayaṅkalkaṇ ṭilaiyō eṅkaṇum kaṇṇuṭai entāy purintaciṟ potuvil tirunaṭam puriyum puṇṇiyā eṉṉuyirt tuṇaivā karantiṭātuṟutaṟ kitutaku taruṇam kalantaruḷ kalantaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: I can no longer endure even a little separation. Do you not see that if I even speak of separation, my heart burns like a fire fed with ghee, becoming agitated and faint? O my Father, whose eyes are everywhere! O Virtuous One, my life's companion, who performs the sacred dance in the chosen hall of consciousness! This is the right moment for you to appear without hiding. Merge with me in grace, merge with me in grace.
commentary: The agony of being apart from God is so intense that even speaking of it feels like adding fuel to a fire. The soul pleads with God, who is described as "all-seeing" and dancing in the hall of pure consciousness, to stop hiding and reveal himself. This verse deepens the sense of urgency, framing divine union as the only possible cure for a searing, spiritual pain.

translit: mēlaiē kānta veḷiyilē naṭañcey meyyaṉē aiyaṉē eṉakku mālaiyē aṇinta makiḻnaṉē ellām vallaṉē nallaṉē aruṭceṅ kōlaiyē naṭattum iṟaivaṉē ōreṇ kuṇattaṉē iṉiccakip paṟiyēṉ kālaiyē tarutaṟ kitutaku taruṇam kalantaruḷ kalantaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: O True One who dances in the transcendent, solitary expanse! O Lord! O my beloved husband who wore my garland! O All-powerful One! O Good One! O God who wields the righteous scepter of grace! O You who possess the eight qualities! I can bear this no longer. This is the right moment to grant your union swiftly. Merge with me in grace, merge with me in grace.
commentary: God is everything to the soul: the ultimate reality, a beloved husband, an all-powerful king, and a good friend. By calling on God in all these roles, Vallalar emphasizes the depth of their relationship, making the current separation feel like a total violation of that intimacy. The "eight qualities" (eṇ kuṇam) are the classical attributes of a perfect, supreme being in the Saiva tradition.

translit: paṇṭukoṇ ṭeṉaittāṉ piḻaikuṟi yāta paṇpaṉē tirucciṟṟam palattē toṇṭukoṇ ṭaṭiyar kaḷikkaniṉ ṟāṭum tūyaṉē nēyaṉē piramaṉ viṇṭukaṇ ṭaṟiyā muṭiaṭi eṉakkē viḷaṅkuṟak kāṭṭiya vimalā kaṇṭukoṇ ṭuṟutaṟ kitutaku taruṇam kalantaruḷ kalantaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: O Gracious One who took me as your own long ago, overlooking my faults! O Pure One, O Loving One, who dances in sacred Chitrambalam, accepting your devotees' service and making them rejoice! O Stainless One, who clearly showed me the crown and feet that Brahma and Vishnu could not find! This is the right moment for me to see and attain you. Merge with me in grace, merge with me in grace.
commentary: Vallalar reminds God of his past acts of grace: overlooking the devotee's faults, accepting his service, and revealing the divine form that even other gods could not perceive. This history of intimacy makes the current withholding of grace all the more painful. He pleads from Thiru Chitrambalam, the sacred center of consciousness where God dances, asking to see and merge with that divine presence once again.

translit: taṉittuṇai eṉumeṉ tantaiyē tāyē talaivaṉē ciṟcapai taṉilē iṉittateḷ ḷamutē eṉṉuyirk kuyirē eṉṉiru kaṇṇuḷmā maṇiyē aṉittamē nīkki āṇṭaeṉ kuruvē aṇṇalē iṉippiri vāṟṟēṉ kaṉittuṇai tarutaṟ kitutaku taruṇam kalantaruḷ kalantaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: O my Father, my Mother, my Lord, my only companion! O sweet, clear ambrosia in the Hall of Consciousness! O life of my life! O great jewel within my two eyes! O my Guru who removed all that is impermanent and made me your own! O great Lord, I can no longer bear this separation! This is the right moment to grant your ripe companionship. Merge with me in grace, merge with me in grace.
commentary: Separation from God is an existential crisis because God is the soul's only true relation: father, mother, lord, and life itself. God is addressed as the sweet ambrosia within the Chit Sabhai (Hall of Consciousness) and the very Guru who initiated the spiritual path. Having been led this far, the soul finds the final separation from its own ultimate reality unbearable.

translit: tuṉpelām tavirkkum tirucciṟṟam palattē cōtiyuṭ cōtiyē aḻiyā iṉpelām aḷikkum iṟaivaṉē eṉṉai īṉṟanal tantaiyē tāyē aṉpelām āki niṟaintatōr niṟaivē aṇṇalē iṉippiri vāṟṟēṉ poṉpatan tarutaṟ kitutaku taruṇam puṇarntaruḷ puṇarntaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: O Jothi within the Jothi in the sacred Chitrambalam that dispels all suffering! O Lord who grants all imperishable bliss! O my good father and mother who bore me! O perfect fullness that has become all love and fills everything! Great one, I can no longer bear separation. This is the right moment to grant me your golden feet. Unite with me in grace, unite with me.
commentary: The ultimate reality of God is a Light within light, a Jothi that dispels all suffering from the sacred Chitrambalam (Hall of Consciousness). More than that, God is the very substance of love, a perfect fullness filling everything. To be separate from this source is to be separate from love, bliss, and reality itself. The plea for the "golden feet" is a classic symbol for attaining divine grace and union.

translit: ētumoṉ ṟaṟiyāp pētaiyām paruvat teṉṉaiāṭ koṇṭeṉai uvantē ōtumiṉ moḻiyāl pāṭavē paṇinta oruvaṉē eṉṉuyirt tuṇaivā vētamum payaṉum ākiya potuvil viḷaṅkiya vimalaṉē ñāṉa pōtakam tarutaṟ kitutaku taruṇam puṇarntaruḷ puṇarntaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: In my innocent youth when I knew nothing, you joyfully took me as your own. O singular one who commanded me to sing with sweet, uttered words! O companion of my very life! O immaculate one who shines in the common space that is both the Vedas and their fruit! This is the right moment to grant me the teaching of wisdom. Unite with me in grace, unite with me.
commentary: The poet recalls his own spiritual history, remembering how God chose him in his youth and gave him the gift of poetry. He sees the divine as the intimate companion of his life. The "common space" (Podu) is the universal stage where God is accessible to all, beyond any single scripture or tradition; it is both the sacred texts (Vedas) and the ultimate truth they point to. Having received the gift of song, he now asks for the final gift: the direct experience of divine wisdom.

translit: eṇṇiya eṉatuḷ eṇṇamē eṇṇat ticaintapē riṉpamē yāṉtāṉ paṇṇiya tavamē tavattuṟum palaṉē palattiṉāl kiṭaittaeṉ patiyē taṇṇiya matiyē matimuṭi aracē taṉittaciṟ capainaṭat tamutē puṇṇiyam aḷittaṟ kitutaku taruṇam puṇarntaruḷ puṇarntaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: O the very thought within my thoughts! O great bliss that arises in my mind! O the spiritual discipline I performed! O the fruit of that discipline! O my Master, obtained through that fruit's power! O cool moon! O King with the moon on your crown! O nectar of the dance in the unique Chit Sabhai! This is the right moment to grant me your grace. Unite with me in grace, unite with me.
commentary: God is experienced as the very fabric of the poet's inner life: the thought inside his mind, the bliss that arises from it, the spiritual discipline (tavam) he performs, and even the resulting reward. This suggests a closeness where the divine is the very process and substance of seeking. The final address to the "nectar of the dance" in the Chit Sabhai (Hall of Consciousness) points to God as the dynamic, blissful reality experienced within.

translit: malappakai tavirkkum taṉippotu maruntē mantira mēoḷir maṇiyē nilaippaṭa eṉaiaṉ ṟāṇṭaruḷ aḷitta nēyaṉē tāyaṉai yavaṉē palappaṭu poṉṉam palattilē naṭañcey paramaṉē paramaciṟ cukantāṉ pulappaṭat tarutaṟ kitutaku taruṇam puṇarntaruḷ puṇarntaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: O unique and universal medicine that removes the enemy, malam! O mantra! O shining gem! O loving one who took me as your own that day, granting me grace to make me steadfast! O you who are like a mother! O supreme one who performs the dance in the glorious Golden Hall! This is the right moment to make the supreme bliss of consciousness manifest to me. Unite with me in grace, unite with me.
commentary: God is the one true "medicine" for the soul's fundamental affliction, malam, the primal impurity and ignorance that separates us from our true nature. This grace provides stability and is offered with the love of a mother. The plea is for the supreme bliss of consciousness to be made fully real and tangible, an experience associated with the divine dance in the Ponnambalam, the "Golden Hall" of the enlightened heart.

translit: kaḷippuṟum aṭiyēṉ kaiyilē kiṭaitta kaṟpakat tīñcuvaik kaṉiyē veḷippuṟat tōṅkum viḷakkamē akattē viḷaṅkumōr viḷakkamē eṉakkē oḷippilā taṉṟē aḷittaciṟ potuvil oruvaṉē iṉippiri vāṟṟēṉ puḷippaṟa iṉittaṟ kitutaku taruṇam puṇarntaruḷ puṇarntaruḷ eṉaiyē.
translation: O sweet-tasting fruit from the wish-fulfilling tree that has fallen into the hands of me, your joyous devotee! O lamp that shines high outside! O the one lamp that shines within! O singular one in the Hall of Consciousness who openly gave yourself to me that day! I can no longer bear separation. This is the right moment to grant a sweetness that has no trace of sourness. Unite with me in grace, unite with me.
commentary: Divine grace is pictured as a rare, sweet fruit from the mythical wish-fulfilling tree (karpagam), a gift that has unexpectedly fallen into the devotee's hands. God is both the light seen in the world and the light of consciousness shining within. Having already received a taste of this grace in the Chit Podu (Hall of Consciousness), the poet now longs for the full experience: a perfect, pure sweetness with no lingering trace of worldly sorrow or bitterness.

sections.title: The Loss of the Sense of Self

translit: avvaṇṇam paḻuttavarum aṟintilarcaṟ ṟeṉiṉum aṟintaṉamōr ciṟitukuru aruḷālē antac cevvaṇṇam paḻuttataṉit tiruvurukkaṇ ṭevarkkum teriyāmal iruppameṉac cintaṉaicey tiruntēṉ ivvaṇṇam iruntaeṉaip piṟaraṟiyat teruvil iḻuttuviṭut tatukaṭavuḷ iyaṟkaiaruṭ ceyalō mavvaṇṇap perumāyai taṉceyalō aṟiyēṉ maṉamālai pāyvatukāṇ maṉṟilnaṭat taracē.
translation: Even the most perfected ones have not known it in the slightest, yet I, by the Guru's grace, came to know a little. Having seen that unique, sacred form, ripened to its ruddy hue, I intended to remain hidden from everyone's sight. But that it dragged me, who was in that state, into the street for others to see, is this God's natural act of grace, or is it the work of great Māyai? I do not know. See how my mind is crushed like a sugarcane press, O King of Dance in the Hall!
commentary: Vallalar describes a painful dilemma. After receiving a rare vision of the divine through his Guru's grace, his only wish was to remain in solitude to deepen his experience. Instead, he feels he has been forcibly "dragged... into the street," exposed to the world, and is tormented by the uncertainty of whether this is God's plan or a deception.

translit: kaḷḷirunta malaritaḻic caṭaikkaṉiniṉ vaṭivam kaṇṭukoṇṭēṉ ciṟitaṭiyēṉ kaṇṭukoṇṭa paṭiyē naḷḷirunta vaṇṇamiṉṉum kaṇṭukaṇṭu kaḷittē nāṭaṟiyā tiruppameṉṟē naṉṟuniṉain torucār uḷḷirunta eṉaitteruvil iḻuttuviṭut tatutāṉ uṉceyalō perumāyai taṉceyelō aṟiyēṉ vaḷḷirunta kuṇakkaṭaiyēṉ itainiṉaik kuntōṟum maṉamālai pāyvatukāṇ maṉṟilnaṭat taracē.
translation: I saw your form, the fruit ripened on your braided hair adorned with honey-filled konrai flowers. Having seen it, I resolved to remain in seclusion, continuing to see it again and again in the dead of night and exulting, unknown to the world. But that it dragged me, who was inside, into the street, is this your act, or the act of great Māyai? I do not know. I am the basest of beings with harsh, sword-like qualities; whenever I think of this, see how my mind is crushed like a sugarcane press, O King of Dance in the Hall!
commentary: He again contrasts the deep intimacy of his vision with the painful exposure of being forced into public view. His plan was to cherish this communion with God in secret, "unknown to the world." The anguish of this unwanted publicity is so great that he feels his mind is being destroyed, unable to reconcile his private path with this new public role.

translit: ikattirunta vaṇṇamelām mikattirunta aruṭpē riṉpavaṭi vamciṟiyēṉ muṉpurinta tavattāl cakattiruntār kāṇātē ciṟitukaṇṭu koṇṭa taramniṉaintu peritiṉṉum tāṉkāṇpēm eṉṟē akattirunta eṉaippuṟattē iḻuttuviṭut tatutāṉ āṇṭavaniṉ aruṭceyalō maruṭceyalō aṟiyēṉ makattiruntār eṉaḷavil eṉniṉaippār antō maṉamālai pāyvatukāṇ maṉṟilnaṭat taracē.
translation: By a penance I performed before, I saw a little of the form of grace, of great bliss, which perfects all states of being in this world, a sight the people of the world have not seen. Thinking I could see it even more fully, I remained inside. But that it dragged me, who was inside, to the outside, is this your act of grace, Lord, or an act of delusion? I do not know. Alas, what will the great ones think of me? See how my mind is crushed like a sugarcane press, O King of Dance in the Hall!
commentary: Vallalar explains that his vision was a reward for past spiritual efforts, and he hoped to build on it in seclusion. Being forced into the open leaves him wondering if it is an act of grace or delusion. He now adds a new anxiety: what will other respected spiritual figures think of his public appearance and claims? This concern for how he is perceived by his peers adds to the mental torment he feels.

translit: karuṅkaḷiṟu pōlmatattāl kaṇcorukki vīṇē kālamelām kaḻikkiṉṟa kaṭaiyarkaṭait talaivāy oruṅkuciṟi yēṉtaṉaimuṉ valintaruḷē vaṭivāy uḷamarntē uḷḷataṉai uḷḷapaṭi uṇarttip peruṅkaruṇai yālaḷitta pēṟataṉai iṉṉum piṟaraṟiyā vakaiperitum peṟatumeṉa uḷḷē maruṅkirunta eṉaiveḷiyil iḻuttuviṭṭa teṉṉō maṉamālai pāyvatukāṇ maṉṟilnaṭat taracē.
translation: Like a black elephant with eyes drooping from the intoxication of rut, I was wasting all my time in vain. You forcefully came and sat within me, this lowly one at the very doorstep of the base, as Grace itself, making me realize what is inside, just as it is. I was staying close by, inside, hoping to receive even more of the blessing you granted out of great compassion, all without others knowing. But what is this that dragged me out into the open? See how my mind is crushed like a sugarcane press, O King of Dance in the Hall!
commentary: Vallalar contrasts his former self, lost in arrogance, with the person he became after God's grace forcefully entered him. The experience was a pure gift, not something he earned. His desire was simply to stay close to that inner grace, but being pulled into a public role feels like a bewildering and painful interruption of that sacred relationship.

translit: nāṭukiṉṟa maṟaikaḷelām nāmaṟiyōm eṉṟu nāṇiurait talamaravē nallamaṇi maṉṟil āṭukiṉṟa cēvaṭikaṇ ṭāṉantak kaṭalil āṭumaṉpar pōlnamakkum aruḷkiṭaitta teṉiṉum vīṭukiṉṟa piṟarciṟitum aṟiyāmal irukka vēṇṭumeṉa iruntaeṉṉai veḷiyiliḻut tiṭṭu vāṭukiṉṟa vakaipurinta vitiyainiṉain taiyō maṉamālai pāyvatukāṇ maṉṟilnaṭat taracē.
translation: While the searching Vedas, ashamed, declare, "We do not know," and wander in confusion, I saw the sacred feet that dance in the good, jeweled hall. Although I received grace, just like the devotees who bathe in the ocean of bliss, I wished to remain completely unknown to others who are perishing. Ah, when I think of the fate that has made me suffer by dragging me outside, see how my mind is crushed like a sugarcane press, O King of Dance in the Hall.
commentary: The speaker has had a direct vision of God that surpasses the knowledge of the ancient Vedas, or scriptures. He felt he had received the ultimate blessing, but his only wish was to keep it hidden from a world not ready for it. To be dragged into the open feels like a cruel twist of fate, turning a source of bliss into a cause of suffering.

translit: natikalanta caṭaiacaiyat tirumēṉi viḷaṅka nallatiruk kūttāṭa vallatiru vaṭikaḷ katikalantu koḷacciṟiyēṉ karuttiṭaiyē kalantu kaḷḷamaṟa uḷḷapaṭi kāṭṭiṭakkaṇ ṭiṉṉum patikalantu koḷummaṭṭum piṟaraṟiyā tirukkap parintuḷḷē iruntaeṉṉai veḷiyil iḻut tiṭṭu matikalantu kalaṅkavaitta vitiyainiṉain taiyō maṉamālai pāyvatukāṇ maṉṟilnaṭat taracē.
translation: As your river-filled matted locks swayed and your sacred body shone, your sacred feet, skilled in the fine sacred dance, entered my base mind to grant me refuge and showed me things as they are, without deceit. I intended to remain inside, unknown to others, until I could merge with you, my Lord. But alas, when I think of the fate that dragged me out into the open, confounding and agitating my mind, my mind churns like a sugarcane press, you see, O King who dances in the Hall.
commentary: The goal of the speaker's spiritual path is clear: to merge completely with God. The vision of the dancing Lord was the means to that end, a private process of purification. Being forced into the public eye is a deep disruption that agitates his mind and stalls his progress toward that final union.

translit: mañcaṉaiya kuḻalammai eṅkaḷciva kāma vallimakiḻ tirumēṉi vaṇṇamatu ciṟitē nañcaṉaiya koṭiyēṉkaṇ ṭiṭappurinta aruḷai nāṭaṟiyā vakaiiṉṉum nīṭaniṉait tiruntēṉ añcaṉaiya piṟarellām aṟintupala pēci alartūṟṟa aḷiyaeṉai veḷiyiliḻut tiṭṭu vañcaṉaicey tiṭavanta vitiyainiṉain taiyō maṉamālai pāyvatukāṇ maṉṟilnaṭat taracē.
translation: Your grace allowed this wretch, who is like poison, to see a little of the beauty of the sacred body that delights our Mother Sivakama Valli, she of the cloud-like tresses. I had intended for this to continue long, unknown to the world. But now, others dark as kohl have learned of it, and they speak endlessly, spreading scandal. Alas, when I think of the fate that came to betray me, dragging my pitiful self out into the open, my mind churns like a sugarcane press, you see, O King who dances in the Hall.
commentary: Here, the pain of public exposure becomes intensely personal. The speaker's sacred vision has become the subject of gossip and scandal among others. What was a moment of grace from God, experienced in private, is now a source of public shame and betrayal. This verse captures the deep anguish of having a sublime inner experience misunderstood and judged by the outside world.

translit: aripiramar uruttirarum aṟintukoḷa māṭṭā talamaravum īteṉṉa aticayamō malattil puripuḻuvil iḻintēṉaip poruḷākki aruḷām poruḷaḷikkap peṟṟaṉaṉip putumaipiṟar aṟiyā turimaipeṟa iruppaṉeṉa uḷirunta eṉṉai ulakaṟiya veḷiyiliḻut talakilvirut tiyiṉāl varitalaiyiṭ ṭāṭṭukiṉṟa vitiyainiṉain taiyō maṉamālai pāyvatukāṇ maṉṟil naṭat taracē.
translation: While Hari, Brahma, and Rudra are unable to know you and reel in confusion, what wonder is this? You took me, who am lower than a worm that delights in filth, and made me a person of worth, and I received the substance that is grace. I intended to stay inside, possessing this new marvel by right, without others knowing. But alas, when I think of the fate that dragged me out for the world to see and now ensnares and torments me with endless worldly affairs, my mind churns like a sugarcane press, you see, O King who dances in the Hall.
commentary: The grace Vallalar received is a treasure beyond the reach of even the highest gods, yet it was given to him, who feels lower than a worm. This experience of unmerited, astonishing grace is something he wanted to possess in quiet solitude. But "fate" has pulled him into the world's endless distractions, tormenting him and making his inner peace impossible to maintain. Hari (Vishnu), Brahma (the creator), and Rudra (a form of Siva) represent the highest celestial beings in the Hindu pantheon.

translit: viḻaṟkiṟaittuk kaḷikkiṉṟa vīṇarkaḷiṟ ciṟanta viṉaikkoṭiyēm poruṭṭāka virumpieḻun taruḷik kaḻaṟkicainta poṉaṭinam talaimēlē amaittuk karuṇaiceyap peṟṟaṉamik karuṇainammai iṉṉum niḻaṟkicaitta mēlnilaiyil ēṟṟumeṉa makiḻntu niṉṟaeṉṉai veḷiyiliḻut tulakaviyā pāra vaḻakkilvaḷait talaikkavanta vitiyainiṉain taiyō maṉamālai pāyvatukāṇ maṉṟilnaṭat taracē.
translation: For the sake of me, a wretched sinner, foremost among the useless who rejoice in watering the reeds, you willingly came and graced us by placing your ankleted golden feet upon our head. I stood there rejoicing, thinking, ‘This grace will lift us still higher, to a state worthy of your protective shade.’ But alas, when I think of the fate that came, dragged me out, and trapped and tormented me in the ways of worldly business, my mind churns like a sugarcane press, you see, O King who dances in the Hall.
commentary: Vallalar expresses a classic devotional sentiment of unworthiness, calling himself the foremost of sinners. Despite this, God came directly to him and offered the highest blessing, symbolized by placing the divine feet on his head. He rejoiced, believing this grace would lead him to ever higher spiritual states. Instead, he finds himself ensnared in worldly business, a path he did not expect or desire.

translit: aṭipiṭittut tirikiṉṟa maṟaikaḷelām kāṇā aruḷvaṭivaik kāṭṭinammai āṇṭukoṇṭa karuṇaik koṭipiṭitta kurumaṇiyaik kūṭumaṭṭum vēṟōr kuṟippiṉṟi iruppameṉak koṇṭakattē iruntēṉ paṭipiṭitta palarpalavum pakarntiṭa:iṅ keṉaittāṉ paṭuvaḻakkiṭ ṭulakiyalām veḷiyiliḻut talaittē maṭipiṭittup paṟikkavanta vitiyainiṉain taiyō maṉamālai pāyvatukāṇ maṉṟil naṭat taracē.
translation: You showed me the form of grace that all the Vedas, which wander about trying to grasp your feet, cannot see. I was staying inside, resolved to have no other purpose until I could unite with the gem-like Guru who held the banner of compassion and took me as his own. But it dragged me out here into the world's ways, tormenting me and entangling me in ruinous affairs so that the worldly could gossip endlessly. Alas, when I think of this fate that came to seize and violently rob me, my mind churns like a sugarcane press, you see, O King who dances in the Hall.
commentary: He was shown a vision of God that even the holy Vedas (the most ancient Hindu scriptures) cannot find. Having received this direct initiation from God as his Guru, Vallalar wanted only to focus inwardly on achieving complete union. But this inner resolve was broken when he was thrust into a public life, where he feels exposed to gossip and worldly corruption that threaten to rob him of his spiritual treasure.

translit: tiṭukkaṟa eṉaittāṉ vaḷarttiṭap paraiyām cevilipāṟ cērttaṉai avaḷō eṭukkavum niṉaiyāḷ paṭukkavum oṭṭāḷ eṉceyvēṉ iṉṉumeṉ ṉiṭaippāl maṭukkanaṟ ṟāyum vantilaḷ nīyum vanteṉaip pārttilai antō taṭukkaruṅ karuṇait tantaiyē taḷarntēṉ taṉaiyaṉēṉ taḷarntiṭal aḻakō.
translation: To raise me without fear, you placed me with the wet nurse, Parai. But she does not think to pick me up, nor does she let me lie down. What can I do? My good mother has not yet come to nurse me, and you have not come to see me either. Alas, O Father of unstoppable compassion, I have grown weary. Is it proper for me, your son, to languish?
commentary: The soul's spiritual life is imagined as an infant's life. God, the Father, places the soul in the care of Parai, the Supreme Mother, or universal Shakti (divine energy). But instead of comfort, the soul finds itself in a state of neglect and suspense, neither held nor allowed to rest. It is a powerful image of spiritual abandonment, with the soul crying out in weariness to the Father who seems to have forgotten it.

translit: taḷarntiṭēl makaṉē eṉṟeṉai eṭuttōr tāykaiyil koṭuttaṉai avaḷō vaḷarntiṭā vakaiyē niṉaittaṉaḷ pōṉṟu māyamē purintiruk kiṉṟāḷ kiḷarntiṭa eṉaittāṉ peṟṟanaṟ ṟāyum kēṭpataṟ kaṭaintilaṉ antō uḷantaru karuṇait tantaiyē nīyum uṟṟilai peṟṟavark kaḻakō.
translation: Saying, “Do not falter, my son,” you picked me up and gave me into a mother’s hands. But she, as if determined that I should not thrive, practices only deceit. My good mother who bore me has not come to check on my cries. Alas, O Father of heart-given compassion, you too have not appeared. Is this proper for parents?
commentary: God offers a word of comfort but then hands the soul to another "mother." This new caretaker represents māyā, the power of cosmic illusion, whose very nature is to deceive. Instead of nurturing the soul, she seems determined to prevent its spiritual growth. The feeling of being trapped by deceit deepens, and the soul's cry becomes more plaintive: is it right for parents to be so absent?

translit: tāṅkaeṉ taṉaiōr tāykaiyil koṭuttāy tāyavaḷ nāṉtaṉit tuṇarntu tūṅkavum oṭṭāḷ eṭukkavum tuṇiyāḷ cūtaiyē niṉaittiruk kiṉṟāḷ ōṅkunaṟ ṟāyum vantilāḷ antō uḷantaḷar vuṟṟaṉaṉ nīyum īṅkuvan tilaiyēl eṉceykēṉ itutāṉ entainiṉ tiruvaruṭ kaḻakō.
translation: To care for me, you gave me into a mother’s hands. That mother will not let me sleep in self-awareness, nor does she dare to pick me up. She is intent only on trickery. My exalted, good mother has not come, alas. I have grown weary of heart. If you do not come here, what will I do? Is this, my Father, befitting your sacred grace?
commentary: The deception of māyā (illusion) is explained here: she prevents the soul from achieving a state of deep, peaceful self-awareness. She will neither comfort the soul nor let it find rest within itself, keeping it in a state of agitated distraction. The soul's cry becomes a desperate plea, asking what it will do if God, the Father, does not personally intervene.

translit: attanī eṉaiōr tāykaiyil koṭuttāy āṅkavaḷ makaḷkaiyil koṭuttāḷ nittiya makaḷōr nīlipāṟ koṭuttāḷ nīliyō taṉpuṭai āṭum tattuva maṭavār taṅkaiyil koṭuttāḷ taṉittaṉi avaravar eṭuttē kattavem payamē kāṭṭiṉar nāṉum kalaṅkiṉēṉ kalaṅkiṭal aḻakō.
translation: Father, you gave me into a mother’s hands. She then gave me to her daughter. Her eternal daughter gave me to a Nīli. The Nīli, in turn, gave me into the hands of the ignorant women of the Tattvas who dance at her side. One by one, they each picked me up and only showed me terrible fears that made me scream. I became distressed. Is it proper that I should be distressed?
commentary: This verse vividly traces the soul's descent into bondage. The soul is passed down from māyā (illusion) to even more limiting powers, represented by her daughter and the dark figure of Nīli. Finally, it lands in the hands of the tattvas, the fundamental cosmic principles that constitute the mind, body and material world. Instead of being neutral building blocks, they are portrayed as terrifying forces that frighten the helpless soul, illustrating how we become trapped and tormented by the very fabric of reality.

translit: vāṅkiya cevili aṟivoṭum tuyiṟṟa makaḷkaiyil koṭuttaṉaṉ eṉaittāṉ īṅkivaḷ karuttil etuniṉait taṉaḷō eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉaiyē uṇarntu tūṅkavum oṭṭāḷ aṭikkaṭi kiḷḷit toṭṭilum āṭṭiṭu kiṉṟāḷ ēṅkuṟu kiṉṟēṉ piḷḷaitaṉ arumai īṉṟavar aṟivarē entāy.
translation: The wet nurse who received me, intending to put me to sleep with wisdom, gave me to her daughter. What this one has conceived in her mind, I do not know. What can I do? She will not let me sleep in self-awareness. Instead, she constantly pinches me while rocking the cradle. I am wailing. O my Mother, only those who have given birth truly know the preciousness of a child.
commentary: The soul’s tormentor both agitates it with pain (the pinch) and distracts it with superficial comforts (rocking the cradle). This captures the nature of worldly life, which constantly stimulates the mind and senses, preventing the soul from finding the deep peace of self-awareness. The final line is a poignant cry to God: as the true parent, only you can understand my preciousness and my suffering.

translit: valattilē cevili eṭuttiṭac cōmpi makkaḷpāl kāṭṭiviṭ ṭiruntāḷ malattilē uḻaittuk kiṭantaḻal kēṭṭum vanteṉai eṭuttilār avarum ilattilē kūṭi āṭukiṉ ṟaṉarnāṉ eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉuṭai arumai nilattilē avarkaḷ aṟintilār peṟṟōy nīyumiṅ kaṟintilai yēyō.
translation: The nurse on my right, too lazy to pick me up, pointed me out to the other children and left me there. Even though they heard me crying as I lay struggling in filth, they also did not come and pick me up. They are all gathered together, playing games. What can I do? They did not recognize my worth on this earth. O my parent, have you also failed to recognize it here?
commentary: The "filth" in which the baby lies represents the soul's entanglement in the impurities of worldly existence. The "other children" playing nearby are other souls, so lost in worldly distractions that they are deaf to another's suffering. This verse expresses a deep loneliness, where the soul feels its inherent value is unrecognized by anyone and wonders if even God has forgotten it.

translit: tummiṉēṉ vetumpit toṭṭiliṟ kiṭantē cōrntaḻu tiḷaittumeṉ kuralum kammiṉēṉ cevili ammipōl acaiyāḷ kātuṟak kēṭṭiruk kiṉṟāḷ cemmiyē maṭavār kommiyē pāṭic cirittiruk kiṉṟaṉar antō immiyē eṉiṉum īntiṭār pōla iruppatō nīyumen tāyē.
translation: Lying in the cradle, I sneezed and grew feverish. I grew weary, cried, became exhausted, and my voice went hoarse. The nurse is as unmoving as a grinding stone; she hears it all clearly. The fine women are singing, clapping, and laughing. Alas! Is it your way too, O my mother, to be like those who would not give even the tiniest bit?
commentary: The imagery of the unmoving nurse and the laughing women highlights the world's cold indifference to the soul's suffering. The baby's hoarse voice is a powerful metaphor for a soul exhausted by its long, unanswered search for grace. The final question is a desperate plea, challenging God by asking if divine compassion, too, is empty and ungiving.

translit: turuvilā vayirat toṭṭilē taṅkat toṭṭilē pala:irun tiṭavum tiruvilāp pottait toṭṭiliṟ cevili ciṟiyaṉaik kiṭattiṉaḷ entāy pirivilāt taṉimait talaivanī peṟṟa piḷḷaināṉ eṉakkitu peṟumō karuvilāy nīit taruṇamvan titaṉaik kaṇṭiṭil cakikkumō niṉakkē.
translation: Though there were many flawless diamond cradles and golden cradles, the nurse laid this little one in a wretched, hollow cradle. My mother! I am the child born to you, the inseparable, solitary Lord. Is this what I deserve? O one without a womb, if you were to come at this moment and see this, could you yourself endure it?
commentary: The soul remembers its true home. The diamond and gold cradles represent its rightful state of luminous purity, while the "wretched, hollow cradle" is its current confinement in the imperfect physical body and material world. This is a complaint and an assertion of identity: as the child of God, the soul knows it is meant for something more than this suffering.

translit: kāyntiṭu maṉattāḷ pōṉṟaṉaḷ ciṟitum kaṉivilāḷ kāmamā tikaḷām pāyntiṭu vēṭap payalkaḷāl eṉakkup payampuri vittaṉaḷ palakāl tēyntiṭu matieṉ ṟeṇṇiṉāḷ kuṟaiyāt tirumati eṉaniṉain taṟiyāḷ cāynta:ic cevili kaiyilē eṉṉait tantatu cālumen tāyē.
translation: She seems to have a harsh heart, with not the slightest tenderness. Many times, she has allowed the pouncing, disguised ruffians of lust and its kin to frighten me. She thought of me as a waning moon; she failed to realize I am the flawless, sacred moon that never wanes. Entrusting me to the hands of this biased nurse is quite enough, O my mother!
commentary: The "nurse" is identified as the world's harsh, unloving influence, which allows inner demons like lust and greed to torment the soul. The soul laments that this worldly consciousness fails to see its true, eternal nature, mistaking it for something temporary and flawed. The verse is a plea for rescue from the corrupting and distracting forces of material existence.

translit: ñāṉaā ṉanta valliyām piriyā nāyaki yuṭaṉeḻun taruḷi īṉamār iṭarnīt teṭutteṉai aṇaittē iṉṉamu taṉaittaiyum arutti ūṉamoṉ ṟillā tōṅkumeyt talattil uṟappurin teṉaippiri yāmal vāṉamum puviyum matikkavāḻn taruḷka māmaṇi maṉṟilen tāyē.
translation: Arise and come with your inseparable consort, the divine creeper of wisdom-bliss. Remove my lowly suffering, lift me up, and embrace me. Feed me all of the sweet ambrosia. In the exalted place of truth where there is no flaw, make me one with you and never be separate from me. Grant me the grace to live, esteemed by heaven and earth, O my father in the Hall of the Great Gem.
commentary: After lamenting its state, the soul now states exactly what it wants: complete and final union with God. This rescue is about ending suffering and about total spiritual transformation. It involves being fed "ambrosia" (divine grace and wisdom), being embraced by God, and being permanently established in the "place of truth," a state of pure, non-dual consciousness.

translit: āṭaka maṇippoṟ kuṉṟamē eṉṉai āṇṭukoṇ ṭaruḷi poruḷē vīṭakat tēṟṟum viḷakkamē viḷakkiṉ meyyoḷik kuḷḷoḷi viyappē vāṭakac ciṟiyēṉ vāṭṭaṅkaḷ ellām tavirttaruḷ vaḻaṅkiya maṉṟil nāṭakak karuṇai nātaṉē uṉṉai nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: O mountain of gems and refined gold! O Essence who took me as your own and graced me! O Lamp that guides to the home of liberation! O Wonder, the Light within the lamp's true light! O Lord of compassionate drama in the Hall, you who granted grace and removed all the sorrows of this lowly, transient self! I have trusted in you; do not abandon me.
commentary: The soul declares its total trust in God as the only refuge from sorrow. The various names for God, like "mountain of gold" and "Lamp that guides," are more than poetic praise; they are statements of faith in the specific divine qualities the soul is relying upon for its salvation. Having experienced grace before, the soul uses that memory as the basis for its plea to never be abandoned.

translit: vaṭṭavāṉ cuṭarē vaḷaroḷi viḷakkē vayaṅkuciṟ cōtiyē aṭiyēṉ iṭṭamē iṭṭat tiyaintuḷē kalanta iṉpamē eṉperum poruḷē kaṭṭamē tavirttiṅ keṉṉaivāḻ vitta kaṭavuḷē kaṉakamaṉ ṟakattē naṭṭamē puriyum pēraru ḷaracē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: O perfect, vast Flame! O ever-growing Lamp of light! O radiant Jothi of consciousness! O my own desire! O Bliss that, fulfilling my desire, mingled deep within me! O my great Treasure! O God who removed my bonds and gave me life here! O King of great grace who performs the dance within the golden hall! I have trusted in you; do not abandon me.
commentary: God is addressed as an intimate and personal reality: the soul's deepest desire, the bliss within, and the great Treasure. This verse expresses trust based on a lived experience of God's grace, which has already removed the soul's "bonds" (kaṭṭam) and given it life. The repeated refrain, "I have trusted in you; do not abandon me," is the heart of the prayer, a complete surrender to the dancing Lord of grace.

translit: pullavā maṉattēṉ eṉṉiṉum camayam pukutavā poynneṟi oḻukkam collavā piṟarait tutikkavā ciṟitōr coppaṉat tāyiṉum niṉaiyēṉ kallavā maṉattōr uṟavaiyuṅ karutēṉ kaṉakamā maṉṟilē naṭikkum nallavā ellām vallavā uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: Though I am of a base mind, I will not enter any religion, speak of the conduct of false paths, or praise others. I would not think of it even for a moment, not even in a dream. I do not contemplate relationships with those of stone-like hearts. O good One, O all-powerful One, who dances in the great golden hall! I have trusted in you alone; do not abandon me.
commentary: Trust in the one God requires a radical turning away from all other dependencies. Vallalar makes a startling declaration: he will not follow any formal religion, false spiritual path, or even associate with hard-hearted people. His commitment is direct and exclusive, focused only on the divine reality.

translit: puṇpaṭā uṭampum puraipaṭā maṉamum poypaṭā oḻukkamum poruntik kaṇpaṭā tiravum pakalumniṉ taṉaiyē karuttilvait tēttutaṟ kicaintēṉ uṇpaṉē eṉiṉum uṭuppaṉē eṉiṉum ulakarai nampilēṉ eṉatu naṇpaṉē nalañcār paṇpaṉē uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: With an unwounded body, a flawless mind, and conduct free from falsehood, I have resolved to praise you day and night without sleep, keeping you alone in my thoughts. Whether I eat or whether I dress, I do not trust worldly people. O my friend, my paragon of goodness! I have trusted in you alone; do not abandon me.
commentary: The goal of spiritual life is a state of constant, steady remembrance of God. To achieve this, Vallalar resolves to live with a pure body, mind, and conduct, renouncing all reliance on worldly people for even the most basic needs like food and clothing. God is the only true friend and provider.

translit: puṇṇilē pukunta kōleṉat tuyaram pukunteṉaik kalakkiya pōtum kaṇṇilē eṉatu karuttilē kalanta karuttaṉē niṉṟaṉai allāl maṇṇilē vayaṅkum vāṉilē piṟarai matittilēṉ matikkiṉṟār tamaiyum naṇṇilēṉ vēṟoṉ ṟeṇṇilēṉ uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: Even when sorrow pierced and agitated me like a rod thrust into a wound, O true Essence who has mingled in my eye and in my very thought, I have valued no one but you, whether they shine on earth or in the sky. I do not draw near to those who value them, and I think of nothing else. I have trusted in you alone; do not abandon me.
commentary: Even in moments of agonizing pain, the poet's focus remains fixed on God. He experiences the divine as an immediate, internal presence "mingled in my eye and in my very thought." This sense of inner connection makes praise for any other being, human or celestial, impossible.

translit: ūṉpeṟum uyirum uṇarcciyum aṉpum ūkkamum uṇmaiyum eṉṉait tāṉpeṟu tāyum tantaiyum kuruvum taṉipperun teyvamun tavamum vāṉpeṟu poruḷum vāḻvumnaṟ ṟuṇaiyum makkaḷum maṉaiviyum uṟavum nāṉpeṟu naṇpum yāvumnī eṉṟē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I have trusted that you are everything: the life that inhabits this body, feeling, love, drive, and truth; my own mother and father, my guru, the supreme singular God, and my austerity; the treasure of heaven, my life and my good companion, my children, wife, and relatives, and the friends I have. Do not abandon me.
commentary: This final verse brings the theme of total dependence to its climax. Vallalar declares that God is the true substance of everything that gives life meaning: family, guru, self, love, and life itself. Every relationship and aspect of his existence is seen as a manifestation of the divine, making the final plea, "do not abandon me," a prayer to not be separated from the source of all being.

translit: vāṭṭamum tuyarum accamum tavirtteṉ vaṭivamum vaṇṇamum uyirum tēṭṭamum nīyē koṇṭuniṉ karuṇait tēkamum uruvummeyc civamum īṭṭamum ellām vallaniṉ ṉaruṭpē riṉpamum aṉpummeyñ ñāṉa nāṭṭamum koṭuttuk kāppatuṉ kaṭaṉnāṉ nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: Having removed my fatigue, sorrow, and fear, you have taken my very form, appearance, life, and all my pursuits. It is now your duty to protect me by giving me your body of compassion, your form, true Sivam, your wealth, your all-powerful, supremely blissful grace, your love, and a focus on true wisdom. I have trusted you; do not abandon me.
commentary: This is a statement of complete surrender. He sees that God has already taken over his life, removing his suffering and absorbing his very identity. Having given everything, he now claims that God has a duty in return: to bestow a new, divine self, made of compassion, grace, and wisdom. It is a bold, intimate transaction based on absolute trust.

translit: vampaṉēṉ piṟarpōl vaiyamum vāṉum maṟṟavum matittilēṉ matañcār umpaṉēr akaṅkā rantavirn tellā ulakamum vāḻkaveṉ ṟiruntēṉ cempoṉē karuṇait teyvamē ellām ceyavalla cittaṉē civaṉē nampaṉē ñāṉa nātaṉē uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I, a worthless fellow, have not valued the earth, the sky, and other things as others do. I have given up the pride that rages like an elephant in rut, and have simply lived wishing for all worlds to thrive. O pure gold! O God of compassion! O Siddhan who can do all things! O Sivan! O Lord whom I trust! O master of wisdom! I have trusted in you alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: He contrasts his way with the way of others. He has not prized the earth, the heavens or anything in them as others do, and he has put away the swollen pride that rages like an elephant in rut. Emptied of that, he lives with a single intention: that all worlds may live well. This compassionate, universal prayer is what he presents to God.

translit: āyakāl iruntum naṭantiṭa valiyil lāmaiyāl aḻuṅkuvār eṉa:uṇ mēyakāl iruntum tiruvaruḷ uṟaōr viruppilā maiyiṉmika melintēṉ tīyakāṉ vilaṅkait tūyamā ṉiṭañcey cittaṉē cattiya capaikku nāyakā uyirkku nayakā uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: Just as some grieve because they cannot walk despite having legs, I have grown very weak because, though I have a soul that can truly perceive, I lack the desire to attain your sacred grace. O Siddhan, who transforms a wicked forest beast into a pure human being! O Lord of the Hall of Truth! O Benefactor to all souls! I have trusted in you alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: He describes a painful paradox in his spiritual life. He knows his soul has the ability to connect with God's grace, just as a person has legs to walk. Yet he feels paralyzed, lacking the deep desire needed to make that connection. He appeals to God as the ultimate transformer, the Siddhan (one of perfected spiritual power) who can turn a wild beast into a pure human, asking for that same power to work on his own inert will.

translit: aṟṟamum maṟaikkum aṟivilā tōṭi āṭiya ciṟuparu vattē kuṟṟamum kuṇaṅkoṇ ṭeṉṉaiāṭ koṇṭa kuṇapperuṅ kuṉṟamē kuruvē ceṟṟamum viruppum tīrttameyt tavartam cintaiyil iṉikkiṉṟa tēṉē naṟṟaka vuṭaiya nātaṉē uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: Even in my early childhood, when I ran and played without the sense to cover my own nakedness, you accepted my faults as virtues and made me your own, O great mountain of virtue! O Guru! O Honey that is sweet in the minds of true ascetics who have shed both hatred and desire! O Lord of virtuous character! I have trusted in you alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: He recalls that God's grace has been present throughout his entire life. Even in his unthinking childhood, God saw past his flaws, treating them as strengths, and claimed him. This verse speaks of an unconditional acceptance that precedes any conscious spiritual effort. He describes God as the sweet essence enjoyed by perfected beings who are free from the turbulence of hatred and desire.

translit: paṭampuri pāmpiṟ koṭiyaṉēṉ koṭiya pāviyiṟ pāviyēṉ tīmaik kiṭampuri maṉattēṉ irakkamoṉ ṟillēṉ eṉṉiṉum tuṇaienta vitattum tiṭampuri niṉpoṉ aṭittuṇai eṉavē cintaṉai ceytiruk kiṉṟēṉ naṭampuri karuṇai nāyakā uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I am more cruel than a hooded snake, the sinner of sinners. My mind is a place for evil; I have no compassion at all. Nevertheless, I am constantly thinking that in every way, my only firm support is your golden feet. O Lord of compassionate dance, I have trusted you. Do not abandon me.
commentary: In a stark confession, the speaker describes himself as completely devoid of virtue and compassion, a "sinner of sinners." Yet this self-condemnation serves to magnify the power of grace. His single saving grace is his unceasing focus on God's feet as his only hope. This single act of surrender, he believes, is enough to connect him to the "Lord of compassionate dance," even from the lowest state.

translit: paṭittaṉaṉ ulakap paṭippelām meynnūl paṭittavar taṅkaḷaip pārttu noṭittaṉaṉ kaṭintu nōkkiṉēṉ kāma nōkkiṉēṉ poyyartam uṟavu piṭittaṉaṉ ulakil pētaiyar mayaṅkap periyaril periyarpōl pēci naṭittaṉaṉ eṉiṉum niṉṉaṭit tuṇaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I have studied all worldly subjects. I have scoffed at and harshly regarded those who studied the true scriptures. I have looked with lust and cherished the company of liars. To make the ignorant swoon, I acted in the world, speaking as if I were the greatest of the great. Even so, I have trusted the support of your feet. Do not abandon me.
commentary: This is a confession of a life misspent on ego and illusion. The speaker admits to intellectual pride, looking down on spiritual seekers while pursuing worldly knowledge and false company. He pretended to be a great man to impress others, living a life of hypocrisy. Despite this long list of failures, his final hope remains unshaken: a complete trust in the support of God's feet, which he holds onto even now.

translit: pañcunēr ulakap pāṭṭilē melinta pāviyēṉ cāviyē pōṉa puñceyē aṉaiyēṉ puḻuttalaip pulaiyēṉ poyyelām pūritta vañca neñciṉēṉ pāpa neṟiyiṉēṉ ciṉattil neṭiyaṉēṉ koṭiyaṉēṉ kāma nañciṉēṉ eṉiṉum añciṉēṉ uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I am a sinner weakened by worldly affairs as flimsy as cotton; I am like a dry field of failed grain; I am a base one with a worm-eaten head. I possess a treacherous heart brimming with lies, walk the path of sin, am great in anger, cruel, and poisoned by lust. Even so, I have feared you; I have trusted you. Do not abandon me.
commentary: The speaker uses powerful images of decay, a failed crop, a worm-eaten head, to express his deep sense of spiritual bankruptcy. He feels weakened by the world, walking a path of sin (pāpam) and filled with anger, lies, and lust. From this place of utter desolation, two feelings remain that connect him to the divine: fear and trust. The fear is a reverent awe of God's power, and the trust is his only hope for salvation.

translit: kayantuḷē uvaṭṭum kāñciraṅ kāyil kaṭiyaṉēṉ kāmamē kalantu viyantuḷē makiḻum vīṇaṉēṉ koṭiya vekuḷiyēṉ veyyaṉēṉ veṟiyēṉ mayarntuḷēṉ ulaka vāḻkkaiyai maṉaiyai makkaḷai okkalai matittē nayantuḷēṉ eṉiṉum payantuḷēṉ uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I am more vile than the bitterest, most sickening fruit. I am a worthless man who mingles with, marvels at, and inwardly delights in lust. I possess cruel rage, I am harsh, I am frenzied. I have been deluded, esteeming and desiring worldly life, home, children, and kin. Even so, I have feared you; I have trusted you. Do not abandon me.
commentary: This verse continues the unflinching self-critique, focusing on the core delusion of valuing worldly life above all else. He confesses to having a nature that delighted in lust and anger, completely lost in attachments to family and home. The power of the poem is in its constant refrain: despite this catalog of deep personal failings, a fundamental fear of and trust in God remained. This faith is his only redeeming quality.

translit: ōṭiṉēṉ perumpē rācaiyāl ulakil ūrtoṟum uṇṭiyē uṭaiyē tēṭiṉēṉ kāmac cēṟṟilē viḻuntu tiyaṅkiṉēṉ mayaṅkiṉēṉ tikaittu vāṭiṉēṉ ciṟiya vāriyāṉ makiḻntēṉ vañcamē poruḷeṉa matittu nāṭiṉēṉ eṉiṉum pāṭiṉēṉ uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: Driven by immense greed, I ran about the world, seeking food and clothing in every town. I fell into the mud of lust; bewildered, deluded, and perplexed, I withered away. I rejoiced in petty gains. I esteemed deceit as a valuable thing and pursued it. Even so, I have sung of you; I have trusted you. Do not abandon me.
commentary: He portrays a life spent in a frantic and greedy pursuit of basic survival and fleeting pleasures. In this chase, he became lost, confused, and spiritually withered, even taking pride in deceit. But then comes the turn: even in the midst of that chaos, he still sang God's praises. This one act of devotion, however inconsistent, is offered as proof of an underlying trust that never completely died.

translit: kāṭṭilē tiriyum vilaṅkiṉiṟ kaṭaiyēṉ kaivaḻak kattiṉāl oṭinta ōṭṭilē eṉiṉum ācaiviṭ ṭaṟiyēṉ uluttaṉēṉ oruciṟu turumpum ēṭṭilē eḻutik kaṇakkiṭṭa koṭiyēṉ eccilum umiḻntiṭēṉ naraka nāṭṭilē periyēṉ eṉṉiṉum uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I am lower than a beast wandering the forest. I have never let go of desire, even for a broken potsherd in my hand. I am a miser; a cruel man who would write down and account for even a tiny speck. I will not even spit out my own saliva. I am a great man in the land of hell. Yet, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: Vallalar calls himself lower than a forest beast, unable to let go even of a broken potsherd, a miser who writes every speck into his accounts and would not even spit out his own saliva. He is great only in the land of hell. From that lowest point he holds to one thing: he has trusted in God alone, and he asks not to be abandoned.

translit: tuṉittavem maṭavār pakalvanta pōtu tuṟaviyiṉ kaṭukaṭut tiruntēṉ taṉittira vatilē vantapō tōṭit taḻuviṉēṉ taṭamulai viḻaintēṉ iṉittacol pukaṉṟēṉ eṉpiṉaik kaṟittē iṭarppaṭṭa nāyeṉa iḷaittēṉ naṉittava ṟuṭaiyēṉ eṉṉiṉum uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: When fierce, passionate women came by day, I remained stern like an ascetic. When they came alone at night, I ran to embrace them, desiring their full breasts. I spoke sweet words. I grew weary like a dog that suffers gnawing on a bone. I am a man of immense wrongdoing. Yet, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: In a moment of brutal honesty, Vallalar confesses to deep hypocrisy. He admits to playing the part of a stern ascetic in public while secretly indulging his lusts at night. He compares this pursuit of pleasure to a dog gnawing on a dry bone: an unsatisfying, exhausting act that brings only suffering. By admitting to being a man of "immense wrongdoing," he strips himself of any pretense of holiness, resting his entire case on trust in God alone.

translit: tārttaṭa mulaiyār nāṉpala roṭuñcār talattilē vantapō tavaraip pārttilēṉ vārttai pakarntilēṉ tavacup pātakap pūṉaipōl iruntēṉ pērttunāṉ taṉitta pōtupōy valintu pēciṉēṉ vañcariṟ periyēṉ nārttiṭar uḷattēṉ eṉṉiṉum uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: When women with garlanded, full breasts came to a place where I was with many others, I did not look at them or speak a word. I was like a wicked, ascetic cat. Later, when I was alone, I went and spoke to them insistently. I am the greatest of deceivers. My heart is a knot of affliction. Yet, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: The image of the "wicked, ascetic cat" perfectly captures the speaker's self-loathing for his own hypocrisy. He sees himself as someone who feigns spiritual purity in public, only to prey on others in private. This confession is about weakness and about the deeper failing of calculated deception.

translit: peṇmaiyē viḻaintēṉ avarmaṉam aṟiyēṉ pēyeṉap piṭittaṉaṉ maṭavārk kuṇmaiyē pukalvāṉ pōṉṟavar tamaittoṭ ṭuvantakaṅ kaḷittapoy yuḷattēṉ taṇmaiyē aṟiyēṉ vemmaiyē uṭaiyēṉ cāttiram pukaṉṟuvāy taṭittēṉ naṇmaiyē aṭaiyēṉ eṉṉiṉum uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I desired only women. I did not know their minds. I clung to them like a ghost. With a false heart, I rejoiced inwardly, touching women while pretending to speak only truth to them. I do not know coolness; I possess only heat. My mouth grew calloused from reciting scriptures. I have attained no goodness. Yet, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: The speaker admits that his desire was purely selfish, reducing others to objects without understanding their inner lives. He highlights the painful gap between his spiritual knowledge and his actual state: his mouth is "calloused from reciting scriptures," but his heart is filled with the "heat" of passion, not the "coolness" of divine peace.

translit: vaṉmaiyil poruḷmēl iccaiil lavaṉpōl vātipōl vārttaikaḷ vaḻaṅki aṉmaiyil piṟarpāl uḷaviṉāl poruḷai aṭikkaṭi vāṅkiya koṭiyēṉ iṉmaiyuṟ ṟavaruk kutavilēṉ poruḷai eṉaiviṭak koṭiyaruk kīntēṉ naṉmaiyuṟ ṟaṟiyēṉ eṉṉiṉum uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: Speaking like a debater, as if I had no desire for worldly wealth, I am the cruel one who, with false affection, repeatedly acquired goods from others through cunning. I did not help those in poverty. I gave my wealth to those more cruel than I am. I have never experienced goodness. Yet, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: This confession turns from lust to greed, exposing another layer of hypocrisy. The speaker presents himself as a philosopher above worldly concerns, while secretly manipulating others for financial gain. His self-condemnation is sharpest when he admits to withholding help from the poor, thus compounding the world's suffering.

translit: kaṭṭamē aṟiyēṉ aṭuttavar iṭattē kācilē ācaiyil lavaṉpōl paṭṭamē kāṭṭip paṇampaṟit tuḻaṉṟēṉ pakalelām tavacipōl iruntēṉ iṭṭamē iravil uṇṭayal puṇarntē iḻutaiyiṟ ṟūṅkiṉēṉ kaḷittu naṭṭamē purintēṉ eṉṉiṉum uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I knew nothing of the hardships of those who came to me. Posing as one who had no desire for money, I paraded my titles and went about extorting funds. All day, I posed as an ascetic. At night, I ate as I pleased, had illicit sex, and then slept blissfully like a fool. I only caused loss. Even so, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: This verse summarizes the speaker's double life: a holy man by day, a hedonist by night. He recognizes that his entire performance of spirituality was a sham, used to extort money and live a life of secret indulgence. By calling his actions a "loss," he acknowledges that this path has brought no real profit or peace, leaving him spiritually bankrupt.

translit: kāṇiyē karutum karuttiṉaip piṟarkkuk kāṭṭiṭā tampelām aṭaṅkum tūṇiyē eṉaccārn tiruntaṉaṉ cōṟṟuc cukattiṉāl cōmpiṉēṉ utavā ēṇiyē aṉaiyēṉ irappavark kumiyum īntilēṉ īntavaṉ eṉavē nāṇilēṉ uraittēṉ eṉṉiṉum uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I coveted property but hid my intentions from others; I was like a large storage bin, keeping everything for myself. I grew lazy from the pleasure of food. I am like a useless ladder. I never gave even chaff to those who begged, yet I shamelessly claimed to be a benefactor. Even so, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: Here, the speaker admits to a life of greed and laziness, using the powerful image of a "useless ladder" to describe himself as someone who offers no help to others. He confesses to the specific hypocrisy of hoarding resources while shamelessly pretending to be a great philanthropist. It is a moment of painful self-awareness about his own uselessness and deceit.

translit: aṭuttavar mayaṅki matittiṭa niṉaittēṉ aṭikkaṭi poykaḷē puṉaintē eṭutteṭut turaittēṉ eṉakketir ilaieṉ ṟikaḻntaṉaṉ akaṅkarit tiruntēṉ koṭuttavar tamaiyē mikavupa carittēṉ koṭātavar tamaiikaḻn turaittēṉ naṭuttaya vaṟiyēṉ eṉṉiṉum uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I wanted others to be deluded into respecting me. I frequently fabricated lies and declared them emphatically. I scornfully said, ‘There is no one to equal me,’ and was full of ego. I treated only those who gave to me with great hospitality, while I spoke contemptuously of those who did not. I knew no impartial compassion. Even so, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: This verse focuses on the sin of ego, confessing to a constant need for others' admiration, which was fed by lies and arrogance. He admits his relationships were purely transactional: he was kind only to those who gave him things. This lack of genuine, impartial compassion is presented as a core spiritual sickness.

translit: eḷiyavar viḷaitta nilamelāṅ kavarum eṇṇamē perituḷēṉ puṉceyk kaḷiyuṇum maṉaiyil carkkarai kalantu kāyccupāl kēṭṭuṇṭa kaṭaiyēṉ tuḷiyavark kutavēṉ viruppilāṉ pōlac cuvaipeṟac cuvaittanāk kuṭaiyēṉ naḷireṉac cuḻaṉṟēṉ eṉṉiṉum uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I was filled with the great desire to seize all the land cultivated by the poor. I am the lowest of the low, who, in a house that eats only coarse porridge, demanded and drank milk boiled with sugar. I would not help them even a little. I have a tongue that relished fine flavors while I pretended to have no desire. I spun about aimlessly like a top. Even so, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: The confession turns to social cruelty and a complete lack of empathy for the poor. The image of demanding rich, sweetened milk in a home that could barely afford basic food is a shocking admission of callousness. It shows that spiritual degradation is tied to a failure to see and care for the suffering of others.

translit: kolaipala purintē pulainukarn tiruntēṉ kōṭuṟu kuraṅkiṉiṟ kutittē alaitaru maṉattēṉ aṟivilēṉ ellām aṟintavaṉ pōlpiṟark kuraittēṉ malaivuṟu camaya valaiakap paṭṭē mayaṅkiya matiyiṉēṉ nallōr nalaiyala eṉavē tirintaṉaṉ eṉiṉum nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I committed many murders and fed on flesh. My mind wanders, leaping about like a monkey on a branch. I am without wisdom, yet I spoke to others as if I knew everything. I am a person of deluded intellect, caught in the net of bewildering religions. I wandered about, dismissing good people as a nuisance. Even so, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: This verse confesses to the gravest of wrongs: many murders and the eating of flesh, with a restless mind leaping like a monkey on a branch. The speaker also admits to being caught in the net of religions that bewilder the mind: Vallalar names the religions themselves as the trap. The plea for grace comes after acknowledging a total corruption of conduct, intellect and understanding.

translit: īyeṉap paṟantēṉ eṟumpeṉa uḻaṉṟēṉ eṭṭiyē eṉamikat taḻaittēṉ pēyeṉac cuḻaṉṟēṉ pittaṉē eṉavāyp pitaṟṟoṭum ūrtoṟum peyarntēṉ kāyeṉak kāyttēṉ kaṭaiyeṉa naṭantēṉ kalleṉak kiṭantaṉaṉ kuraikkum nāyeṉat tirintēṉ eṉṉiṉum uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I flew about like a fly and toiled like an ant; I flourished exceedingly like a poison tree. I spun like a demon and wandered from town to town, babbling like a madman. I was hard like an unripe fruit, I acted like the lowest of the low, and I lay like a stone. I roamed like a barking dog. Yet, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: The imagery here is intentionally shocking. By comparing himself to a fly, a poison tree, a demon, and a barking dog, Vallalar expresses a deep sense of his own unworthiness. This is a complete stripping away of ego, showing how far he feels he has strayed from his true nature. This total self-abasement becomes the very foundation of his trust in God.

translit: oṉṟiyē uṇavai uṇṭuṭal parutta ūttaiyēṉ nāttaḻum puṟavē veṉṟiyē uraittu viṉaikaḷē viḷaitta vīṇaṉēṉ ūrtoṟuñ cuḻaṉṟa paṉṟiyē aṉaiyēṉ kaṭṭuvār aṟṟa pakaṭeṉat tirikiṉṟa paṭiṟēṉ naṉṟiyē aṟiyēṉ eṉṉiṉum uṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I am a filthy person who only ate food and fattened my body, a useless man who spoke of victories until my tongue was calloused, cultivating only karmic deeds. I am like a pig that roams from town to town, a deceiver who wanders like an untethered bull. I do not know gratitude. Yet, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: This verse focuses on sins of the body and ego. He sees himself as a base creature who lived for physical gratification and self-promotion, comparing his mindless wandering to that of a pig or an untamed bull. The final admission, "I do not know gratitude," is a devastating self-indictment, yet it leads directly to the ultimate act of faith: trusting in the one being to whom all gratitude is owed.

translit: kavaiyelān tavirnta veṟumaram aṉaiyēṉ kaḷḷaṉēṉ kaḷḷuṇṭa kaṭiyēṉ cuvaiyelām virumpic cuḻaṉṟatōr kaṭaiyēṉ tuṭṭaṉēṉ tītelān tuṇintēṉ ivaiyelām annāḷ uṭaiyaṉō alaṉō intanāḷ iṟaivaniṉ aruḷāl navaiyelām tavirntēṉ tūyaṉāy niṉaiyē nampiṉēṉ kaiviṭēl eṉaiyē.
translation: I am like a bare tree that has lost all its branches. I am a thief, a harsh man who drank alcohol, one of the lowest who wandered about craving all worldly tastes. I am a wicked man who dared to do every evil. Whether or not I possessed all these faults in those days, today, O Lord, by Your grace, I have been freed from all flaws. Having become pure, I have trusted in You alone. Do not abandon me.
commentary: After a long and harsh self-condemnation, this verse marks a shift. He acknowledges his past as a "thief," a "drunkard," and a "wicked man" but declares that God's grace has already transformed him. The purification is a gift he received. This change from despair to purity makes his final plea an expression of trust in a relationship that has already begun to heal him.

tamil: போக மாட்டேன் பிறரிடத்தே பொய்யிற் கிடந்து புலர்ந்துமனம்
வேக மாட்டேன் பிறிதொன்றும் விரும்ப மாட்டேன் பொய்யுலகன்
ஆக மாட்டேன் அரசேஎன் அப்பா என்றன் ஐயாநான்
translit: pōka māṭṭēṉ piṟariṭattē poyyiṟ kiṭantu pularntumaṉam vēka māṭṭēṉ piṟitoṉṟum virumpa māṭṭēṉ poyyulakaṉ āka māṭṭēṉ aracēeṉ appā eṉṟaṉ aiyānāṉ cāka māṭṭēṉ uṉaippirintāl tarikka māṭṭēṉkaṇṭāyē.
translation: I will not go to others. I will not lie in falsehood, wither, and let my mind burn. I will not desire anything else. I will not become a person of this false world. O King, my Father, my Master, I will not die, but if I am separated from you, I cannot bear it, you see.
commentary: Vallalar makes a chain of vows: he will not go to others, will not wither in falsehood, will not desire anything else, will not become one of this false world. Then he states two things together: “I will not die,” and “if I am parted from You, I cannot bear it.” What he refuses to endure is not death, which he has already refused, but separation from God.

tamil: செல்ல மாட்டேன் பிறரிடத்தே சிறிதுந் தரியேன் தீமொழிகள்
சொல்ல மாட்டேன் இனிக்கணமுந் துயர மாட்டேன் சோம்பன்மிடி
புல்ல மாட்டேன் பொய்யொழுக்கம் பொருந்த மாட்டேன் பிறஉயிரைக்
கொல்ல மாட்டேன் உனைஅல்லால் குறிக்க மாட்டேன் கண்டாயே.
translit: cella māṭṭēṉ piṟariṭattē ciṟitun tariyēṉ tīmoḻikaḷ colla māṭṭēṉ iṉikkaṇamun tuyara māṭṭēṉ cōmpaṉmiṭi pulla māṭṭēṉ poyyoḻukkam porunta māṭṭēṉ piṟa:uyiraik kolla māṭṭēṉ uṉaiallāl kuṟikka māṭṭēṉ kaṇṭāyē.
translation: I will not go to others; I cannot bear it even a little. I will not speak harsh words. I will not grieve for a single moment more. I will not cling to sloth and want. I will not take up false conduct. I will not kill other lives. I will not set my mind on anything but You. Know this.
commentary: A list of vows, each one a door shut. Most are about the inner life: no harsh speech, no sloth, no false conduct. In the middle stands the one that holds them up: "I will not kill other lives." For Vallalar this is not one virtue among many. It is Jeevakarunyam, the ground of the whole path, and it sits here beside his vow to fix his mind on God alone.

tamil: வெறுக்க மாட்டேன் நின்றனையே விரும்பிப் பிடித்தேன் துயர்சிறிதும்
பொறுக்க மாட்டேன் உலகவர்போல் பொய்யிற் கிடந்து புரண்டினிநான்
சிறுக்க மாட்டேன் அரசேநின் திருத்தாள் ஆணை நின்ஆணை
மறுக்க மாட்டேன் வழங்குவன எல்லாம் வழங்கி வாழியவே.
translit: veṟukka māṭṭēṉ niṉṟaṉaiyē virumpip piṭittēṉ tuyarciṟitum poṟukka māṭṭēṉ ulakavarpōl poyyiṟ kiṭantu puraṇṭiṉināṉ ciṟukka māṭṭēṉ aracēniṉ tiruttāḷ āṇai niṉāṇai maṟukka māṭṭēṉ vaḻaṅkuvaṉa ellām vaḻaṅki vāḻiyavē.
translation: I will not hate. I have desired and held onto you alone. I cannot bear even a little suffering. Like the people of the world, I will not lie in falsehood, wallow, and be diminished anymore. O King, I swear on your sacred feet, I swear on you, I will not refuse. Grant all that you grant, and may you live long.
commentary: The verse is a chain of vows. He will hate no one; he holds to God alone; he will no longer lie in falsehood and shrink like the people of the world. He swears on God's own feet that he will not refuse what God commands. Having given himself completely, he asks God to grant all that God grants, and blesses God in return.

tamil: கருணைப் பெருக்கே ஆனந்தக் கனியே என்னுட் கலந்தொளிரும்
தருணச் சுடரே எனைஈன்ற தாயே என்னைத் தந்தோனே
வருணப் படிக மணிமாலையே மன்றில் நடஞ்செய் வாழ்வேநற்
பொருண்மெய்ப் பதியே இனித்துயரம் பொறுக்க மாட்டேன் கண்டாயே.
translit: karuṇaip perukkē āṉantak kaṉiyē eṉṉuṭ kalantoḷirum taruṇac cuṭarē eṉaiīṉṟa tāyē eṉṉait tantōṉē varuṇap paṭika maṇimālaiyē maṉṟil naṭañcey vāḻvēnaṟ poruṇmeyp patiyē iṉittuyaram poṟukka māṭṭēṉ kaṇṭāyē.
translation: O great flood of compassion! O fruit of bliss! O youthful flame that mingles and shines within me! O mother who gave birth to me! O father who begot me! O garland of beautiful crystal gems! O Life that performs the dance in the Hall! O Lord of good and true substance! From now on, I cannot bear suffering, you see.
commentary: The experience of God's presence makes any remaining suffering feel completely unbearable. Vallalar addresses God with a flood of intimate names: mother, father, and life-giving flame. The maṉṟam, or sacred hall, is the inner space of consciousness where this divine dance of life happens. Having tasted this reality, he can no longer tolerate the pain of the old one.

tamil: திண்ணமும் பழுத்த சிந்தையிலே தித்தித் துலவாச் சுயஞ்சோதி
வண்ணம் பழுத்த தனிப்பழமே மன்றில் விளங்கு மணிச்சுடரே
தண்ணம் பழுத்த மதிஅமுதே தருவாய் இதுவே தருணம்என்றன்
எண்ணம் பழுத்த தினிச்சிறியேன் இறையுந் தரியேன் தரியேனே.
translit: tiṇṇamum paḻutta cintaiyilē tittit tulavāc cuyañcōti vaṇṇam paḻutta taṉippaḻamē maṉṟil viḷaṅku maṇiccuṭarē taṇṇam paḻutta matiamutē taruvāy ituvē taruṇameṉṟaṉ eṇṇam paḻutta tiṉicciṟiyēṉ iṟaiyun tariyēṉ tariyēṉē.
translation: O self-emergent Jothi that sweetly pervades the mind ripened in firmness! O unique fruit ripened in beauty! O gem-like flame that shines in the Hall! O nectar of the moon, ripened in coolness! My thought has ripened. Grant it, this is the moment! From now on, this lowly one cannot endure, not even for an instant, I cannot endure!
commentary: The speaker feels he is spiritually "ripe" and ready for God, making any further delay an agony. He addresses the divine as a self-emergent Jothi, or light, that fills a mind that has become mature and firm. Having reached this point of readiness, he pleads that the moment of union must be now, as he cannot endure waiting any longer.

tamil: நாட்டுக் கிசைந்த மணிமன்றில் ஞான வடிவாய் நடஞ்செயருள்
ஆட்டுக் கிசைந்த பெருங்கருணை அப்பா என்றன் அரசேஎன்
பாட்டுக் கிசைந்த பதியேஓர் பரமா னந்தப் பழமேமேல்
வீட்டுக் கிசைந்த விளக்கேஎன் விவேகம் விளங்க விளக்குகவே.
translit: nāṭṭuk kicainta maṇimaṉṟil ñāṉa vaṭivāy naṭañceyaruḷ āṭṭuk kicainta peruṅkaruṇai appā eṉṟaṉ aracēeṉ pāṭṭuk kicainta patiyēōr paramā ṉantap paḻamēmēl vīṭṭuk kicainta viḷakkēeṉ vivēkam viḷaṅka viḷakkukavē.
translation: O Father of great compassion, who agreed to perform the dance of grace as the form of wisdom in the gem-hall that befits the world! O my King, O Lord who befits my songs, O rare fruit of supreme bliss, O lamp that befits the supreme abode! Illuminate me, that my discernment may shine.
commentary: God's compassionate action in the world is an expression of perfect wisdom. Vallalar asks for this same divine light to illuminate his own mind, sharpening his vivekam, or spiritual discernment. The prayer is for the clarity to see things as they truly are.

tamil: வேதந் தலைமேற் கொளவிரும்பி வேண்டிப் பரவு நினதுமலர்ப்
பாதந் தலைமேற் சூட்டிஎனைப் பணிசெய் திடவும் பணித்தனைநான்
சாதந் தலைமேல் எடுத்தொருவர் தம்பின் செலவும் தரமில்லேன்
translit: vētan talaimēṟ koḷavirumpi vēṇṭip paravu niṉatumalarp pātan talaimēṟ cūṭṭieṉaip paṇicey tiṭavum paṇittaṉaināṉ cātan talaimēl eṭuttoruvar tampiṉ celavum taramillēṉ ētan talaimēṟ cumantēṉuk kiccīr kiṭaittatevvāṟē.
translation: You placed upon my head Your flower-like feet, which the Vedas yearn to place upon their own heads, seeking and praising them, and you commanded me to do your service. I, who am not even worthy to walk behind a man carrying a pot of rice on his head, who carry only blame upon my head, how did I receive this glory?
commentary: The speaker expresses deep humility, feeling completely unworthy of the immense grace he has been given. In this tradition, having a guru's or God's feet placed on one's head is the highest possible blessing. Vallalar notes that even the ancient scriptures, the Vedas, long for this honor. He sees himself as less than the lowliest person, yet he has received this supreme gift, leaving him in a state of wondering gratitude.

tamil: பொய்விட் டகலாப் புலைக்கொடியேன் பொருட்டா இரவில் போந்தொருநின்
கைவிட் டகலாப் பெரும்பொருள்என் கையிற் கொடுத்தே களிப்பித்தாய்
மைவிட் டகலா விழிஇன்ப வல்லி மகிழும் மணவாளா
மெய்விட் டகலா மனத்தவர்க்கு வியப்பாம் உனது மெய்யருளே.
translit: poyviṭ ṭakalāp pulaikkoṭiyēṉ poruṭṭā iravil pōntoruniṉ kaiviṭ ṭakalāp perumporuḷeṉ kaiyiṟ koṭuttē kaḷippittāy maiviṭ ṭakalā viḻiiṉpa valli makiḻum maṇavāḷā meyviṭ ṭakalā maṉattavarkku viyappām uṉatu meyyaruḷē.
translation: For my sake, this lowly, cruel one who never abandons falsehood, you came in the night. You placed in my hand the great treasure that never leaves your own and made me rejoice. O Bridegroom, delighted by the blissful, creeper-like one whose eyes are always dark with kohl! Your true grace is a wonder even to those whose minds never stray from the truth.
commentary: Divine grace is so surprising that it is a wonder even to the most virtuous souls. Vallalar describes himself as deeply flawed, yet God came to him secretly and gave him a priceless treasure: the direct experience of the divine. This grace is a mysterious gift given out of pure compassion. The address to God as the Bridegroom frames this encounter as an act of intimate love.

tamil: சாமத் திரவில் எழுந்தருளித் தமியேன் தூக்கந் தடுத்துமயல்
காமக் கடலைக் கடத்திஅருட் கருணை அமுதங் களித்தளித்தாய்
நாமத் தடிகொண் டடிபெயர்க்கும் நடையார் தமக்கும் கடையானேன்
ஏமத் தருட்பே றடைந்தேன்நான் என்ன தவஞ்செய் திருந்தேனே.
translit: cāmat tiravil eḻuntaruḷit tamiyēṉ tūkkan taṭuttumayal kāmak kaṭalaik kaṭattiaruṭ karuṇai amutaṅ kaḷittaḷittāy nāmat taṭikoṇ ṭaṭipeyarkkum naṭaiyār tamakkum kaṭaiyāṉēṉ ēmat taruṭpē ṟaṭaintēṉnāṉ eṉṉa tavañcey tiruntēṉē.
translation: You came to me in the middle of the night, stopped my lonely sleep, and helped me cross the ocean of delusive passion. You joyfully gave me the nectar of gracious compassion. I, who am lower than even the mendicants who walk measuring their steps with a marked staff, have attained the treasure of your protective grace. What penance could I have possibly performed?
commentary: Divine grace is a direct intervention that can rescue a person from their own inner turmoil. The experience of God's presence is described as a force that stops delusion and worldly desire, replacing them with the "nectar of gracious compassion." Again, Vallalar's extreme self-abasement serves to magnify the sheer generosity of this unearned gift.

tamil: பாதி இரவில் எழுந்தருளிப் பாவி யேனை எழுப்பிஅருட்
சோதி அளித்தென் உள்ளகத்தே சூழ்ந்து கலந்து துலங்குகின்றாய்
நீதி நடஞ்செய் பேரின்ப நிதிநான் பெற்ற நெடும்பேற்றை
ஓதி முடியா தென்போல்இவ் வுலகம் பெறுதல் வேண்டுவனே.
translit: pāti iravil eḻuntaruḷip pāvi yēṉai eḻuppiaruṭ cōti aḷitteṉ uḷḷakattē cūḻntu kalantu tulaṅkukiṉṟāy nīti naṭañcey pēriṉpa nitināṉ peṟṟa neṭumpēṟṟai ōti muṭiyā teṉpōliv vulakam peṟutal vēṇṭuvaṉē.
translation: O treasure of supreme bliss who performs the dance of justice! You came at midnight, woke me, a sinner, and bestowed the Jothi of grace. You surround, merge with, and shine within my very self. The great blessing I have received is impossible to describe. I desire that this world receive it just as I have.
commentary: The personal experience of God's light immediately transforms into a universal wish for all of humanity. After describing how the Jothi (divine light) of grace filled his being, Vallalar’s first impulse is gratitude and a deep desire that every other person in the world might receive this same incredible blessing. This reveals a core principle of his path: enlightenment is not complete until it is shared.
NOTES
Note 242

translit: kaṇṭāyē - mutaṟpatippu, po. ka., ca.mu.ka.
translation: kaṇṭāyē — reading of the first edition, and of the Po. Ka. and S. Mu. Ka. editions.
Note 243

tamil: கொடுத்த - முதற்பதிப்பு, பொ. சு., பி. இரா. ச.மு.க.,
translit: koṭutta - mutaṟpatippu, po. cu., pi. irā. ca.mu.ka.,
translation: koṭutta — reading of the first edition, and of the Po. Su., P. Irā., and S. Mu. Ka. Editions.

translit: appānāṉ paṟpalakāl aṟaivateṉṉē aṭiyēṉ accamelām tuṉpamelām aṟuttuvirain tuvantē ippāril itutaruṇam eṉṉaiaṭain taruḷi eṇṇamelām muṭitteṉṉai ēṉṟukoḷāy eṉilō tappāmal uyirviṭuvēṉ cattiyañcat tiyamniṉ tāḷiṇaikaḷ aṟika:itu tayavuṭaiyōy evarkkum tuppākit tuṇaiyākit tulaṅkiyameyt tuṇaiyē cuttacivā ṉantaaruṭ cōtinaṭat taracē.
translation: Father, what more can I say? I have told you so many times. Cut away all my fear and suffering, come to me quickly and joyfully, and on this earth, at this very moment, reach me with your grace, fulfill all my wishes, and accept me. If you do not, I will surely give up my life. This is the truth, the truth, and your twin feet know it. O Gracious One, true companion who is the brilliant strength and support for all! O King of the Dance, who is the Arut Jothi of Pure Siva-Bliss!
commentary: The pain of being separate from God has become so unbearable that devotion turns into a desperate ultimatum. Vallalar declares that life itself is meaningless without union, vowing to die if God does not accept him at this very moment. This expresses absolute sincerity, where spiritual fulfillment has become more essential than life.

translit: āṇaiuṉmēl āṇaiuṉmēl āṇaiuṉmēl aiyā araikkaṇamum niṉaippirintē iṉittarikka māṭṭēṉ kōṇainilat tavarpēcak kēṭṭatupōl iṉṉum kuṟumpumoḻi cevikaḷuṟak koṇṭiṭavum māṭṭēṉ ūṇaiuṟak kattaiyumnāṉ viṭukiṉṟēṉ nītāṉ uvantuvarāy eṉileṉṟaṉ uyiraiyumviṭ ṭiṭuvēṉ māṇaimaṇip potunaṭañcey vaḷḷālnī eṉatu maṉamaṟivāy iṉamuṉakku vakutturaippa teṉṉē.
translation: I swear it on you, I swear it on you, I swear it on you, my Lord! Henceforth, I cannot bear to be parted from you for even half an instant. I will no longer allow my ears to hear deceitful words, like those spoken by the crooked people of this world. I am giving up food and sleep. If you do not come to me joyfully, I will give up my very life. O great benefactor who dances in the magnificent, gem-like hall! You know my mind; what is the point of my explaining it all to you in detail now?
commentary: To prove his seriousness, the devotee begins to sever all ties to worldly existence. By giving up food, sleep, and even the sound of worldly conversation, he makes his life a single-pointed offering. The triple oath sworn upon God himself is the ultimate expression of commitment, leaving no room for retreat. His plea is simple: since you already know my heart, there is nothing left to say; only your arrival matters.

translit: paṭamuṭiyā tiṉittuyaram paṭamuṭiyā taracē paṭṭatellām pōtumintap payantīrttip poḻuteṉ uṭaluyirā tiyaellām nīeṭuttut koṇṭuṉ uṭaluyirā tiyaellām uvanteṉakkē aḷippāy vaṭaluṟuciṟ ṟampalattē vāḻvāyeṉ kaṇṇuḷ maṇiyēeṉ kurumaṇiyē māṇikka maṇiyē naṭaṉacikā maṇiyēeṉ navamaṇiyē ñāṉa naṉmaṇiyē poṉmaṇiyē naṭarāja maṇiyē.
translation: I cannot bear it, I can no longer bear this suffering, O King! All that I have endured is enough. End this fear and, this very moment, take my body, life, and all that I am, and in return, joyfully grant me Your body, Your life, and all that You are. O You who live in the little hall at Vadalur! O jewel within my eye! O my Guru-jewel! O ruby-jewel! O crest-jewel of dance! O my nine-gem jewel! O good jewel of wisdom! O golden jewel! O jewel of the King of Dance!
commentary: Here, the purpose of his desperate plea becomes clear: he asks for a complete and mutual exchange. He wants God to take his mortal body and life and, in return, grant him God's own immortal nature. He asks for a total transformation of being. The string of loving names he calls God, like "ruby-jewel" and "jewel within my eye," reveals the deep intimacy behind this radical request.

translit: vāḻaiyaṭi vāḻaieṉa vantatiruk kūṭṭa marapiṉilyāṉ oruvaṉaṉṟō vakaiaṟiyēṉ inta ēḻaipaṭum pāṭuṉakkun tiruvuḷaccam matamō itutakumō itumuṟaiyō itutaruman tāṉō māḻaimaṇip potunaṭañcey vaḷḷālyāṉ uṉakku makaṉalaṉō nīeṉakku vāyttatantai alaiyō kōḻaiula kuyirttuyaram iṉippoṟukka māṭṭēṉ koṭuttaruḷniṉ aruḷoḷiyaik koṭuttaruḷip poḻutē.
translation: Am I not one in the sacred lineage that comes in unbroken succession? I am one who does not know the way. Is the suffering this poor soul endures also acceptable to your divine will? Is this fitting? Is this proper? Is this justice itself? O great benefactor who dances in the beautiful, gem-like hall! Am I not your son? Are you not the father destined for me? I can no longer bear the suffering of the beings in this feeble world. Grant me your light of grace, grant it this very moment!
commentary: Vallalar shifts his argument, appealing to God's sense of justice and their father-son relationship. He questions if it is right for God to let his own child suffer. Crucially, his motivation expands beyond his personal pain: he asks for the light of grace because he can no longer stand the suffering of all other beings in the world. This connects his own liberation to his compassion for all life.

translit: ceyvakaieṉ eṉattikaittēṉ tikaiyēleṉ ṟorunāḷ tirumēṉi kāṭṭieṉait teḷivittāy nīyē poyvakaiaṉ ṟituniṉatu puntiaṟin tatuvē poṉṉaṭiyē tuṇaieṉanāṉ eṉuyirvait tiruntēṉ eyvakaieṉ namperumāṉ aruḷpurivāṉ eṉṟē entaivara vetirpārttē iṉṉumiruk kiṉṟēṉ aivakaiiv uyirttuyaram iṉippoṟukka māṭṭēṉ aruṭcōtip perumporuḷai aḷittaruḷip poḻutē.
translation: I was bewildered, wondering what to do. It was you who once clarified my mind, showing me your sacred form and saying, “Do not be dismayed.” This is no lie; your own intelligence knows it is true. I have sustained my life with the thought, “Your golden feet are my only refuge.” I am still waiting, anticipating my Father’s arrival, believing, “Our great Lord will surely bestow his grace.” I can no longer bear these five-fold sufferings of life. Grant me the Great Substance of the Arut Jothi, grant it this very moment!
commentary: He reminds God of a past mystical experience, a vision where God appeared and promised him not to fear. Vallalar explains that this memory has been his sole reason for living, but his capacity to endure the world's suffering is now exhausted. His plea for the "Great Substance of the Arut Jothi" is a call for God to fulfill that earlier promise and finally end his trial.

translit: muṉorunāḷ mayaṅkiṉaṉnī mayaṅkēleṉ ṟeṉakku muṉṉiṉuruk kāṭṭiṉaināṉ mukamalarntiṅ kiruntēṉ iṉṉumvarak kāṇēṉniṉ varavaietir pārttē eṇṇieṇṇi varuntukiṉṟēṉ eṉṉaceyvēṉ antō aṉṉaiyiṉum tayavuṭaiyāy niṉtayavai niṉaittē āruyirvait tirukkiṉṟēṉ āṇaiitu kaṇṭāy eṉirukaṇ maṇiyēeṉ aṟivēeṉ aṉpē eṉṉuyirkkup peruntuṇaiyē eṉṉuyirnā yakaṉē.
translation: One day, when I was bewildered, you told me not to be and showed me your form. My face blossomed, and I have stayed here since. I still do not see you coming; I suffer, thinking and thinking, as I watch for your arrival. What can I do? Alas! You who are more compassionate than a mother, I hold on to my precious life only by thinking of your compassion. This is my vow, you see. O apple of my two eyes, my intelligence, my love, O great companion to my life, O Lord of my life.
commentary: Again, he recalls the divine vision that gave him hope, contrasting that moment of joy with his current pain of waiting. He declares that the only thing keeping him alive is his faith in God's compassion, which he describes as even greater than a mother's.
