sections.title: The State of the Divine Feet

translit: ulakupal kōṭi kōṭikaḷ iṭaṅkoḷ uvappilā aṇṭattiṉ pakuti alakukāṇ pariya periyakūṭ ṭatta avaielām puṟattiṟaic cārpil vilakuṟā aṇuvil kōṭiyuḷ orukūṟ ṟirunteṉa viruntaṉa miṭaintē ilakupoṟ potuvil naṭampuri taruṇat teṉparvāṉ tiruvaṭi nilaiyē.
translation: The many billions and billions of worlds, the regions of the cosmos that are beyond measure, all these great assemblies are packed together. In relation to the Lord who is beyond them, they are like one-billionth of an inseparable atom. This, they say, is the state of the magnificent Divine Feet at the moment of the dance in the radiant Golden Hall.
commentary: To express the sheer immensity of God, Vallalar uses a startling comparison. He says that the entire physical universe, with its billions of worlds, is less than a tiny fraction of a single atom when compared to the Lord. This almost unimaginable smallness is what he calls the "state of the Divine Feet," the ground upon which God stands.

translit: taṭaiyuṟāp piramaṉ viṇṭurut tiraṉmā yēccuraṉ catācivaṉ vintu naṭaiyuṟāp piramam uyarparā catti navilpara civameṉum ivarkaḷ iṭaiyuṟāt tirucciṟ ṟampalat tāṭum iṭatukāṟ kaṭaiviral nakattiṉ kaṭaiyuṟu tukaḷeṉ ṟaṟintaṉaṉ ataṉmēṟ kaṇṭaṉaṉ tiruvaṭi nilaiyē.
translation: Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, Mahesvara, Sadasiva, Vindu (the subtle point), Nadam (the principle of vibration), Brahman that is beyond movement, the exalted Para Sakti, and the one proclaimed as Para Sivam, I have known that all of these beings, in relation to the One who dances in the ceaseless Thiru Chitrambalam, are but a final particle of dust on the nail of the little toe of His left foot. Above that, I have seen the state of the Divine Feet.
commentary: This verse makes a radical claim about the divine hierarchy. The great gods of the Hindu pantheon, from Brahma and Vishnu up to the formless realities like Para Sivam, are traditionally seen as the highest powers in the cosmos. Vallalar states that all of them, together, are less than a particle of dust on the toenail of the ultimate God who dances in the Thiru Chitrambalam (sacred hall of consciousness). His vision is of a God who transcends all other gods.

translit: aṭarmalat taṭaiyāl taṭaiyuṟum ayaṉmāl araṉmayēc curaṉcatā civaṉvāṉ paṭartaru vintu piraṇavap piramam paraiparam paraṉeṉum ivarkaḷ cuṭarmaṇip potuvil tirunaṭam puriyum tuṇaiyaṭip pātukaip puṟattē iṭarkeṭa vayaṅku tukaḷeṉa aṟintē ēttuvaṉ tiruvaṭi nilaiyē.
translation: Brahma, Vishnu, Aran, Mahesvara, and Sadasiva, who are obstructed by the impediment of dense primal impurity; the spreading Vindu, Pranava, Brahman, Parai, Param, and Paran, I have known them to be like shining specks of dust, their troubles removed, on the outside of the sandals of the twin feet of the One who performs the sacred dance in the radiant Jeweled Hall. And so, I praise the state of the Divine Feet.
commentary: Reinforcing the previous verse's point, Vallalar again lists the great cosmic gods and principles. He notes that they are all bound by malam (primal impurity), an inherent limitation. In his vision, these powerful beings are like specks of dust on the outside of the sandals worn by the one true God. By placing them on the sandals, not even on the foot itself, he emphasizes their external and secondary relationship to the supreme reality he has realized.

translit: ikattuḻal pakutit tēvarin tiraṉmāl piramaṉī cāṉaṉē mutalām makattuḻal camaya vāṉavar maṉṟiṉ malaraṭip pātukaip puṟattum pukattaram poruntā malattuṟu ciṟiya puḻukkaḷeṉ ṟaṟintaṉaṉ ataṉmēl cekattoṭar pikantār uḷattamar oḷiyil terintaṉaṉ tiruvaṭi nilaiyē.
translation: The devas of this world who toil here, such as Indra, Vishnu, Brahma, and Isana, along with the celestial beings of the great, toiling religions, I have known them to be tiny worms trapped in malam, lacking the worth to even approach the outside of the sandals on the flower-like feet in the Hall. Above all that, in the Light that dwells within the hearts of those who have transcended worldly attachments, I have perceived the state of the Divine Feet.
commentary: Vallalar now reveals where the ultimate reality can truly be found: not in heavens ruled by gods, but within the human heart. He uses the shocking image of "tiny worms" to describe the celestial beings (devas) of various religions, emphasizing their powerlessness. In contrast, he perceives the true divine state as a Light shining inside those who have let go of worldly desire. This marks a deep shift from external worship to internal realization; the highest truth is present within you, accessible through inner purity.

translit: poṉvaṇap poruppoṉ ṟatucaku ṇāntam pōntavāṉ muṭiyatāṅ kataṉmēl maṉvaṇac cōtit tampamoṉ ṟatumā vayintuvān tattatāṇ ṭataṉmēl eṉvaṇac cōtik koṭipara nātān tattilē ilaṅkiya tataṉmēl taṉvaṇam maṇakkum oḷimala rākat taḻuviṉaṉ tiruvaṭi nilaiyē.
translation: A golden mountain forms the vast crown that reaches the end of the manifest realm with attributes. Above it, a pillar of enduring, brilliant Jothi stands at the end of the great Vaindava. Above that, a flag of my brilliant Jothi shines at the end of Paranada. Above that, as a flower of light, fragrant with its own nature, I embraced the state of the Divine Feet.
commentary: Vallalar maps his spiritual ascent to the highest state using cosmic symbols. The ascent begins at the edge of the manifest universe with its forms (saguṇa), represented as a mountain. It moves through a pillar of Jothi (divine Light) signifying the point of creation (Vaindava), and a flag of light for the primordial sound (Paranada). At the peak, he experiences the divine as a "flower of light" that he embraces directly, showing that realization culminates in an intimate, loving union with the ultimate.

translit: maṇmutal pakarpoṉ vaṇṇatta vuḷavāṉ maṟṟavaṟ ṟuṭpuṟaṅ kīḻmēl aṇṇuṟu naṉantar pakkameṉ ṟivaṟṟiṉ amaintaṉa cattikaḷ avaṟṟiṉ kaṇṇuṟu cattar eṉumiru puṭaikkum karuturu mutaliya viḷaṅka naṇṇuṟum upayam eṉamaṉṟil eṉṟu naviṉṟaṉar tiruvaṭi nilaiyē.
translation: They have declared the state of the sacred feet to be the instrumental cause in the Hall. It enables the conceived forms and other attributes to manifest for both the Saktis and their corresponding Saktas. These Saktis are established within and without, below and above, in the vast spaces, and on the sides of all that exists, from the earth element up to the golden-hued realm.
commentary: The ultimate reality, symbolized by the sacred feet, is the very principle that allows the universe to take shape. This divine state is the "instrumental cause" (ubhayam) which makes it possible for all powers (Saktis) and the conscious beings who wield them (Saktas) to exist with distinct forms. This shows that God is the active, enabling presence that gives form and function to everything in existence, at every moment and in every place.

translit: tokaiyaḷa vivaieṉ ṟaṟivarum pakutit tollaiyiṉ ellaiyum avaṟṟiṉ vakaiyoṭu viriyum uḷappaṭa āṅkē maṉṉieṅ kaṇumiru pāṟkut takaiyuṟu mutalā vaṇaṅkaṭai yākat tayaṅkamaṟ ṟatuvatu karuvic cikaiyuṟa upayam eṉamaṉṟil āṭum eṉparāl tiruvaṭi nilaiyē.
translation: They say the state of the sacred feet dances in the Hall as the instrumental cause. This dance happens within the unknowable bounds of ancient Prakṛti, including all its types and expansions, abiding there and everywhere. It allows the principles, from the qualified primary cause down to the final object of worship, to shine forth for both sides, and allows their respective instruments to reach their peak.
commentary: The divine dance is the continuous act of creation that brings the entire universe into being. This dance occurs within Prakṛti (primordial matter), activating it and causing all of existence to unfold, from the highest universal causes down to the simple objects people worship. This presents a living cosmos, constantly animated by the divine presence. Creation is an ongoing dance that sustains everything that is.

translit: maṉṟaōṅ kiyamā māyaiyiṉ pēta vakaitokai virieṉa malinta oṉṟiṉoṉ ṟaṉanta kōṭikō ṭikaḷā uṟṟaṉa maṟṟavai ellām niṉṟaan nilaiyiṉ uruccuvai viḷaṅka niṉṟacat tikaḷoṭu cattar ceṉṟati karippa naṭittiṭum potuvil eṉparāl tiruvaṭi nilaiyē.
translation: They say the state of the sacred feet dances in the Common Space. This dance allows the established Saktis and Saktas to go and exercise their authority, making manifest the form and essence of all things in their respective states. "All things" refers to the distinctions, types, totals, and expansions of Mahāmāyā, exalted in the Hall, which abound as endless crores upon crores, one arising from another.
commentary: The "state of the sacred feet" is the dance in the common space (potu). That dance lets the powers (Saktis) and those who wield them carry out their work, so that every form and essence in creation becomes manifest. All the countless levels of great māyā arise from it. Everything that appears, however vast, moves by the dance of the sacred feet.

translit: pēcumōṅ kāram īṟatāp pēcāp periyaōṅ kāramē mutalā ēcaṟum aṅkam upāṅkamvē ṟaṅkam eṉṟavaṟ ṟavaṇavaṇ icainta mācaṟu catti cattarāṇ ṭamaittu maṉati kāramain tiyaṟṟat tēcucey taṇipoṉ ṉampalat tāṭum eṉparāl tiruvaṭi nilaiyē.
translation: They say the state of the sacred feet dances in the beautiful, radiant Golden Hall. It establishes flawless Saktis and Saktas there in their respective places, enabling them to perform the five great cosmic functions. This occurs throughout the flawless main limbs, secondary limbs, and other limbs of creation, which extend from the great unuttered Omkara as the beginning to the uttered Omkara as the end.
commentary: The "state of the sacred feet" is a poetic way of describing God's dynamic presence, which "dances" in the Ponnampalam (Golden Hall of consciousness). This divine power organizes the entire cosmos, from the unmanifest, unuttered sound of creation (Omkara) to the material world. It delegates authority to the divine energies (Saktis) and their conscious agents (Saktas), empowering them to carry out the five fundamental cosmic functions like creation and preservation.

translit: paraitaru cutta nilaimutal atītap pativarai niṟuviāṅ kataṉmēl uraitara oṇṇā veṟuveḷi veṭṭa veṟuveḷi eṉa:ula kuṇarnta puraiaṟum iṉpa aṉupavam taraṟkōr tiruvuruk koṇṭupoṟ potuvil tiraiaṟum iṉpa naṭampuri kiṉṟa eṉparāl tiruvaṭi nilaiyē.
translation: They say the state of the sacred feet performs the dance of unveiled bliss in the Golden Common Space. Having established everything from the pure state given by Parai up to the transcendent Lord, and even higher, in what the world knows as the indescribable veṟuveḷi and veṭṭaveṟuveḷi, it takes a sacred form to grant the flawless experience of bliss.
commentary: The divine presence is a "dance of unveiled bliss" happening in the Golden Common Space. This power is the foundation for all reality, establishing everything from the highest divine principles like Parai (the supreme creative energy) up to the ultimate, indescribable void, or "utter empty space" (veṭṭaveṟuveḷi). Though its nature is formless emptiness, it graciously takes on a sacred form for one reason: to give souls the direct experience of flawless joy.

translit: karuttaṉaieṉ kaṇmaṇiyaik kaṇṇutalaip peruṅkaruṇaik kaṭalai vētat tiruttaṉaieṉ civapatiyait tīṅkaṉiyait teḷḷamutat teḷivai vāṉil oruttaṉaieṉ uyirttuṇaiyai uyirkkuyirai uyirkkuṇarvai uṇartta ṉāti aruttaṉaicciṟ ṟampalatteṉ aruṭperuñcō tiyaippeṟṟēṉ accō accō.
translation: I have attained the Creator, the apple of my eye, the one with the forehead eye, the ocean of great compassion, the sacred one of the Vedas, my Lord Sivapati, the sweet fruit, the clarity of pure ambrosia, the unique one in the heavens, my life-companion, the life of my life, the consciousness of my life, the beginningless, precious one who grants realization, my ArutPerunJothi in the Chitrambalam. Oh wonder, oh wonder!
commentary: This is a cry of ecstatic fulfillment, announcing the attainment of God. Vallalar describes the divine in the most intimate terms: the apple of his eye, his life's companion, the very consciousness within his own life. This ultimate reality, which he names ArutPerunJothi (Vast Grace-Light), is experienced within the Chitrambalam (the inner space of consciousness).

translit: meyyaṉaieṉ tuyartavirtta vimalaṉaieṉ itayattē viḷaṅku kiṉṟa tuyyaṉaimeyt tuṇaivaṉaivāṉ turiyanilait talaivaṉaicciṟ cukantan tāṉaic ceyyaṉaiveṇ niṟattaṉaieṉ civapatiyai oṉṟāṉa teyvan taṉṉai ayyaṉaicciṟ ṟampalatteṉ aruṭperuñcō tiyaippeṟṟēṉ accō accō.
translation: I have attained the True One, the immaculate one who dispelled my sorrow, the pure one who shines in my heart, the true companion, the Lord of the celestial state of Turiya, the one who gave the bliss of consciousness, the ruddy one, the white-complexioned one, my Lord Sivapati, the one and only God, the Master, my ArutPerunJothi in the Chitrambalam. Oh wonder, oh wonder!
commentary: The experience of God is the experience of absolute Truth and purity, dispelling all sorrow. This divine companion is the lord of Turiya, the fourth state of consciousness that lies beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. Vallalar's wonder comes from realizing this ultimate state and its master, the one and only God, who shines within his own heart.

translit: epporuḷum evvuyirum evvulakum viḷaṅkaviḷak kiṭuvāṉ taṉṉaic ceppariya periyaoru civapatiyaic civakatiyaic civapō kattait tuppuravu peṟaeṉakkē aruḷamutam tuṇintaḷitta tuṇaiyai eṉṟaṉ appaṉaicciṟ ṟampalatteṉ aruṭperuñcō tiyaippeṟṟēṉ accō accō.
translation: I have attained the one who illuminates all things, all beings, and all worlds that they may shine; the great, indescribable Lord Sivapati, the state of Siva-gati, the experience of Siva-bhogam; the companion who, for my perfection, resolved to grant me the ambrosia of grace; my Father, my ArutPerunJothi in the Chitrambalam. Oh wonder, oh wonder!
commentary: God is the light that illuminates everything in existence, allowing all beings and worlds to shine. To attain him is to attain the final spiritual destination, Siva-gati (the state of Siva), and experience its supreme bliss, Siva-bhogam. For Vallalar, this attainment feels like a personal gift of grace from a loving Father.

translit: piṟiveṉaittun tōṟṟāteṉ uḷaṅkalanta peruntakaiem perumāṉ taṉṉaic ceṟivaṉaittum eṉmaṉattuk kaḷitteṉakkup peruṅkaḷippuc ceytāṉ taṉṉai muṟiveṉaittum iṉṟiaruḷ amutuṇavu koṭutteṉakku muṉṉiṉ ṟāṉai aṟivaṉaicciṟ ṟampalatteṉ aruṭperuñcō tiyaippeṟṟēṉ accō accō.
translation: I have attained my Lord, the great, noble one who merged with my soul without a trace of separation; the one who gave my mind every fullness and brought me immense joy; the one who stood before me, feeding me the ambrosia of grace without interruption; the embodiment of knowledge, my ArutPerunJothi in the Chitrambalam. Oh wonder, oh wonder!
commentary: The wonder here is the completeness of the union. God merges with the soul so perfectly that no sense of separation remains. This is a continuous state of being nurtured, where God himself provides uninterrupted nourishment through the "ambrosia of grace." The experience is one of total fulfillment and communion with the divine, who is the very embodiment of knowledge.

translit: poṉpuṉaiuḷ ḷoḷikkoḷiyaip pūraṇamām perumporuḷaip puṉitan taṉṉai eṉpiḻaiyaip poṟutteṉaiyum ēṉṟukoṇṭa peruṅkaruṇai iyaṟkai taṉṉai iṉpiṉaieṉ itayattē iruntaruḷum peruvāḻvai eṉṉuḷ ōṅkum aṉpiṉaicciṟ ṟampalatteṉ aruṭperuñcō tiyaippeṟṟēṉ accō accō.
translation: I have attained the light of the inner light adorned in gold, the great substance that is fullness, holiness itself, the very nature of great compassion that forgave my faults and accepted me, the one who is bliss, the great life that graciously abides in my heart, the love that soars within me, my ArutPerunJothi in the Chitrambalam. Oh wonder, oh wonder!
commentary: God is the light within our own inner light, the absolute fullness and holiness at the very core of our being. This divine reality is defined by great compassion, a nature that forgives all personal faults and accepts the soul. This is why God is experienced as pure bliss and love abiding within one's own heart.

translit: ittaṉaieṉ ṟiṭamuṭiyāc cattielām uṭaiyāṉai ellām valla cittaṉaieṉ civapatiyait teyvamelām virittaṭakkum teyvan taṉṉai ettaṉaiyum eṉpiḻaikaḷ poṟuttataṉip peruntāyai eṉṉai īṉṟa attaṉaicciṟ ṟampalatteṉ aruṭperuñcō tiyaippeṟṟēṉ accō accō.
translation: I have attained Him who possesses all powers that cannot be quantified, the all-powerful Siddha, my Sivapati, the Divinity who both emanates and encompasses all other divinities, the singular great Mother who forgave my countless faults, the Father who gave me birth, my ArutPerunJothi in the Chitrambalam, oh wonder, oh wonder!
commentary: God is both the infinite, all-powerful source from whom all other gods and powers emerge, and at the same time, an intimate, personal parent. Vallalar calls this being a Siddha (a perfected one), his Father, and a great Mother who forgives countless mistakes. The ultimate reality is deeply relational and merciful.

translit: emmaiyumeṉ taṉaippiriyā teṉṉuḷamē iṭaṅkoṇṭa iṟaivaṉ taṉṉai immaiyileṉ taṉakkaḻiyāt tiruvaṭivam tantāṉai ellām valla cemmaitaru cittaṉaieṉ civapatiyait teḷḷamutat tiraḷai eṉṟaṉ ammaiyaicciṟ ṟampalatteṉ aruṭperuñcō tiyaippeṟṟēṉ accō accō.
translation: I have attained the Lord who, never separating from me, took my own heart as His place; Him who gave me an imperishable sacred form in this very life; the all-powerful, perfection-granting Siddha; my Sivapati; a mass of clear amrita; my Mother; my ArutPerunJothi in the Chitrambalam, oh wonder, oh wonder!
commentary: Here, God has made Vallalar's own heart His home. This verse also states one of the most distinctive claims of Vallalar's path: that grace can grant an "imperishable sacred form" in this very life. This divine presence is experienced as a Mother, a Lord, and a mass of pure amrita, the nectar of immortality.

translit: eṉṉaiyumeṉ poruḷaiyumeṉ āviyaiyum tāṉkoṇṭiṅ keṉpāl aṉpāl taṉṉaiyumtaṉ poruḷaiyumtaṉ āviyaiyum kaḷittaḷitta talaivaṉ taṉṉai muṉṉaiyumpiṉ ṉaiyumeṉakkē muḻuttuṇaiyāy iruntamuḻu mutalvaṉ taṉṉai aṉṉaiyaicciṟ ṟampalatteṉ aruṭperuñcō tiyaippeṟṟēṉ accō accō.
translation: I have attained the Master who, taking me, my possessions, and my very soul, then out of love for me, joyfully gave Himself, His possessions, and His very soul in return; the absolute Primal Being who was my complete companion before and has been ever since; the Mother; my ArutPerunJothi in the Chitrambalam, oh wonder, oh wonder!
commentary: Spiritual union is a total, mutual self-giving. The soul surrenders everything it is and has, and in response, God joyfully gives His entire being in return. This is a loving exchange that makes God the soul's constant companion, the source of its being, and its own Mother.

translit: eṇṇalaivē ṟiraṅkalainiṉ eṇṇamelām tarukiṉṟōmiṉṉē eṉṟeṉ kaṇnirampa oḷikāṭṭik karuttilamarn tirukkiṉṟa karuttaṉ taṉṉaip puṇṇiyaṉai uḷattūṟum puttamutai meyiṉpap poruḷai eṉṟaṉ aṇṇalaiciṟ ṟampalatteṉ aruṭperuñcō tiyaippeṟṟēṉ accō accō.
translation: I have attained the Master who, saying, "Do not worry, do not grieve; We grant all your heart's desires this very instant," showed me light until my eyes overflowed and now resides in my consciousness; the Virtuous One, the fresh amrita springing forth in my heart, the substance of true bliss, my great Lord, my ArutPerunJothi in the Chitrambalam, oh wonder, oh wonder!
commentary: God's presence brings an end to all spiritual anxiety. Instead of striving and worrying, the devotee receives a direct, personal assurance from God, who promises to fulfill every need instantly. This is experienced as a tangible inner light and a feeling of bliss, which Vallalar compares to amrita, the sweet nectar of immortality, bubbling up within him.

translit: cātiyainīḷ camayattai matattaielām viṭuvitteṉ taṉṉai ñāṉa nītiyilē cuttaciva caṉmārkka nilaitaṉilē niṟutti ṉāṉaip pātiyaioṉ ṟāṉavaṉaip paramparaṉaip parāparaṉaip patia ṉāti ātiyaicciṟ ṟampalatteṉ aruṭperuñcō tiyaippeṟṟēṉ accō accō.
translation: I have attained Him who made me abandon caste, far-reaching religions, and creeds, and established me in the law of wisdom, in the state of the Suddha Siva Sanmarkkam; Him who is the half and the one, the Transcendent Lord, the Transcendent-Immanent One, the Master, the beginningless Primal Origin, my ArutPerunJothi in the Chitrambalam, oh wonder, oh wonder!
commentary: True spiritual life, as Vallalar describes it, lies beyond the boundaries of all organized religions. He celebrates that God has personally liberated him from the divisions of caste, creed, and religious doctrine. Instead, he is established in a universal path called Suddha Siva Sanmarkkam, a state of pure wisdom (Gnana) and direct union with the divine, which is open to all.
NOTES
Note 323

translit: civapōkattē - mutaṟpatippu. po. cu. patippu.
translation: civapōkattē — reading of the first edition and of the Po. Su. edition.
Note 324

translit: tarukiṉṟām - pi. irā. patippu.
translation: tarukiṉṟām — reading of the P. Irā. Edition.

translit: aruṭcōtit teyvameṉai āṇṭukoṇṭa teyvam ampalattē āṭukiṉṟa āṉantat teyvam poruṭcārum maṟaikaḷelām pōṟṟukiṉṟa teyvam pōtāntat teyvamuyar nātāntat teyvam iruṭpāṭu nīkkioḷi īntaruḷun teyvam eṇṇiyanāṉ eṇṇiyavā ṟeṉakkaruḷun teyvam teruṭpāṭal uvanteṉaiyum civamākkum teyvam ciṟcapaiyil viḷaṅkukiṉṟa teyvamatē teyvam.
translation: The divine Grace-Light, the divinity that has taken me as its own, the divinity of bliss that dances in the sacred hall. It is the divinity praised by all the Vedas rich in meaning, the divinity beyond perception, the sublime divinity beyond sound. It is the divinity that removes the affliction of darkness and graciously gives light, the divinity that grants me whatever I desire. It is the divinity that delights in songs of clarity and makes even me into Sivam. The divinity that shines in the Chit Sabhai is the one true divinity.
commentary: The one true divinity is the Grace-Light (Aruṭjōti) that actively engages with the soul. This God is a dynamic presence who takes you as its own, dances in bliss, removes ignorance, grants your prayers, and finally transforms you into a divine being (Sivam). Vallalar concludes that only this responsive, light-giving divinity, which he experiences in the Chit Sabhai (hall of consciousness), is real.

translit: ellāñcey vallateyvam eṅkumniṟai teyvam eṉṉuyiril kalanteṉakkē iṉpanalkum teyvam nallārkku nallateyvam naṭuvāṉa teyvam naṟcapaiyil āṭukiṉṟa naṭarājat teyvam kallārkkuṅ kaṟṟavarkkuṅ kaḷipparuḷun teyvam kāraṇamān teyvamaruṭ pūraṇamān teyvam cellāta nilaikaḷelāñ cellukiṉṟa teyvam ciṟcapaiyil viḷaṅkukiṉṟa teyvamatē teyvam.
translation: The all-powerful divinity that can do anything, the divinity that fills all space, the divinity that has mingled with my very life and gives me bliss. It is the divinity that is good to the good, the impartial divinity, the divine Nataraja dancing in the sacred hall. It is the divinity that graciously gives joy to the unlearned and the learned alike, the divinity that is the First Cause, the divinity that is the fullness of grace. It is the divinity that reaches all unreachable states. The divinity that shines in the Chit Sabhai is the one true divinity.
commentary: God's power and presence are universal and impartial. This divinity can do anything and is everywhere, yet is also intimately mingled with your own life, bringing personal bliss. Joy is given equally to the wise and the unlearned, because this God, the dancing Nataraja, is the very fullness of grace and the ultimate cause of all that exists.

translit: tāyākit tantaiyumāyt tāṅkukiṉṟa teyvam taṉṉainikar illāta taṉittalaimait teyvam vāyāra vāḻttukiṉṟōr maṉattamarnta teyvam malaraṭieṉ ceṉṉimicai vaittaperun teyvam kāyātu kaṉiyākik kalantiṉikkun teyvam karuṇainitit teyvammuṟṟuṅ kāṭṭuvikkun teyvam cēyāka eṉaivaḷarkkun teyvamakā teyvam ciṟcapaiyil āṭukiṉṟa teyvamatē teyvam.
translation: The divinity that sustains me as both mother and father, the peerless, sovereign divinity. It is the divinity that abides in the minds of those who praise it with full hearts, the great divinity that placed its flower-like feet upon my head. It is the divinity that is sweet like a perfectly ripened fruit, mingling with me, the divinity that is a treasury of compassion, the divinity that reveals all. It is the great divinity, the supreme divinity, that raises me as its own child. The divinity that dances in the Chit Sabhai is the one true divinity.
commentary: The focus now becomes intensely personal, describing God's relationship to the soul. God is a loving parent, a sweet fruit melting into one's being, and a compassionate guide. The image of the divine placing its feet on his head signifies a direct blessing and initiation, showing that the path to the Chit Sabhai is one of intimate love and surrender.

translit: eṉṉitaya kamalattē iruntaruḷun teyvam eṉṉiraṇṭu kaṇmaṇikkuḷ ilaṅkukiṉṟa teyvam poṉṉaṭieṉ ceṉṉiyilē poruntavaitta teyvam poyyāta teyvamiṭar ceyyāta teyvam aṉṉiyamal lātateyvam aṟivāṉa teyvam avvaṟivuk kaṟivāmeṉ aṉpāṉa teyvam ceṉṉilaiyil cemporuḷāyt tikaḻkiṉṟa teyvam ciṟcapaiyil viḷaṅkukiṉṟa teyvamatē teyvam.
translation: The divinity that graciously abides in the lotus of my heart, the divinity that shines from within the pupils of my two eyes. It is the divinity that placed its golden feet perfectly upon my head, the divinity that is never false, the divinity that does no harm. It is the divinity that is not other than me, the divinity that is pure consciousness, the consciousness of that consciousness, my beloved divinity. It is the divinity that shines as the ultimate reality in the highest state. The divinity that shines in the Chit Sabhai is the one true divinity.
commentary: This verse makes the teaching's most direct statement of non-separation. God is not simply inside the heart or behind the eyes; it is "not other than me." Vallalar describes divinity as pure consciousness, and, deeper still, as the awareness that perceives that consciousness. This is the core of the experience in the Chit Sabhai: the realization that the divine you seek is your own fundamental being.

translit: eṇṇiyavā viḷaiyāṭeṉ ṟeṉaiaḷitta teyvam ellāñcey vallacittē eṉakkīnta teyvam naṇṇiyapoṉ ṉampalattē naṭampuriyun teyvam nāṉākit tāṉāki naṇṇukiṉṟa teyvam paṇṇiyaeṉ pūcaiyilē palittaperun teyvam pāṭukiṉṟa maṟaimuṭiyil āṭukiṉṟa teyvam tiṇṇiyaṉeṉ ṟeṉaiulakam ceppavaitta teyvam ciṟcapaiyil viḷaṅkukiṉṟa teyvamatē teyvam.
translation: The divinity that created me, telling me to play as I desire; the divinity that bestowed on me the siddhi to do all things. It is the divinity that performs its dance in the golden hall it has reached; the divinity that draws near, being both itself and me. It is the great divinity that came to fruition in the worship I performed; the divinity that dances on the crest of the chanted Vedas. It is the divinity that caused the world to call me steadfast. The divinity that shines in the Chit Sabhai is the one true divinity.
commentary: The fruits of divine union become manifest in the world. Vallalar describes receiving the freedom to "play as I desire" and the siddhi (spiritual power) to do all things, indicating that grace empowers action, not negates it. His own worship has come to fruition, and his spiritual maturity is now recognized by others. All these outer signs are the result of the inner reality where the soul and the divine become one in the Chit Sabhai.

translit: iccaielām eṉakkaḷittē eṉaikkalanta teyvam iṟantavarkaḷ aṉaivaraiyum eḻuppukiṉṟa teyvam eccamayat teyvamuntāṉ eṉaniṟainta teyvam ellāñcey vallateyvam eṉatukula teyvam piccakaṟṟum perunteyvam civakāmi eṉumōr peṇkoṇṭa teyvameṅkum kaṇkaṇṭa teyvam ceccaimalareṉaviḷaṅkun tirumēṉit teyvam ciṟcapaiyil viḷaṅkukiṉṟa teyvamatē teyvam.
translation: The God who granted all my desires and united with me, the God who raises all who have died, the God who is immanent as the God of every religion, the all-powerful God who can do anything, my ancestral God, the great God who removes delusion, the God who took a woman named Sivakami, a God witnessed everywhere, the God whose sacred form shines like the red ixora flower, the God shining in the Hall of Consciousnessis the true God.
commentary: This verse presents God's ultimate, universal power. It makes two remarkable claims: that this God is the same divinity worshiped in all religions, and that it holds the power to raise the dead. While referencing Sivakami (the consort of the dancing God at Chidambaram) grounds the vision in tradition, the message is one of radical inclusivity. This God, who is beyond all limits and present in all faiths, is the very same light that shines within the Chit Sabhai (hall of consciousness).

translit: cākāta varameṉakkē tantataṉit teyvam caṉmārkka capaiyileṉait taṉikkavaitta teyvam mākāta lāleṉakku vāyttaoru teyvam mātavarā tiyarellām vāḻttukiṉṟa teyvam ēkāta nilaiataṉmēl eṉaiēṟṟum teyvam eṇṇutoṟum eṉṉuḷattē iṉikkiṉṟa teyvam tēkāti ulakamelāñ ceyappaṇitta teyvam ciṟcapaiyil viḷaṅkukiṉṟa teyvamatē teyvam.
translation: The unique God who gave me the boon of never dying, the God who placed me alone in the Sanmarkkam assembly, a God who came to be mine through great love, the God whom great ascetics and all others praise, the God who raises me to the changeless state and beyond, the God who sweetens my heart each time I think of him, the God who ordained the creation of the body and all worlds, the God shining in the Hall of Consciousness is the true God.
commentary: The path to God is love. Through this loving relationship, Vallalar receives the ultimate boons: the promise of immortality and elevation to a "changeless state" of being. He is placed in the Sanmarkkam (the True Path), a universal spiritual brotherhood, because a loving God "came to be mine."

translit: tūṇṭāta maṇiviḷakkāyt tulaṅkukiṉṟa teyvam turiyateyvam ariyateyvam periyaperun teyvam māṇṭārai eḻuppukiṉṟa maruntāṉa teyvam māṇikka valliyaiōr valattilvaitta teyvam āṇṭārai āṇṭateyvam aruṭcōtit teyvam ākamavē tātielām aṟivaritān teyvam tīṇṭāta veḷiyilvaḷar tīṇṭāta teyvam ciṟcapaiyil viḷaṅkukiṉṟa teyvamatē teyvam.
translation: The God who shines as a jeweled lamp that needs no tending, the God of Turiya, the rare God, the great, great God, the God who is the medicine that raises the dead, the God who placed the ruby-like vine on his right, the God who rules the rulers, the God of Arut Jothi, the God who is difficult to comprehend through the Agamas, Vedas, and other texts, the God who grows in the untouched space, the untouchable God, the God shining in the Hall of Consciousness is the true God.
commentary: God is a self-luminous reality that exists beyond ordinary understanding. Described as a lamp that needs no fuel, this God belongs to the state of Turiya (pure consciousness beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep). This being, the Arut Jothi (Grace-Light), cannot be fully captured by scriptures. It is "untouchable," dwelling in a pristine inner space beyond human concepts.

translit: evvakaittān tavañceyiṉum eytaritān teyvam eṉakkeḷitiṟ kiṭaitteṉmaṉam iṭaṅkoṇṭa teyvam avvakaittān teyvamataṟ kappālān teyvam appālum peruveḷikkē appālān teyvam ovvakattē oḷiyāki ōṅkukiṉṟa teyvam oṉṟāṉa teyvammika naṉṟāṉa teyvam cevvakaitteṉ ṟaṟiñarelāñ cērperiya teyvam ciṟcapaiyil viḷaṅkukiṉṟa teyvamatē teyvam.
translation: The God who is difficult to attain no matter what penance one performs, the God who came to me with ease and took my mind as his dwelling, that very God, and the God beyond him, the God beyond even that, and beyond the great void, the God who rises as light within every single thing, the one God, the supremely good God, the great God whom all the wise join, declaring him the right way, the God shining in the Hall of Consciousness is the true God.
commentary: Here, Vallalar expresses a central paradox of grace. The ultimate God, impossible to attain through any amount of penance, came to him with ease and made his heart a home. This divinity is both the light within every single thing and the mystery that lies infinitely beyond creation, even "beyond the great void." It is the one, good reality that all wise people recognize as the true way.

translit: cattiyamān taṉitteyvam taṭaiyaṟiyāt teyvam cattikaḷālel lāmviḷaṅkat tāṉōṅkum teyvam nittiyataṉ mayamāki niṉṟateyvam ellā nilaikaḷuntaṉ aruḷveḷiyil nilaikkavaitta teyvam pattivalaip paṭukiṉṟa teyvameṉak kellāp paricumaḷit taḻiyāta patattilvaitta teyvam cittielān taruteyvam cittāntat teyvam ciṟcapaiyil viḷaṅkukiṉṟa teyvamatē teyvam.
translation: The true, unique God, the God who knows no obstacle, the God who soars, making everything manifest through his powers, the God who stands as eternal righteousness, the God who established all states of being within the space of his grace, the God who is caught in the net of devotion, the God who gave me all gifts and placed me in the indestructible state, the God who grants all siddhis, the God of Siddhanta, the God shining in the Hall of Consciousness is the true God.
commentary: God is both the absolute, unshakable foundation of all reality and a personal being who responds to simple love. He is the ultimate truth of Siddhanta (a major philosophical path) and the source of all siddhis (supernatural powers), yet he is also "caught in the net of devotion." For Vallalar, this cosmic God is the one who personally bestowed gifts and placed him in an indestructible state of being.
NOTES
Note 267

translit: ceccaimalar - veṭcimalar. mutaṟpatippu.
translation: ceccaimalar — veṭcimalar, reading of the first edition.

sections.title: The Supreme State of Great Bliss

translit: aṇivaḷar tirucciṟ ṟampalat tāṭum āṉanta pōkamē amutē maṇivaḷar oḷiyē oḷiyiṉuḷ oḷiyē maṉṉumeṉ āruyirt tuṇaiyē tuṇivuṟu cittān tapperum poruḷē tūyavē tāntattiṉ payaṉē paṇivuṟum uḷattē iṉittiṭa eṉakkē paḻuttapē rāṉantap paḻamē.
translation: O blissful experience who dances in the beautifully adorned Thiru Chitrambalam, O Nectar! O gem-like growing light, light within the light, my abiding, precious life-companion! O great substance of definitive Siddhanta, O fruit of pure Vedanta! O fruit of great bliss that has ripened just for me, sweetening the submissive heart!
commentary: God is experienced as an intimate, blissful presence, like a sweet fruit ripening within one's own heart. Vallalar addresses the divine as the dancer in Thiru Chitrambalam (the sacred hall of consciousness) and a constant companion. He calls this experience the true purpose of both Vedanta and Siddhanta, suggesting that these complex philosophical paths culminate in this simple, sweet, and personal realization.

translit: tiruvaḷar tirucciṟ ṟampalat tāṭum teyvamē meypporuṭ civamē uruvaḷar oḷiyē oḷiyiṉuḷ oḷiyē ōṅkumeṉ uyirpperun tuṇaiyē orutaṉit talaimai aruḷveḷi naṭuvē uvantara caḷikkiṉṟa aracē paruvaral nīkki iṉittiṭa eṉakkē paḻuttapē rāṉantap paḻamē.
translation: O God who dances in the grace-filled Thiru Chitrambalam, O Sivam who is the true substance! O light that grows in form, light within the light, my exalted, great life-companion! O King who joyfully holds singular, supreme rule in the midst of the space of grace! O fruit of great bliss that has ripened just for me, removing my distress and sweetening my being!
commentary: The supreme being who governs the entire cosmos is also an intimate companion who personally removes an individual's suffering. Vallalar calls this being Sivam (the auspicious one) and the king who rules from the center of the "space of grace." This cosmic ruler is the same sweet, ripened fruit of bliss tasted within, bringing an end to personal sorrow and distress.

translit: tutivaḷar tirucciṟ ṟampalat tāṭum cōtiyuṭ cōtiyē eṉatu mativaḷar maruntē mantira maṇiyē maṉṉiya peruṅkuṇa malaiyē katitaru turiyat taṉiveḷi naṭuvē kalantara cāḷkiṉṟa kaḷippē patiyuṟum uḷattē iṉittiṭa eṉakkē paḻuttapē rāṉantap paḻamē.
translation: O Jothi within Jothi who dances in the praise-filled Thiru Chitrambalam! My medicine that expands the mind, my mantra-gem, O mountain of abiding, great qualities! O bliss who mingles and reigns in the midst of the singular space of Turiya that grants liberation! O fruit of great bliss that has ripened just for me, sweetening the devoted heart!
commentary: The experience of God is a form of healing that expands the mind and a blissful light that guides one's awareness. Vallalar calls the divine a "medicine," a Jothi (divine light) within light, and the joy found in the state of Turiya (pure, liberated consciousness beyond waking and sleep). This divine presence, which reigns in the highest spiritual state, is the same sweet fruit of bliss that becomes real within a devoted heart.

translit: cīrvaḷar tirucciṟ ṟampalat tōṅkuñ celvamē eṉperuñ ciṟappē nīrvaḷar neruppē neruppiṉuḷ oḷiyē niṟaioḷi vaḻaṅkumōr veḷiyē ērtaru kalānta mātiā ṟantat tiruntara caḷikkiṉṟa patiyē pāruṟum uḷattē iṉittiṭa eṉakkē paḻuttapē rāṉantap paḻamē.
translation: O wealth exalted in the excellence-filled Thiru Chitrambalam, O my great glory! O fire that flourishes in water, O light within the fire, O a space that grants abundant light! O Lord who resides and rules within the six excellent philosophical systems, from Kalanta onward! O fruit of great bliss that has ripened just for me, sweetening the perceiving heart!
commentary: The divine is the unifying essence hidden within all of creation and all systems of thought. It is the light that shines even within fire and the core truth present in the six major schools of Indian philosophy, beginning with Kalanta. This universal presence is the source of all glory, a personal treasure that sweetens the perceptive mind.

translit: uraivaḷar tirucciṟ ṟampalat tōṅkum oḷḷiya teḷḷiya oḷiyē varaivaḷar maruntē mavuṉaman tiramē mantirat tāṟpeṟṟa maṇiyē niraitaru cutta nilaikkumēl nilaiyil niṟaintara cāḷkiṉṟa nitiyē paraiyuṟum uḷattē iṉittiṭa eṉakkē paḻuttapē rāṉantap paḻamē.
translation: O brilliant, clear light exalted in the scripture-filled Thiru Chitrambalam! O medicine that grows on the mountain, O mantra of silence, O gem obtained through mantra! O treasure who pervades and reigns in the state above the pure state! O fruit of great bliss that has ripened just for me, sweetening the heart that attains Parai!
commentary: True communion with God happens in silence, beyond scriptures and spoken mantras. While these tools can help, the path to the real "gem" is through a "mantra of silence." This way leads to a state above the ordinary pure state, a union with Parai (the supreme consciousness), which is experienced as a treasure that fills and sweetens the heart.

translit: mēlvaḷar tirucciṟ ṟampalat tōṅkum meyyaṟi vāṉanta viḷakkē kālvaḷar kaṉalē kaṉalvaḷar katirē katirnaṭu vaḷarkiṉṟa kalaiyē āluṟum upacān tappara veḷikkap pālara cāḷkiṉṟa aracē pāluṟum uḷattē iṉittiṭa eṉakkē paḻuttapē rāṉantap paḻamē.
translation: O lamp of true-knowledge-bliss that soars in the ever-ascending Thiru Chitrambalam! O fire that grows from the wind! O ray that grows from the fire! O subtle art that grows within the ray! O King who rules beyond the transcendent space of all-pervading supreme peace! O fruit of supreme bliss, ripened to be sweet for me in my loving heart!
commentary: The divine is the source from which all cosmic elements unfold in a cascade of creation: fire grows from wind, light from fire, and the subtle art of existence from light. God, the "lamp of true-knowledge-bliss," is the king who reigns even beyond this cosmic process, in a state of absolute peace. Yet this supreme king is also the personal bliss ripened for the loving soul.

translit: icaivaḷar tirucciṟ ṟampalat tōṅkum iṉpamē eṉṉuṭai aṉpē ticaivaḷar aṇṭa kōṭikaḷ aṉaittum tikaḻuṟat tikaḻkiṉṟa civamē micaiyuṟu mauṉa veḷikaṭan tataṉmēl veḷiara cāḷkiṉṟa patiyē pacaiyuṟum uḷattē iṉittiṭa eṉakkē paḻuttapē rāṉantap paḻamē.
translation: O Bliss that soars in the harmony-filled Thiru Chitrambalam! O my Love! O Sivam, who shines, making the countless crores of universes that expand in every direction also shine! O Lord, who rules the space beyond the supernal space of silence! O fruit of supreme bliss, ripened to be sweet for me in my devoted heart!
commentary: The divine is simultaneously the vast cosmic light and the most intimate personal love. It is Sivam, the being whose radiance illuminates countless universes (crores meaning tens of millions). Yet this same Lord, who rules a space beyond even the highest mystical silence, is experienced directly as "my Love," a blissful sweetness filling the devoted heart.

translit: aruḷvaḷar tirucciṟ ṟampalat tōṅkum arumperuñ cōtiyē eṉatu poruḷvaḷar aṟivuk kaṟivutan teṉṉaip puṟamviṭā tāṇṭameyp poruḷē maruvumōr nāta veḷikkumēl veḷiyil makiḻntara cāḷkiṉṟa vāḻvē paruvaral nīkki iṉittiṭa eṉakkē paḻuttapē rāṉantap paḻamē.
translation: O rare, great Jothi that soars in the grace-filled Thiru Chitrambalam! O true substance that gave knowledge to my own developing knowledge and ruled me, never letting me go! O Life that joyfully rules in the space beyond the space of primal sound! O fruit of supreme bliss, ripened to be sweet for me, removing all my anguish!
commentary: Here, God is the great Jothi, the divine light of grace that awakens our own capacity for knowledge. This is a guiding presence that holds the soul securely and actively removes suffering. The experience is one of complete safety and illumined understanding, culminating in a sweet bliss.

translit: vāṉvaḷar tirucciṟ ṟampalat tōṅkum māperuṅ karuṇaiem patiyē ūṉvaḷar uyirkaṭ kuyiratāy ellā ulakamum niṟaintapē roḷiyē māṉmutaṉ mūrtti māṉilaik kappāl vayaṅkumōr veḷinaṭu maṇiyē pāṉmaiyuṟ ṟuḷattē iṉittiṭa eṉakkē paḻuttapē rāṉantap paḻamē.
translation: O my Lord of immense compassion, who soars in the celestial Thiru Chitrambalam! O great effulgence that is the life within lives growing in flesh, filling all worlds! O gem at the center of a radiant space, beyond the great state of divine forms like Vishnu! O fruit of supreme bliss, ripened to be sweet for me in the heart that has attained its true nature!
commentary: The divine is the compassionate life-force animating every creature, "the life within lives growing in flesh." This verse makes a significant point: this ultimate reality is found beyond all specific divine forms, such as Vishnu, pointing to a direct experience of the formless source. That formless immensity, however, is a sweet "gem" found within the heart that has realized its own true nature.

translit: talamvaḷar tirucciṟ ṟampalat tōṅkum taṉittameyp poruṭperuñ civamē nalamvaḷar karuṇai nāṭṭamvait teṉaiyē naṇpukoṇ ṭaruḷiya naṇpē valamuṟu nilaikaḷ yāvaiyuṅ kaṭantu vayaṅkiya taṉinilai vāḻvē palamuṟum uḷattē iṉittiṭa eṉakkē paḻuttapē rāṉantap paḻamē.
translation: O supreme Sivam, the unique, true substance, soaring in the Thiru Chitrambalam that pervades all sacred planes! O Friend who graciously befriended me, casting Your ever-growing, benevolent gaze of grace upon me! O Life of the radiant, unique state that surpasses all powerful states! O fruit of supreme bliss, ripened to be sweet for me in my strengthening heart!
commentary: The supreme reality, Sivam, is a personal Friend who actively initiates a relationship with the soul. In this divine friendship, it is God's benevolent gaze that strengthens the heart and makes it capable of receiving the bliss that surpasses all other spiritual states. The relationship itself is the path to the highest experience.

sections.title: Marveling at the Wonder of His Gracious Rule

translit: ampalat tāṭum amutamē eṉkō aṭiyaṉēṉ āruyir eṉkō empalat tellām vallacit teṉkō eṉṉiru kaṇmaṇi eṉkō nampiṭil aṇaikkum naṟṟuṇai eṉkō nāṉpeṟṟa peruñcelvam eṉkō imparip piṟappē meyppiṟap pākki eṉṉaiāṇ ṭaruḷiya niṉaiyē.
translation: Shall I call You the nectar that dances in the Ambalam? Shall I call You the dear life of this devotee? Shall I call You the all-powerful perfection that is my strength? Shall I call You the apple of my two eyes? Shall I call You the good companion who embraces me when I trust You? Shall I call You the great treasure I have received? You, who made this very birth on earth my true birth and graciously took me into Your rule.
commentary: No single name can contain the nature of God, who is experienced in a multitude of ways. The devotee cycles through powerful metaphors: God is the blissful energy dancing in the Ambalam (the inner hall of consciousness), the very breath of life, and the most intimate companion. The final lines reveal the culmination of all these roles: by grace, this divine presence has transformed an ordinary life into a "true birth," a life of authentic purpose.

translit: ammaiyē eṉkō appaṉē eṉkō aruṭperuñ cōtiyē eṉkō cemmaiyē ellām vallacit teṉkō tirucciṟṟam palattamu teṉkō tammaiyē uṇarntār uḷattoḷi eṉkō tamiyaṉēṉ taṉittuṇai eṉkō immaiyē aḻiyāt tiruuru aḷittiṅ keṉṉaiāṇ ṭaruḷiya niṉaiyē.
translation: Shall I call You my Mother? Shall I call You my Father? Shall I call You the Vast Grace-Light? Shall I call You the perfect, all-powerful Siddhi? Shall I call You the nectar of the sacred Cirrambalam? Shall I call You the light in the hearts of those who have realized themselves? Shall I call You the sole companion for me in my loneliness? You, who gave me an undying, sacred form in this very life and graciously took me into Your rule.
commentary: The divine contains all relationships, being both Mother and Father, while also being the ultimate reality of ArutPerunJothi (the Vast Grace-Light). This light is the source of all supernatural perfection (siddhi) and the inner radiance found by those who have realized their true selves. For Vallalar, this great being is also a personal companion, the one who granted him an immortal body in this very life.

translit: eyppilē kiṭaitta vaippatu eṉkō eṉṉuyirk kiṉpamē eṉkō tuyppilē niṟainta peruṅkaḷip peṉkō cōtiyuṭ cōtiyē eṉkō tappelām poṟutta tayāniti eṉkō taṉipperun talaivaṉē eṉkō ippiṟap patilē meyppayaṉ aḷittiṅ keṉṉaiāṇ ṭaruḷiya niṉaiyē.
translation: Shall I call You the treasure I found when I was destitute? Shall I call You the bliss of my life? Shall I call You the great delight that fills my every experience? Shall I call You the Light within the light? Shall I call You the treasury of compassion who forgave all my wrongs? Shall I call You the peerless, great Master? You, who granted me the true fruit in this very birth and graciously took me into Your rule.
commentary: The experience of God is one of deep consolation and complete fulfillment. For a soul who felt destitute, grace is a discovered treasure; for a life that knew suffering, it is pure bliss. This divine "Light within the light" is also a treasury of compassion that has forgiven every mistake, making this birth the one in which life's true purpose is realized.

translit: accamnīk kiyaeṉ āriyaṉ eṉkō ampalat tempirāṉ eṉkō niccalum eṉakkē kiṭaittavāḻ veṉkō nīṭumeṉ nēyaṉē eṉkō piccaṉēṟ kaḷitta piccaṉē eṉkō periyariṟ periyaṉē eṉkō iccakat taḻiyāp perunalam aḻittiṅ keṉṉaiāṇ ṭaruḷiya niṉaiyē.
translation: Shall I call You my noble Guru who dispelled my fear? Shall I call You my Lord of the Ambalam? Shall I call You the life that is mine forever? Shall I call You my eternal beloved? Shall I call You the Madman who bestowed grace upon this madman? Shall I call You the Greatest of the great? You, who granted me undying, great well-being in this world and graciously took me into Your rule.
commentary: God is addressed as the noble teacher (guru) who removes all fear and as the eternal beloved. The most striking names here are "the Madman who bestowed grace upon this madman." This suggests a love and grace so boundless they defy worldly logic, a divine "madness" that gives itself completely to a devotee whose own intense love makes them appear mad to the world.

translit: attamnēr kiṭaitta cuvaikkaṉi eṉkō aṉpilē niṟaiamu teṉkō cittelām valla cittaṉē eṉkō tirucciṟṟam palaccivam eṉkō mattaṉēṉ peṟṟa periyavāḻ veṉkō maṉṉumeṉ vāḻmutal eṉkō ittaṉip piṟappai nittiyam ākki eṉṉaiāṇ ṭaruḷiya niṉaiyē.
translation: Shall I call You the sweet fruit that came directly into my hand? Shall I call You the full nectar of love? Shall I call You the Siddha who is master of all powers? Shall I call You the Siva of the sacred Cirrambalam? Shall I call You the great life that I, in my madness, received? Shall I call You the eternal source of my life? You, who made this unique birth an eternal one and graciously took me into Your rule.
commentary: Grace is a sweet fruit placed directly into one's hand. Here, the divine is the perfected one (Siddha) with all powers, the ultimate reality, Siva, experienced in the Cirrambalam (the intimate inner space of consciousness). This grace makes what was a singular, mortal life into an eternal one.

translit: maṟappelām tavirtta matiamu teṉkō mayakkanīt taruḷmarun teṉkō paṟappelām oḻitta patipatam eṉkō pataccuvai aṉupavam eṉkō ciṟappelām eṉakkē ceytatāy eṉkō tirucciṟṟam palattantai eṉkō iṟappilā vaṭivam immaiyē aḷittiṅ keṉṉaiāṇ ṭaruḷiya niṉaiyē.
translation: Shall I call You the nectar of wisdom that removes all forgetfulness? Shall I call You the medicine of grace that dispels delusion? Shall I call You the state of the Lord that has ended all worldly concerns? Shall I call You the experience of the flavor of that state? Shall I call You the mother who gave me every excellence? Shall I call You the father of the sacred golden hall? You who graciously ruled me here, granting me a deathless form in this very life.
commentary: God is the medicine that cures the soul's sicknesses of delusion and forgetfulness of its true nature. Here, the divine is both mother and father, the source of all good things. Vallalar points to a specific, extraordinary result of this grace: the attainment of a deathless physical body, right here in this life. Thiru Chitrambalam is another name for the sacred inner hall of consciousness.

translit: aṉpilē paḻutta taṉippaḻam eṉkō aṟivilē aṟivaṟi veṉkō iṉpilē niṟainta civapatam eṉkō eṉṉuyirt tuṇaippati eṉkō vaṉpilā maṉattē vayaṅkoḷi eṉkō maṉṉumam palattara ceṉkō eṉpuri aḻiyāp poṉpuri ākki eṉṉaiāṇ ṭaruḷiya niṉaiyē.
translation: Shall I call You the unique fruit ripened in love? Shall I call You the knowledge of knowledge within wisdom? Shall I call You the state of Siva filled with bliss? Shall I call You the lordly companion to my life? Shall I call You the brilliant light in a mind free of hardness? Shall I call You the King of the eternal sacred hall? You who graciously ruled me, transforming my perishable body of bone into an imperishable golden one.
commentary: The divine is found at the very core of experience: as the essence of love, the ultimate source of knowledge, and a brilliant light that shines in a softened, open mind. This inner realization has a tangible, physical result. Vallalar describes the transformation of his own body from perishable bone into an imperishable golden form, a literal physical immortality granted by grace.

translit: taṭaiyilā teṭutta aruḷamu teṉkō carkkaraik kaṭṭiyē eṉkō aṭaivuṟu vayirak kaṭṭiyē eṉkō ampalat tāṇippoṉ eṉkō uṭaiya māṇikkap perumalai eṉkō uḷḷoḷik kuḷḷoḷi eṉkō iṭaitalaṟ ṟōṅkum tiruaḷit tiṅkē eṉṉaiāṇ ṭaruḷiya niṉaiyē.
translation: Shall I call You the nectar of grace drawn without obstruction? Shall I call You a block of raw sugar? Shall I call You a solid block of diamond? Shall I call You the purest gold of the sacred hall? Shall I call You the great mountain of ruby that I possess? Shall I call You the light within the inner light? You who graciously ruled me here, granting me a prosperity that flourishes without interruption.
commentary: The divine is portrayed as the ultimate treasure, using metaphors of intense sweetness, value, and permanence: raw sugar, diamond, pure gold, and a mountain of ruby. This is a solid, inexhaustible treasure that one comes to possess. This treasure is the "light within the inner light," the deepest source of consciousness itself.

translit: maṟaimuṭi viḷaṅku perumporuḷ eṉkō maṉṉumā kamapporuḷ eṉkō kuṟaimuṭit taruḷcey teyvamē eṉkō kuṇapperuṅ kuṉṟamē eṉkō piṟaimuṭik kaṇinta peruntakai eṉkō periyaam palattara ceṉkō iṟaimuṭip poruḷeṉ uḷampeṟa aḷittiṅ keṉṉaiāṇ ṭaruḷiya niṉaiyē.
translation: Shall I call You the great substance that shines at the pinnacle of the Vedas? Shall I call You the substance of the eternal Agamas? Shall I call You the God who graciously fulfills all needs? Shall I call You the great mountain of virtue? Shall I call You the great magnate adorned with the crescent moon on his crown? Shall I call You the King of the great sacred hall? You who graciously ruled me here, granting my mind the ultimate substance of the Lord.
commentary: God is the single, ultimate truth that all scriptures point to, the "great substance" found at the peak of the Vedas (ancient Hindu hymns) and in the Agamas (texts on ritual and philosophy). This supreme reality is also deeply personal, a "mountain of virtue" who fulfills every need. By referencing the crescent moon, a traditional symbol of Lord Siva, Vallalar connects his direct experience to the God known through tradition, showing they are one.

translit: eṉuḷam piriyāp pēroḷi eṉkō eṉuyirt tantaiyē eṉkō eṉuyirt tāyē iṉpamē eṉkō eṉuyirt talaivaṉē eṉkō eṉuyir vaḷarkkum taṉiamu teṉkō eṉṉuṭai naṇpaṉē eṉkō eṉoruvāḻviṉ taṉimutal eṉkō eṉṉaiāṇ ṭaruḷiya niṉaiyē.
translation: Shall I call You the great light that never leaves my mind? Shall I call You the father of my life? Shall I call You the mother of my life, my very bliss? Shall I call You the lord of my life? Shall I call You the unique nectar that nurtures my life? Shall I call You my friend? Shall I call You the sole foundation of my one life? You who graciously ruled me.
commentary: The experience of God moves from the cosmic to the deeply personal. Here, the divine is the most intimate presence imaginable: a constant light in the mind, a father, a mother, a lord, and a friend. This shows that the ultimate reality is also the source of all love and relationship, the very foundation of life itself.
NOTES
Note 275

translit: eṉperu - pi. irā. patippu.
translation: eṉperu — reading of the P. Irā. edition.

glossary.def: The five divine functions: creation, preservation, dissolution, veiling and grace. Vallalar says these are done by deities under God, and that God granted them to him.
The Agamas, scriptures of temple worship and doctrine. Vallalar says their truth is known by grace, not by reading.
A Tamil verse form of long, flowing lines. The ArutPerunJothi Agaval, Vallalar's hymn of 1,596 lines, belongs to the Sixth Thirumurai and is published as a separate volume.
Ambalam: the hall or open stage where God dances. It is the hall at Chidambaram and, within, the space of consciousness where God is known.
Nectar, ambrosia. Vallalar's word for the sweetness of grace, tasted within, which brings deathless life.
Bliss, Ananda. The joy of union with God.
The root impurity of the ego, the "I-ness" that veils the soul. The first of the three impurities (malam).
Anma Neya Orumaipadu: the unity of all souls in love. Every living being shares the same essence, so every being is to be seen as one's own.
The universe, the macrocosm. Vallalar sees the same Light filling the countless universes (aṇṭam) and the human body (piṇṭam).
Traditionally a name for Brahmins. Vallalar gives it its root meaning: the gracious ones whose nature is coolness and compassion toward all life, whatever their birth.
Refuge. The cry "apayam, apayam" ("refuge, refuge") runs through the pathigam Apayam Iṭutal, the soul's plea to be held by God.
Virtue, righteous action. For Vallalar its heart is compassion: feeding the hungry and relieving the suffering of every living being.
A name for the Vedas.
The six "ends" (antam) or culminations of the philosophical traditions: Vedanta, Siddhanta, Bodhanta, Nadanta, Yoganta and Kalanta. Vallalar says God is beyond all six.
Grace. The living, compassionate power of God that frees the soul and transforms it. For Vallalar grace is received through compassion for all life.
ArutJothi, the Grace-Light: God as the Light of grace, seen and received within.

ArutPerunJothi, the Vast Grace-Light: Vallalar's name for God in the Sixth Thirumurai. The one infinite Light of grace from which everything comes and in which everything is held, open to every living being.
The deathless education: the knowledge, given by grace, of the life that does not end in death.
The waking state, the first of the states of consciousness. Vallalar speaks of a higher waking beyond the usual states.
Salai, the hall or house. Here the Sathya Dharma Salai, the free kitchen at Vadalur.
Samarasam: perfect harmony, equality of all. Part of the full name of Vallalar's path, Samarasa Suddha Sanmarkkam.
Religion as an organized creed. In the Sixth Thirumurai Vallalar declares the religions, creeds and sects false, and calls people beyond them to the true path.
The conch, blown to announce victory and arrival. Vallalar has it blown to proclaim the coming of God.
Sanmarkkam, the true path. Vallalar's name for the way of grace, compassion and direct knowledge of God, open to every living being.
Satguru, the true teacher. Vallalar's name for God, who taught him directly from within.
Caste. Vallalar declares caste false, a darkness to be thrown away, and calls all people one family.
Sathya Gnana Sabai, the Hall of True Wisdom that Vallalar consecrated at Vadalur in 1872, a hall of light open to all, built for no religion.
Sathya Dharma Salai, the free kitchen Vallalar opened at Vadalur in 1867 so that no one would go hungry. Its fire has not been put out since.
Crest-jewel, the jewel worn at the top of a crown. Used for God as the highest of all.
Chit Sabhai, the Hall of Consciousness, where God dances. Both the hall at Chidambaram and the inner space of awareness.
Chitrambalam, the "small" or subtle hall: the hall of the dance at Chidambaram and the hall of consciousness within. Thiru Chitrambalam is "the sacred Chitrambalam".
Siddhanta, the Saiva philosophical tradition. One of the six "ends" (āṟantam) that Vallalar says God transcends.
Siddhar, a perfected one. Vallalar calls God the Siddhar who can do all things.
Siddhi, attainment or perfect power. Vallalar speaks above all of the Siddhi that can do all things, given by grace.
Sivakami, the Divine Mother, consort of the Lord who dances at Chidambaram.
Sivam, the Auspicious: the supreme Reality. In the Sixth Thirumurai Vallalar says that Sivam alone is the true substance.
Bliss, lasting well-being.
The bliss of simply being: the stillness beyond all effort and thought that Vallalar longs for in the second verse of the Sixth Thirumurai.
Suddha Sanmarkkam, the pure true path that Vallalar names and teaches in the Sixth Thirumurai: compassion for all life, the end of caste and creed, and union with ArutPerunJothi.
The seven levels. In the pathigam on the Hall of Pure Gold, the seven stages of the inner vision, each marked by a change of jewel and color.
Jeeva Karunyam, compassion for all living beings. For Vallalar the foundation of all spiritual life and the key to God's grace.
Jothi, Light. Vallalar's central name for God.
Husband. In the bridal songs the soul is the bride and God the husband, the closest union a human life knows.
Karma: the accumulated effect of one's actions. One of the three impurities (malam).
The evil eye: harm believed to come from an envious look.
The inner faculties: mind, intellect, will and ego. Vallalar asks that they be purified and ruled by grace.
Compassion, mercy. God's compassion toward all, and the compassion the soul must have for every living being.
Kollāmai, non-killing. For Vallalar the condition of the true path: those who kill and eat flesh stand outside it until they give up killing.
Death, personified as Yama, the god of death.
Mahamayai, the great māyai: the subtle, primal form of illusion.
Malam, impurity. The three impurities, ego (āṇavam), karma (kaṉmam) and illusion (māyai), veil the soul until grace removes them.
Manimanram, the Hall of Gems, where God dances.
Creed or doctrine; also pride or madness. Vallalar uses the double meaning: attachment to creed is a kind of madness.
Māyai, illusion: the power that makes the passing world seem the whole of reality. One of the three impurities.
Mettukuppam, the village near Vadalur where Vallalar lived his last years and where, on 30 January 1874, he entered his room and was not seen again.
Silence, the stillness beyond all words.
Mutti, liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
A unit of time of twenty-four minutes.
Gnana Sabai, the Hall of Wisdom: the hall of God's dance, and Vallalar's hall at Vadalur.
Gnanam, wisdom: direct knowledge of God, given by grace and not by study.
The medicine of wisdom: God as the remedy for every ill, above all for birth and death.
Dance. God's dance in the hall is the movement of grace that sustains all things.
Nadam, the primordial sound from which manifestation arises.
Nadanta, "the end of sound": the state beyond primordial sound. One of the six "ends" (āṟantam).
Nataraja, the King of Dance: God as the Dancer in the hall at Chidambaram and in the hall of consciousness.
The central channel, the subtle path at the center of the body in which, Vallalar says, God dances.
Justice. Vallalar speaks of the compassionate justice that rules in God's hall.
The sacred sound Om.
Parai, the supreme Power of God, worshipped as the Divine Mother.
Pati, Lord. God as the sovereign of all souls, as in Sivapati, "the Lord who is Siva".
Pathigam, a hymn, usually of ten verses. The Sixth Thirumurai is arranged in pathigams.
The body, the microcosm, set against aṇṭam, the universe.
Enjoyment. In the Sixth Thirumurai, the bliss of union with God.
The Golden Hall (Pon Sabhai) at Chidambaram, where God dances.
The common space, open to all. God dances in the common space so that all may see.
The heroine of the love songs. In Vallalar's bridal songs she is the soul, and her beloved is God.
Tandavam, the cosmic dance of God.
Tattva, a principle of existence. The tattvas are the levels from the elements to the subtlest powers. God is in them all and beyond them.
Tapas, spiritual discipline or penance.
Thillai, the old name of Chidambaram, the town of the Golden Hall where God dances.
Thirumurai, "sacred book". The Thiru Arutpa is arranged in six Thirumurai; this is the sixth and last.
Thiru Arutpa, "the Divine Songs of Grace": the collected poetry of Vallalar.
The sacred feet of God, the place of refuge and of grace.
The heroine's friend and confidant in the love songs, to whom the soul tells her experience of God.
The evil path, the way of cruelty and falsehood, as opposed to Sanmarkkam.
Turiyam, the "fourth" state of consciousness beyond waking, dreaming and deep sleep.
Turiyatitam, the state beyond the fourth.
The refrain of a traditional Tamil girls' game-song, also used by Manikkavasagar. Vallalar uses it to sing God's deeds as joyful play.
Latent tendencies left in the mind by past experience, which bind the soul until grace frees it.
"Come!" The refrain of the pathigam Ampalavāṇar Varukai, calling God to come.
Vadalur, the town in Tamil Nadu where Vallalar founded the Sathya Dharma Salai and the Sathya Gnana Sabai.
Space, the expanse. Vallalar speaks of many spaces, up to the Space of Siva (Siva veḷi).
Vedanta, the philosophy of the Upanishads. One of the six "ends" (āṟantam) that Vallalar says God transcends.
Open space, the boundless expanse of pure consciousness in which all things are seen to resolve.
Karma: the effect of past actions that binds the soul to birth.
